steps: Pick one service worth designing — something taking at least 1,000 requests a second over a table that grows daily.
Write the capacity estimate first: request rate, read/write split, row growth per day, storage at one year, three named failure modes.
Build the service to that design and nothing more. Every component you add must trace back to a line in the estimate.
Load-test the built version against the estimate. Doing this rather than trusting the estimate is the part everybody skips.
Push past the estimate until it breaks, and record which of your named failure modes actually arrived first.
Measure: estimated versus actual throughput, p99 at the estimated load, and which capacity number was furthest out.
Write the checklist first — error paths, boundary values, rollback, partial failure. Twelve items maximum, on one page.
Review every change to one real repository against it for at least three weeks, your own changes included.
Log every defect twice over: caught in review, or escaped to CI. Logging the escapes is the part everybody skips.
Get a second contributor reviewing under the same checklist, so you can tell a checklist gap from a reviewer gap.
Plant a defect of a kind the checklist covers in one pull request and see whether the review actually catches it.
Measure: defects caught versus escaped per checklist item, review turnaround, and which items never caught anything.
Take one module with real branching — a parser, a pricing rule, a state machine — and write the suite to full line coverage.
Run a mutation tester over it and record the first score before changing anything.
Read the surviving mutants one at a time. Every survivor is a test that passes against broken code, which means it asserts nothing.
Rewrite the tests those mutants survived rather than adding new ones. The rewrite is the project; coverage was never the point.
Wire the mutation run into CI with a threshold, then break a line of production code on purpose and confirm the build fails.
Measure: line coverage and mutation score before and after, and the surviving mutants you could not kill.
Pick the module everyone is afraid of — 500 lines or more, no tests, still in use.
Write characterisation tests recording what it does today, right or wrong, until you can change nothing and stay green.
Prove the pin holds: introduce a deliberate behaviour change and confirm the tests go red before you trust them.
Refactor in steps small enough that each is one commit, revertible alone, with the suite green between every step.
When a characterisation test disagrees with what the code was meant to do, fix the behaviour in a separate labelled commit.
Measure: lines and cyclomatic complexity before and after, steps in the chain, and behaviour changes found while pinning.
Take a feature request from a real requester — a colleague, a club, a user — not one you invented for yourself.
Write the acceptance criteria as numbered, testable statements and get them agreed in writing before the first commit.
Build it behind a flag from the start, so an unfinished path can reach main without reaching anyone.
Demonstrate each criterion back to the requester one at a time. Doing this before the flag comes out is what everybody skips.
Turn the flag off mid-session with someone using the feature, and confirm nothing breaks and nothing is left half-written.
Measure: criteria agreed versus changed after demo, days from request to flag-on, and defects found after release.
Take a real request written in prose — a ticket, an email, a stakeholder paragraph — with at least ten things going on in it.
Split it into numbered requirements, each a single testable statement, marking every place the prose could mean two things.
Send the ambiguous ones back and get answers in writing. Chasing the answer instead of guessing is the part everybody skips.
Build a traceability table: requirement number, where it is implemented, which test proves it.
Find the requirement with no test and the code with no requirement. One is a gap, the other is scope you added yourself.
Measure: requirements raised, ambiguities sent back, answers that changed the design, and code tracing to no requirement.
Take a real reported defect from a repository with history — your own or an open-source issue you can reproduce.
Reproduce it in a failing test before reading the code. If you cannot fail a test, you do not yet understand the bug.
Bisect to the commit that introduced it. Running the test under git bisect makes this mechanical rather than a hunt.
Grep every caller of the function you are about to change. Fixing only the path the report named is the mistake everybody makes.
Fix the shared function, then write a failing test for a sibling caller nobody reported, and confirm it was broken too.
Measure: callers found, tests added, commits between introduction and report, and the diff size of the fix.
Take an application with a database and at least one third-party call. Stand the database up in a container, not in memory.
Stub the third party at the HTTP boundary with recorded responses, so you test your parsing rather than their uptime.
Reset data between every test by truncating or rolling back. Leftover rows are why suites go flaky.
Run the suite fifty times in CI. Anything that fails once is flaky and must be fixed, not retried. This is the step everybody skips.
Kill the database container mid-suite and confirm the failure reads as an infrastructure error, not a silent pass.
Measure: suite runtime, flaky failures per hundred runs, and the paths integration covers that unit tests did not.
Run three nodes of a replicated store — etcd, a Raft library, or Postgres with streaming replicas — with real network between them.
Write down the consistency you are promising before you test it: what a read may return, and what a write may be refused.
Configure leader election and confirm a new leader is chosen when you kill the current one.
Partition the network on purpose with iptables or toxiproxy. Partitioning it deliberately is the whole project.
During the partition, record which reads went stale, which writes were refused, and what happened when it healed.
Measure: election time, stale reads served, writes refused, and time to converge after healing.
Find a real consumer first — another team, a friend's project, a front end written by someone else — and start from the calls they need.
Write the schema before the handlers, with cursor pagination, idempotency keys and an error taxonomy clients can branch on.
Generate the client from the schema and have the consumer integrate against it before you freeze anything.
Take their complaints seriously and change the API. Changing it because a consumer asked is the part everybody skips.
Rename a field on the server and confirm the generated client fails at build time, not at runtime for a user.
Measure: endpoints changed after consumer feedback, round trips for their main screen, and error codes clients actually branch on.
Take a domain with real rules — orders and stock, bookings and rooms — and write the invariants down as sentences first.
Express each one in the database: foreign keys, unique constraints, check constraints, exclusion constraints for overlapping ranges.
For every invariant, write the illegal write and fire it. A constraint you never tried to violate is not proven.
Seed to a realistic volume, at least a million rows, and read the query plan for each screen before adding any index.
Bypass the application entirely and try the illegal writes straight through psql. If any succeed, the rule was in the wrong place.
Measure: invariants held by constraints versus by code, rejected writes per constraint, and write cost added by each index.
Find the slowest real read path in something you built, with traffic you can replay — a log of at least 100,000 requests.
Choose an invalidation rule on purpose and write it down: TTL, write-through, or event-driven. Say what it costs you.
Add single-flight protection so a cold key cannot start a stampede when five hundred requests miss at once.
Measure worst-case staleness by timestamping writes and reads. Measuring it instead of estimating it is the whole project.
Expire every key at once under replayed traffic and record what the origin did.
Measure: hit rate, p99 at hit and at miss separately, worst-case staleness in seconds, and origin load removed.
Build an API over a real domain with at least eight routes, including one that creates and one that lists with filters.
Validate request bodies against a schema, return correct status codes, and give every error one consistent shape.
Generate the OpenAPI document from the code, never by hand. Handwritten documentation drifts within a fortnight.
Add a CI job that regenerates the schema and fails the build if the committed one differs. That gate is the whole project.
Rename a field without updating the schema and confirm the build goes red instead of shipping.
Measure: routes documented versus routes existing, schema-drift failures caught in CI, and validation rejections by error code.
Take a codebase with fat handlers — 200-line controllers where rules, queries and HTTP concerns are tangled together.
List the business rules as sentences before moving any code, so you know what you are meant to end up with.
Move them into a service layer with plain signatures taking domain types, not request objects.
Write tests for that layer that boot no web server at all. If a test needs an HTTP client, the extraction is not finished.
Delete the web framework from the test file's imports and watch what fails to compile. That is the tangle you missed.
Measure: handler line counts before and after, tests that run without a server, and runtime of the rules-only suite.
Map a schema with at least three levels of relation and seed it to 100,000 rows, so a bad query is visibly bad.
Turn the query log on and hit each screen once. Count queries per request before changing anything.
Add eager loading exactly where the log showed N+1 access, then re-count. Reading the log rather than guessing is the whole project.
Find the report the ORM generates badly, write it in raw SQL, and record the plan for both versions.
Assert a query budget in tests, then add a lazy relation on purpose and watch the test fail.
Measure: queries per request before and after per screen, p95 per endpoint, and plan cost of the raw-SQL report.
Build sign-up, sign-in and sign-out over a real user table, with passwords hashed by argon2 or bcrypt at a sane cost factor.
Issue a short-lived access token and a refresh token, and rotate the refresh token on every use.
Detect reuse: a refresh token presented twice means it was stolen, so revoke the whole session family.
Replay a stolen refresh token in a test and confirm the entire session dies. Proving this is the whole project.
Add rate limiting and constant-time comparison on the login path, then time a hundred logins with wrong and right usernames.
Measure: hash cost in milliseconds, token lifetimes, sessions killed by a replayed token, and login attempts allowed per minute.
Take a list of at least 10,000 real rows and render it the naive way first, on a CPU throttled to mid-range.
Record a flame chart while scrolling and find the work that does not fit inside the 16ms frame.
Virtualise the list and memoise the subtrees the profile says are re-rendering. Profiling first is the part everybody skips.
Re-record the identical scroll at the identical throttle. Comparing like with like is the only way the number means anything.
Add a deliberately expensive component mid-list and watch the frame budget break, so you know the measurement is live.
Measure: dropped frames per scroll, long tasks over 50ms, and interaction-to-next-paint before and after.
Take a screen with both kinds of state — server data and local UI state — such as a filtered list with a form open over it.
Put server data in a query cache with keys and invalidation; keep selection, drafts and open panels local. Never mix them.
Add an optimistic update to one mutation, keeping the previous value so a rollback restores exactly what was there.
Force the request to fail mid-flight — throttle it, then return a 500 — and watch the rollback. This is the whole project.
Fail it while a second mutation on the same record is in flight, and decide what the screen shows.
Measure: states the screen can be in, rollback time, and stale reads served after an invalidation.
Pick six primitives real screens need — button, field, select, dialog, table, toast — not a theoretical set.
Give each typed props and both controlled and uncontrolled variants, and say in the docs which one to reach for.
Document them in a workbench with a story per state, including loading, empty and error.
Get someone who did not write them to build a screen from them. The second consumer is who tells you which prop was wrong.
Add visual regression snapshots, then change one token on purpose so you see the diff fail rather than trusting it.
Measure: components adopted by screens the author did not write, props changed after the first outside consumer, and snapshot diffs caught.
Take an app shipping over 500KB of JavaScript and record the baseline with a bundle analyser, per route.
Split by route so a user landing on one page does not download the other nine.
Defer third-party scripts, then find the heaviest dependency — usually date, chart or icons — and replace or trim it.
Put a size budget in CI so a regression fails the pull request. Without the gate the win is gone within a month.
Add a heavy import on purpose and confirm the pull request goes red before it reaches a user.
Measure: transferred bytes per route before and after, largest contentful paint on a throttled connection, and the budget you set.
Take a real design with at least four breakpoints and build it from one fluid grid, not per-device override blocks.
Use the platform's own layout primitives — grid, flex, clamp, container queries — before reaching for a library.
Check it at every supported breakpoint, and at the sizes between them where nothing was designed.
Test on a real low-end handset, not the device emulator. The emulator lies about fonts, scrollbars and viewport height.
Zoom the browser to 200% and raise the system font two sizes, then find what overflows or overlaps.
Measure: breakpoints checked, cumulative layout shift on load, and defects found on hardware that the emulator did not show.
Take a real page built from nested divs — a dashboard or a form — and run an accessibility audit for the baseline count.
Rebuild it on landmarks, a correct heading order and native controls: a button element, not a div with a click handler.
Walk the whole page by keyboard. Everything reachable, focus visible, nothing trapped, order matching the visual order.
Then walk it with an actual screen reader. Doing that rather than trusting the audit tool is the whole project.
Unplug the mouse and complete the page's main task end to end. If you cannot, it is not finished.
Measure: automated violations before and after, tab stops to reach the main action, and what the reader announces per control.
Take a stylesheet over 2,000 lines with at least ten !important declarations, and record its size and selector count.
Pull colours, spacing and the type scale out as tokens, then replace the literals that matched them.
Write down one layering rule — cascade layers or a strict order — and put every rule into a layer.
Remove each !important by fixing the specificity that made it necessary. Fixing the cause rather than adding another one is the project.
Delete the selectors coverage tooling calls dead, then click through every screen to find the one it got wrong.
Measure: stylesheet bytes, selector count, !important declarations, and dead rules removed, before and after.
Build a multi-step form writing to a real backend — at least twelve fields with cross-field rules, not a contact form.
Define the rules once in a shared schema and run that same schema on the client and on the server.
Tie each error to its field with aria-describedby and move focus to the first one, so assistive technology announces it.
Preserve everything typed when a submission is rejected. Making a user retype after a server error is the failure everybody ships.
Reject a valid-looking submission from the server — a duplicate email — and confirm nothing is lost and nothing submits twice.
Measure: rules shared versus duplicated, fields retained after a rejected submit, and duplicate submissions under a double click.
Pick one feature needing a schema change, an API and a screen, and agree the metric it should move before you start.
Write the migration first and run it forward and backward against a copy of real data.
Build the API, then the screen, and note every place your own API design made the front end awkward.
Go back and change the API rather than working around it in the client. That correction is the point of owning both ends.
Ship behind a flag, turn it on for a slice, then turn it off mid-session to confirm both states are safe.
Measure: the agreed metric before and after, API round trips per screen, and rollback time from flag-on to flag-off.
Define one schema as the single source for a real API with at least ten endpoints — OpenAPI, protobuf or a shared validator module.
Generate server validation and client types from it. Nothing hand-written on either side.
Wire generation into the build so a stale generated file fails CI rather than sitting there quietly.
Rename a field on the server and confirm the front-end build breaks. If it only breaks at runtime, the contract is decorative.
Work out what an already-deployed old client does against the new server, and evolve additively rather than break it.
Measure: types generated versus hand-written, build failures caught by the contract, and endpoints needing a version bump.
List the queries the screens actually issue before drawing a single table. The read patterns come first.
Model to those queries, then seed to a realistic volume — a million rows, not a handful.
Read the query plan for every screen query on the seeded data and write down what it says.
Add an index only where the plan justifies it, and record the write cost. Deciding against one is as much of the project as adding one.
Drop an index you thought was essential and re-read the plan, so you know which ones are actually load-bearing.
Measure: rows seeded, plan and timing per screen query, and write throughput before and after each index.
Server-render a real app with signed-in and signed-out pages, over data that takes at least 200ms to fetch.
Stream the slow region so the shell reaches the browser first, and check the page still works with JavaScript disabled.
Mark every part of every page as publicly cacheable or per-user, explicitly. An unmarked default is how leaks happen.
Set the cache headers and CDN rules from that split, and keep per-user responses out of any shared cache.
Request a page as one signed-in user, then as another, and confirm the second never sees the first's data. This is the whole project.
Measure: time to first byte, first contentful paint, cache hit rate on public routes, and cross-user leaks found.
Build and deploy an application people other than you use — a club roster, a booking tool — with real data in it.
Set up a nightly backup of the database and uploaded files, stored somewhere that is not the application server.
Write the restore as numbered steps someone else could follow at three in the morning, not as a paragraph you remember.
Restore onto an empty machine and run the application from it. Rehearsing the restore is the project; a backup alone is a guess.
Note everything missing on the first attempt — secrets, uploads, cron entries — fix the procedure, and do it again.
Measure: restore time end to end, data lost between last backup and restore point, and items missing on the first attempt.
Build create, edit and delete over a record real people share — a shift rota, a price list — with at least two accounts.
Make delete a soft delete with a restore path, and keep an edit history naming who changed which field and when.
Add a version column and check it on save, so a stale form is refused rather than silently overwriting.
Open the same record in two browsers, save the second, then save the first. Doing it by hand is how you find out what the message says.
Design what the loser sees: what changed, by whom, and how to merge. Losing without an explanation is the failure everybody ships.
Measure: conflicts detected versus overwrites, fields tracked in the history, and restore time from a soft delete.
Build a real application on Rails, Django or Laravel using its own conventions — migrations, form objects, background jobs, its test harness.
Resist replacing framework pieces with your own. If you fight a convention, write down why, in a comment.
Get the suite covering the paths you would be afraid to break, and get CI running it on every push.
Upgrade the framework a full major version. This is the project — conventions only pay off at the upgrade.
Run the suite against the upgraded framework and fix each failure at the source, never with a compatibility shim.
Measure: suite runtime and pass rate before and after the upgrade, deprecations fixed, and files the upgrade changed.
Take one Linux box — a cheap VPS is fine — and deploy your application onto it by hand, with no platform-as-a-service.
Configure a reverse proxy, TLS with automated renewal, a process manager that restarts on crash, and log rotation.
Run the app as an unprivileged user, close every port you are not using, and record why each open one is open.
Reboot the machine in the middle of a request and confirm it comes back with no hand-holding. This is the whole project.
Simulate a failed certificate renewal and a full disk, and check you would find out before a user did.
Measure: time from reboot to serving, certificate expiry alert lead time, disk headroom, and restarts after a forced crash.
Build an Android app doing one real thing well, over data that comes from somewhere other than a hard-coded list.
Wire crash reporting and produce a signed release build with R8 on and the mapping file uploaded, so traces are readable.
Ship it to an internal testing track and get people who are not you to install it.
Run it on an actual low-end handset with 2GB of RAM. Testing only on the emulator is the mistake everybody makes.
Turn the network off mid-action, rotate, then background the app for an hour and come back to it.
Measure: cold start on the low-end device, APK size, crash-free sessions, and defects found on hardware but not the emulator.
Take a screen doing at least three concurrent asynchronous things — a fetch, a database read and a timer.
Scope every coroutine to the lifecycle that started it, and collect flows so collection stops when the screen is not visible.
Make cancellation structured: leaving the screen cancels the in-flight request, and the cancellation is not swallowed as an error.
Rotate and back out of the screen fifty times with a leak detector running. Repeating it is what makes the leak show.
Launch one coroutine on a global scope on purpose, repeat the loop, and watch the detector catch it, so you trust the tool.
Measure: leaks reported before and after, requests still in flight after leaving the screen, and memory after fifty navigation cycles.
Take a screen with real unsaved state — a part-filled form, a scroll position, a selection — over a list of at least 200 items.
Put small transient state in saved state and anything larger in a repository, and be able to say why each went where.
Rotate the device and confirm nothing is lost. That is the easy half.
Turn on Do not keep activities and background the app to kill the process. Process death is what everybody skips, and it is the project.
Relaunch from recents, from every screen, and check the app resumes where the user was rather than at the home screen.
Measure: state items restored after rotation versus after process death, restore time, and screens failing the cold relaunch.
Schedule a real background sync with WorkManager — upload queued records, pull updates — over data that actually changes.
Set the constraints honestly: network type, charging, battery not low, and say what each one costs the user.
Use unique work with an explicit policy so the same job cannot be queued twice by two triggers.
Add exponential backoff with a ceiling, and make the worker idempotent so a retry after a partial run duplicates nothing.
Force the device into doze with adb, run the window, reboot mid-queue, and confirm the job neither vanishes nor runs twice.
Measure: jobs queued versus executed, duplicate executions after reboot, latency from trigger to run, and battery use over a day.
Build an iOS app around one real task, over data from a service rather than a fixture file.
Make every build reproducible from a tagged commit, with versioning and signing driven by CI rather than by clicking in Xcode.
Push it to TestFlight and get at least five testers from outside the project onto it.
Symbolicate the crash reports that come back. An unsymbolicated log tells you nothing, and this is where most people stop.
Watch a tester use it without helping, and write down every place they hesitated or did the wrong thing.
Measure: testers installed, crash-free sessions, cold launch time, and defects found by testers that you never hit.
Take code with real shared mutable state — a cache, a download queue — and turn strict concurrency checking up to complete.
Read every warning rather than silencing it. The warnings are the project; unchecked Sendable is how people skip it.
Move shared mutable state behind actors, and confine anything touching the view layer to the main actor.
Replace completion handlers with async/await, keeping cancellation propagating through the whole chain.
Reintroduce one unsynchronised shared variable and confirm the compiler refuses it, so you know the checking is really on.
Measure: concurrency warnings before and after, unchecked conformances remaining, and thread sanitiser reports under a stress loop.
Take an app with at least five screens deep in a navigation stack, holding a selection and a scroll position.
Implement state restoration so a cold launch after termination lands on the screen the user left.
Pair every observer, timer and notification registration with its removal, and say at which lifecycle point each happens.
Terminate the app from the background rather than swiping it away. That is the case restoration exists for, and the one everybody tests wrong.
Cold-relaunch from every screen, and separately leave a screen with a timer running and confirm it stops.
Measure: screens restoring correctly out of screens tested, restore time, and observers still registered after a screen is dismissed.
Take an app with closures, delegates and navigation, and record a baseline in the Allocations instrument.
Navigate one loop — push a screen, use it, pop it — twenty times, and watch whether the allocation graph returns to its floor.
Use the Leaks instrument and the memory graph debugger to find which objects are still alive and what is holding them.
Break the cycles with weak or unowned captures, and be able to say which one you chose and why.
Repeat the identical navigation loop and confirm the graph flattens. Repeating the same loop is the only comparison that counts.
Measure: resident memory after twenty loops before and after, leaked objects per loop, and retain cycles found by class.
Build a real app in one codebase — React Native, Flutter or Kotlin Multiplatform — with at least six screens and a network layer.
Isolate platform-specific code behind a single module with one interface, so the rest of the app never branches on platform.
Get one CI job producing both builds from the same commit. Two hand-run build processes drift within a month.
Write down what you had to write twice anyway — permissions, deep links, notifications — and why it could not be shared.
Run both builds on real devices, oldest supported OS included, and find what the shared layer got wrong on one platform.
Measure: shared code percentage, both build times in CI, app size per platform, and defects appearing on one platform only.
Build eight shared components a real app needs — nav bar, list row, sheet, picker, tab bar — not a theoretical kit.
Honour each platform's conventions: hardware and gesture back on Android, swipe-back and safe areas on iOS.
Scale everything with the system font size up to the largest accessibility setting, and check nothing clips or overlaps.
Walk every component with TalkBack and with VoiceOver. Testing on both readers is the part everybody skips.
Force one component to look identical on both platforms on purpose, use it, and write down what that broke.
Measure: components passing both screen readers, largest font size that still fits, and touch targets under 44pt or 48dp.
Take an app that is actually finished and prepare a real submission to both stores, not a draft.
Fill in the privacy disclosures from what the app genuinely collects — audit your own network calls to find out.
Produce signed builds from CI with release notes, screenshots and age rating as part of the release, not afterwards.
Submit, and record every reviewer query or rejection verbatim. The rejection is where the learning is, and nobody plans for it.
Release with a staged rollout at a small percentage and hold there until crash-free sessions hold steady.
Measure: review turnaround per store, rejections and their reasons, crash-free sessions per rollout stage, and adoption per day.
Make the local database the source of truth: the UI reads from it and never waits on the network.
Write every change into a durable outbox in the same transaction as the local write, so a kill mid-queue loses nothing.
Write the conflict rule down before implementing it — last-write-wins, per-field merge, or server authority — and say who loses what.
Kill the app mid-sync with the process killer and confirm the queue resumes without duplicating or dropping anything.
Edit the same record on two offline devices, reconnect them in each order, and check the rule holds both ways round.
Measure: queued operations surviving a kill, duplicates after resume, sync time per hundred operations, and conflicts resolved per rule.
Find a real spreadsheet-and-email process someone runs weekly — invoices, stock, rotas — and watch a full cycle of it first.
Build the smallest system covering that cycle, with the same fields and the same outputs the spreadsheet produced.
Run both in parallel for a whole cycle. Everyone wants to skip this, and it is the only thing that earns the switch-off.
Reconcile the two outputs line by line and record every disagreement, including the ones where the spreadsheet was right.
Fix the disagreements, run a second parallel cycle, and only then retire the spreadsheet.
Measure: rows reconciled, disagreements per cycle and their cause, and time the process takes before and after.
Sit with the people who actually run the process, at least three of them, and watch rather than interview.
Draw the as-is map from what you saw, then walk it back through them and let them correct it.
Chase the exceptions — the except-when, the manual override, the one customer handled differently. These never come up unprompted and they are the project.
Write the to-be process, name what happens to each exception, and get it signed off before any code exists.
Take one exception you decided to leave out and confirm with the person who handles it what breaks if you do.
Measure: exceptions found per interview round, steps in the as-is versus the to-be, and requirements changed after sign-off.
Integrate two systems where you control only one — a real third-party API, or a stub you agree to treat as unreliable.
Put a queue between them so your system never blocks on theirs, with retries and bounded backoff.
Add a dead-letter path and a replay tool for it. Poison messages are what actually take integrations down.
Build the reconciliation report that compares both sides record by record, and state exactly what it compares.
Take the other system offline halfway through a batch, bring it back, and prove from the report that nothing was lost or applied twice.
Measure: records reconciled, dead-lettered messages and their causes, replay time, and duplicates after the outage.
Take a real approval — expenses, leave, purchase orders — with at least three roles and two decision points.
Model it as explicit states and transitions, and reject any event arriving in a state that does not expect it.
Write an audit entry for every transition: who, when, from which state to which, and on what grounds.
Add timed escalation for the approver who does nothing. Doing nothing is the commonest outcome and nobody models it.
Build a documented manual override, log it louder than everything else, and run a real case through it.
Measure: transitions per case, cases escalated by timeout, overrides used and by whom, and time from request to decision.
Run at least four tasks on FreeRTOS or Zephyr on real hardware, with a hard deadline on one of them.
Measure each task's worst-case execution time with a pin toggle and a scope, and assign priorities from the measurement, not intuition.
Turn on priority inheritance for every shared mutex, and be able to say which inversion it prevents.
Soak it for hours and read the stack high-water marks afterwards. Checking the marks after a soak is the part everybody skips.
Raise the load until a deadline is missed, and record which task went first and why that one.
Measure: worst-case execution time per task, stack headroom after soak, CPU idle percentage, and the load at which the first deadline slipped.
Take a peripheral firing at least 1kHz — a timer, a UART, an encoder — and write its interrupt path.
Keep the handler short: read the hardware, push into a lock-free ring buffer, signal a task, return.
Toggle a GPIO at handler entry and exit and put a scope on it. Measuring rather than reasoning is the whole project.
Find every place interrupts are disabled and add up the worst case, including whatever the vendor library does behind your back.
Flood the peripheral faster than the task drains the buffer, and record what overruns and whether you notice.
Measure: interrupt latency and jitter on the scope, the longest interrupts-disabled window, and samples dropped under flood.
Write a driver for a real peripheral from its datasheet — an I2C sensor or SPI display — with no vendor example open.
Put a documented abstraction between the register writes and the application, so the application never touches a register.
Handle the device that does not acknowledge: a bounded timeout, a defined error, and a bus recovery attempt.
Bench test it by physically pulling the sensor off the bus mid-read. Doing it physically is the project; a mocked failure proves nothing.
Short the bus lines and brown out the supply, and check the driver reports rather than hangs.
Measure: timeout before giving up, recovery attempts, errors reported per fault type, and bus utilisation at your transfer rate.
Take a custom or unfamiliar board and write the bring-up order before applying power: rails, clocks, reset, debug, then peripherals.
Power it through a current-limited supply and measure every rail against the schematic before anything else.
Get the clock configured and verified on a scope, then a debugger attached, then a pin toggling. Nothing else until a pin toggles.
Bring up one peripheral at a time and log each result as you go, pass or fail, with what you measured.
When something does not work, prove whether it is hardware or firmware before fixing either. That decision is the skill here.
Measure: rails within tolerance, actual clock frequency versus intended, peripherals working first time, and schematic errors found.
Write firmware for a real device in C99, with fixed-width types everywhere and every buffer statically allocated.
Ban allocation after boot and prove it: stub the allocator to trap, and run the whole application against the trap.
Run a static analyser and a MISRA checker over it, and drive the findings down rather than filtering them out.
Justify every deviation in writing, at the line. An unjustified deviation is the same as having no rule at all.
Feed the input parser malformed and oversized data and confirm nothing writes past a buffer, with the sanitiser on a host build.
Measure: flash and RAM used, peak stack depth, analyser findings by severity, and MISRA deviations with justifications.
Take a sampled input — ADC, I2S microphone, camera line — running fast enough that polling visibly costs CPU time.
Get it working with a polling loop first and measure the CPU time it eats. That baseline is what justifies the DMA.
Move it to DMA with double buffering, so the CPU processes one half while the peripheral fills the other.
Handle the late CPU explicitly: decide whether you drop a buffer or corrupt one, and make the code say which.
Run it overnight counting dropped samples, then stall the processing task on purpose and confirm the drop counter moves.
Measure: CPU idle percentage polling versus DMA, samples dropped over an overnight run, and overruns under a deliberate stall.
Wire at least two real sensors and log raw readings alongside a known reference instrument for a full day.
Write the calibration procedure as steps someone else could follow, and store the coefficients in non-volatile memory.
Choose the filter from the logged data by comparing candidates against the reference, not by eye on a live plot.
Leave it on the bench for a week logging continuously. Drift only shows up over time, and nobody waits.
Heat and cool the sensor deliberately and see whether the calibration still holds outside the temperature you calibrated at.
Measure: error against the reference before and after calibration, drift across the week, and error across the temperature range tested.
Take control logic with real modes — charging, running, fault, service — and draw the full transition table before writing any code.
Implement it as one explicit transition function, not as flags scattered through the main loop.
Handle every event in every state, including the ones that should not happen, and route the impossible ones to a safe state.
Compile the machine for the host and unit test every cell of the table. Testing the impossible cells is the part everybody skips.
Inject events out of order and during transitions, and confirm it never lands somewhere the table does not define.
Measure: states, events, table cells covered by tests, and unreachable states caught by the trap during a soak.
Build one core loop playable end to end in three minutes — input, feedback, failure, retry — and nothing else.
Put every tuning value in data rather than code, so you can change them between playtests without a rebuild.
Record at least five people who have never seen it, screen and hands, and say nothing at all while they play.
Watch where they got stuck and change the tuning value, not the explanation. Adding a tutorial instead is the escape everybody takes.
Re-test with new players after each change, so you are not measuring people who already learnt it.
Measure: time to first success, deaths before first success, retry rate, and quit points, per playtest round.
Find the content a designer currently needs you for — levels, dialogue, item tables — and build the editor tool for it.
Author the data as engine assets with a custom inspector, so the workflow lives where the designer already works.
Validate in the editor: reject the invalid setup at author time rather than crashing at runtime.
Hand it to an actual designer and watch them use it without helping. What they break is the requirement list.
Feed the tool a deliberately broken asset — missing reference, out-of-range value, a cycle — and check the editor refuses it clearly.
Measure: content authored without a programmer, validation rules and what each catches, and runtime errors from bad content before and after.
Simulate at least 200 interacting bodies on a fixed timestep, with rendering interpolated between steps.
Decouple the physics step from the frame rate entirely, accumulating leftover time rather than scaling the step.
Add continuous collision for the fast bodies, and find the speed at which discrete detection lets one tunnel through.
Record one input sequence and replay it. Determinism only counts if the replay matches on another machine, and that is the test.
Run the replay on a machine with a different CPU and frame rate, hashing the state each step, and compare the hashes.
Measure: physics step time at that body count, the step where the two machines diverge, and the velocity at which tunnelling starts.
Profile a real scene on the target hardware, not your development machine, and take a full frame capture.
Split the budget before optimising anything: state what the CPU gets and what the GPU gets out of your 16.6ms.
Work out which side you are bound on from the capture. Guessing wrong is how people spend a week optimising the wrong half.
Cut draw calls by batching and instancing, and pool the allocations causing collection spikes.
Profile the worst scene rather than the average one and hold the budget there — the average frame was never the problem.
Measure: CPU and GPU frame time separately, draw calls, allocations per frame, and 99th percentile frame time in the worst scene.
Write the design document for one game mode: core loop, win and failure states, and the questions you have not answered.
Build a playable prototype of the loop only — greybox geometry, no menus, no progression, no art.
Hand it to five people who have never seen it. Do not explain the rules; if you must, the document is wrong.
Write down every place the document promised something the prototype did not deliver, or the reverse.
Rewrite the sections the playtest disproved, and mark in the document what changed and why.
Measure: sections rewritten after the playtest, open questions closed versus still open, and time to the player's first correct action.
Block out one level in greybox with an intended route you can state in a sentence.
Instrument it: log player position twice a second, plus every death and every checkpoint reached.
Run eight players through it and draw their real paths over your intended one.
Find where they missed the route the level depends on. Do not add a sign — move geometry.
Change sightlines, cover and blockout lighting, then run eight fresh players over the same build.
Measure: deaths per section, route-completion rate, and time to find the critical path, before and after.
Take one game's combat and cost systems with at least twelve distinct options a player can choose between.
Put every option in a spreadsheet with its cost, its output, and the turn it becomes available.
Write a simulator that plays strategies against each other for thousands of matches with no human in the loop.
Find the dominant strategy. There is always one, and reading the spreadsheet will never show it to you.
Re-tune, re-run, and repeat until no single strategy wins unattended across the whole set.
Measure: win rate per strategy before and after tuning, and the count of options nobody ever picks.
Take a game with at least fifteen stages and write the intended unlock and difficulty curve down first.
Log one event per stage — started, completed, failed, quit — with timestamps, per anonymous player.
Get thirty people playing over a week, not five people for an hour. Retention needs days to show.
Plot retention per stage and find the session where players stop coming back at all.
Rebuild the two stages either side of that point and ship to a fresh cohort with the same events.
Measure: drop-off rate per stage for both cohorts, median session length, and stages reached per player.
Take a scene with at least six passes — depth, shadows, opaque, transparent, post, UI — in Vulkan or D3D12.
Declare each pass with its reads and writes, then derive barriers and transient allocations from the graph.
Wrap every pass in GPU timestamp queries, so the frame breakdown is measured rather than guessed at.
Handle two passes wanting the same resource in different states. That transition is the entire reason for the graph.
Remove a declared dependency on purpose and confirm the validation layer or the corrupted output catches it.
Measure: GPU milliseconds per pass, transient memory peak, and barrier count against the hand-written version.
Write the material and post-process shaders for one scene, with at least three quality variants per material.
Set the frame budget in milliseconds before writing the first variant, and split it across the passes.
Time each variant on the GPU at target resolution. Frame rate is an average and hides everything.
Put the expensive variant beside the cheap one and ask three people which is which. Most cannot tell.
Cut every variant nobody could pick out, then reprofile the whole scene on the same camera path.
Measure: GPU cost per variant, total frame time against budget, and the variants rejected on cost.
Find a real scene that misses its frame budget — your renderer or an open-source engine's stress scene.
Capture the frame in RenderDoc and again in Nsight or PIX, on a camera path you can repeat exactly.
Attribute the spike to one pass, then to one counter: bandwidth, occupancy, or a pipeline stall.
Name the counter that proves it before changing anything. Guessing from the pass name fixes the wrong thing.
Apply the fix and re-capture on the identical scene and camera path, or the comparison means nothing.
Measure: GPU time for that pass before and after, the counter you targeted, and total frame time.
Write a triangle rasteriser in C++ that renders a mesh of at least 50,000 triangles into a buffer.
Add perspective-correct attribute interpolation, a depth buffer, and back-face culling with a stated winding order.
Do near-plane clipping properly. This is where home rasterisers quietly start producing nonsense off-screen.
Render the identical scene, camera and matrices through OpenGL and dump both colour and depth buffers.
Diff them pixel by pixel and classify each disagreement as a bug or a legitimate precision difference.
Measure: pixels differing beyond tolerance, largest depth error, and frames per second at 1080p.
Take one Linux host running something real — a database and two services, not an empty box.
Write the baseline down: accounts and sudo rules, unattended security patching, systemd units, log rotation, firewall.
Wipe a second machine and rebuild it from that document alone, with the original terminal closed.
Anything you reach into shell history for is a gap in the document. Write it down then, not later.
Reboot the rebuilt host under load and confirm every service returns without being touched.
Measure: rebuild time, steps missing from the first pass, and services not running after the reboot.
Pick a running service and record a week of CPU, memory, IOPS and network per host, not fleet averages.
Load-test it until one resource saturates, and note which one gives first and at what load.
Size from the busiest hour's percentiles. Averages hide the peak that is actually going to kill you.
Write the model down: requests a second per host, and the growth rate at which the fleet runs out.
Push one host past that predicted limit on purpose and confirm it fails the way you said it would.
Measure: headroom per resource at peak, the saturation point, and months of runway at current growth.
Take three servers with different roles and write Ansible roles that build all three from a fresh image.
Keep the roles in version control with per-environment variables and no secrets in the repository.
Run every role twice and confirm the second run changes nothing. Idempotence is claimed far more often than checked.
Break a host deliberately: delete a config file, stop a service, change a file's permissions.
Run the playbook again and let it repair the host without you touching anything by hand.
Measure: changed tasks on the second run (should be zero), repair time, and full build time per role.
Build a primary and standby pair for something stateful — Postgres with streaming replication will do.
Add health checks, automatic promotion, and a virtual IP or proxy that the clients actually talk to.
Write the failback path down before you need it. Going back is harder than failing over, and always rushed.
Put steady load through it, then pull the power or the network from the primary without warning.
Check whether any committed write was lost, and time exactly how long clients saw errors.
Measure: failover time, client error window, writes lost, and failback time.
Define a typed SSA intermediate representation for a small language with functions, branches and integers.
Write the front end that lowers source to that IR, and a printer so a human can read it.
Write the verifier: types agree, every use is dominated by its definition, every block ends in a terminator.
Run the verifier after every pass, not once at the end. That is what names the pass that broke it.
Break a pass on purpose — drop a phi node, mistype a value — and confirm the verifier catches it there.
Measure: invariants checked, verifier runtime per pass, and planted breakages caught at the right pass.
Take an IR you already have and write constant folding and dead code elimination over it.
Collect a corpus of at least 200 programs whose output you can run and capture deterministically.
Run the corpus with passes off and on and diff the program output, not the generated code. Everybody diffs the code.
Add a random program generator so the corpus keeps growing past the cases you thought of.
When a program disagrees, shrink it to the smallest one that still disagrees before you open the debugger.
Measure: programs in the corpus, disagreements found, and instructions removed per pass.
Write the calling convention and stack frame layout down before emitting a single instruction.
Lower your IR to x86-64 assembly, assemble it, and link it into a binary that runs.
Get callee-saved registers and stack alignment right. Mistakes there crash late and far from the cause.
Run every corpus program through both the reference interpreter and the compiled binary on the same inputs.
Compare outputs and shrink any program that disagrees until the failing construct is obvious.
Measure: programs matching the interpreter, instructions emitted per program, and runtime against the interpreter.
Write a lexer and recursive-descent parser for a query language with at least twenty grammar rules.
Attach a line and column to every token, so an error can point at something a user recognises.
Add error recovery: report the error, skip to a synchronisation point, and keep parsing for the next one.
Reporting only the first error is what a weekend parser does. Report several from one bad input.
Fuzz it with random bytes and mutated valid inputs until nothing crashes, hangs or blows the stack.
Measure: errors reported from a single broken input, fuzz cases run, and crashes and hangs found.
Take a Cortex-M board and lay flash out as bootloader, slot A, slot B, and a small state area.
Write the bootloader: check the image's CRC and version, then jump to it with the vector table relocated.
Fall back to the other slot when the check fails, and mark the failing slot so it is not retried forever.
Flash a deliberately corrupted image and confirm the device boots the previous one instead of bricking.
Decide what happens when both slots fail and build that recovery path — serial or DFU — rather than assuming it.
Measure: boot time with and without verification, corrupted images rejected, and recovery time from a dead device.
Build the update path for a networked device: the server offers an image, the device writes the inactive slot.
Chunk the transfer with a CRC per chunk and a persisted offset, so a dropped link resumes instead of restarting.
Verify the whole image before marking it bootable. Never commit halfway through a transfer.
Add the confirm step: an image that boots but never checks in gets rolled back automatically. This is the part skipped.
Cut power at every stage — mid-transfer, at the commit, on first boot — and confirm the device still comes up.
Measure: update time over the real link, resumes after interruption, and successful boots after each power cut.
Pick a board and write SPI and timer drivers straight from the reference manual, with no vendor HAL.
Configure the clock tree yourself and confirm the core runs at the frequency you believe it does.
Bring SPI up in order: mode, prescaler, pin alternate functions, then move one byte before anything else.
Put a logic analyser on the bus and check clock polarity, phase and timing against the datasheet. An LED proves nothing.
Drive the timer at a set rate and measure the real interval on the analyser, not from a print statement.
Measure: measured SPI clock against nominal, timer interval error, and interrupt latency at the pin.
Lay flash out for a logger: a partition map, a fixed record format, and a CRC on every entry.
Write records sequentially across erase blocks so wear spreads instead of hammering one block.
Make a half-written record detectable — header written last, or a CRC that cannot pass on a partial write.
Write the mount routine so it scans for the last valid record and recovers the write position from flash alone.
Cut power mid-write a hundred times with a relay or bench supply, remounting after every cut.
Measure: remounts succeeding, records lost per cut (at most one), and erase counts per block after the run.
Take one provider service and two consumers that call it differently — a web client and a batch job.
Have each consumer write its own contract: the requests it sends and the fields it actually reads.
Verify the provider against both contracts in CI on every push, not on a nightly schedule.
Contracts written by the provider are worthless. They must come from the consumer's own tests, or they prove nothing.
Rename a field a consumer depends on and confirm the build goes red while the unit tests stay green.
Measure: contracts verified, fields covered per consumer, and breaking changes caught by contract but not by unit tests.
Write the OpenAPI document first for an API with at least eight operations, error responses included.
Generate the server stubs and two client SDKs in different languages from that single document.
Validate live requests and responses against the schema in middleware, in test and in staging.
Add a CI check that fails when implementation and specification disagree. Without it the document rots within a month.
Add an undocumented field to a response and confirm the validator rejects it rather than passing it through.
Measure: operations covered, drift failures caught in CI, and validation overhead per request in milliseconds.
Ship v1 of an API with at least three named callers you can identify per request.
Design v2 with the breaking change in it and run both versions from the same service.
Add Deprecation and Sunset headers to v1, and track usage per caller so you know exactly who is left.
Publish the window, then actually chase the remaining callers. Retirement is the part that never gets finished.
Switch v1 off only once the caller count reaches zero, and leave it off a fortnight before deleting code.
Measure: callers on v1 over time, days to zero, and requests hitting the retired version after cutoff.
Model the resources for a domain with four related entities and a collection large enough to need paging.
Add cursor pagination, filtering and sorting, with the cursor opaque and stable when rows are inserted.
Return an ETag on every read and require If-Match on every update.
Reject the stale write with 412 rather than merging or silently overwriting. Deciding that is the actual design work.
Fire two concurrent updates carrying the same ETag and confirm exactly one of them wins.
Measure: stale writes rejected under concurrency, pagination correctness across inserts, and p95 per endpoint.
Build the layout for a page with a sidebar, a card grid and a data table — the three things that break.
Use container queries and a fluid type scale rather than a stack of fixed device breakpoints.
Narrow the window continuously from 1600 to 320 pixels and watch for the first thing that breaks.
Fix it by changing the layout rule, not by adding another breakpoint. Breakpoints accumulate and never get removed.
Load it on a real phone and a real tablet. Emulators lie about fonts, scrollbars and the address bar.
Measure: widths tested, breaks found on device but not in the emulator, and breakpoints left in the final CSS.
Take a page built from nested divs and list every wrapper that is carrying meaning it cannot express.
Rewrite it with landmarks, a correct heading order, real lists, and native form controls.
Disable stylesheets entirely and read the page top to bottom. If it reads as nonsense, the markup is wrong.
Walk it with the keyboard only: every control reachable, focus visible, and no trap anywhere.
Run it through a screen reader and write down what each control is announced as, before and after.
Measure: heading-order errors, controls unreachable by keyboard, and controls announced without a name.
Take a stylesheet over 2,000 lines and count its !important declarations and its specificity spikes.
Extract colour, spacing and type into design tokens as custom properties with one naming convention.
Pick one layering rule and keep every selector's specificity flat underneath it.
Remove each !important by fixing the specificity that made it necessary, not by adding a competing one.
Run coverage tooling against the real pages and delete the selectors that nothing on the site uses.
Measure: shipped CSS bytes, !important count, and overriding rules per component, before and after.
Build one non-trivial component — a filterable, sortable list — on plain DOM APIs with no framework.
Delegate events from one container rather than binding per row, so new rows work without rebinding.
Render it on the server first, then enhance it in the browser rather than building it there.
Turn JavaScript off completely and confirm filtering and sorting still work through form submissions.
Operate the whole thing by keyboard, managing focus explicitly after every update to the list.
Measure: script bytes shipped, time to interactive, and features still working with JavaScript disabled.
Take a live site with a CMS and at least ten plugins, and clone it to staging with real content.
Write the maintenance window procedure down: clone, update, check, promote, log.
Apply core and plugin updates on staging first. Nothing goes straight to production, including the small ones.
Run a link checker and a visual diff against production before promoting anything. This is the check people skip.
Let an update break staging on purpose, then use the log to identify which one rather than reverting everything.
Measure: broken links and visual diffs caught on staging, window duration, and updates rolled back.
Export the whole existing zone and list every A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and TXT record with what it is for.
Find the records nobody remembers — SPF, DKIM, DMARC and the verification TXT entries. Those are what break mail.
Lower TTLs to 300 seconds at least a day ahead of the cutover and confirm they have propagated.
Build the new zone, cut over, then query it from several public resolvers, not only your own machine.
Send and receive real mail through the domain and check the headers show SPF and DKIM passing.
Measure: records inventoried versus migrated, resolvers agreeing after cutover, and mail delivery test results.
Set up ACME issuance on a real host serving a real domain, driven by a timer, not by a person.
Add the reload hook so the web server actually starts serving the new certificate.
Force an early renewal rather than waiting sixty days to discover whether any of it works.
Confirm from outside with openssl s_client that the served certificate is the new one. A successful job proves nothing.
Add an independent days-to-expiry check that alerts, so a silently failing renewal is still caught.
Measure: renewal run time, days before expiry the alarm fires, and served-certificate dates after a forced renewal.
List every account on the CMS and what it can actually do today, including the ones nobody uses.
Define roles from the tasks people really do, then cut each account down to the least it needs.
Turn on an audit log covering content changes, settings changes and role changes.
Plant a settings change from one account and confirm the log names who, what and when. Untested logging is decoration.
Delete a page and restore it from backup with an editor watching and timing you.
Measure: accounts holding admin before and after, restore time, and change types the audit log misses.
Pick a real written specification — a file format, a protocol, a tax rule — and number every clause.
Write one conformance test per clause before writing any of the implementation.
Implement until every test passes, keeping the clause number in the test name so traceability is automatic.
List the ambiguous clauses and ask about them, rather than deciding quietly in code. Everybody decides quietly.
Feed it inputs the specification never covers and record what you assumed and where that assumption lives.
Measure: clauses covered by tests, ambiguities raised and answered, and undefined cases handled explicitly.
Take an unowned program with no tests — an old script that still runs in production is ideal.
Capture its current behaviour on real inputs as characterisation tests, including the outputs you think are wrong.
Pin the ugly behaviour too. The point is to detect change, not to approve of what it does.
Make the change you were asked for, and see which characterisation tests move.
For each moved test, decide out loud whether it is the fix or a regression, and record the decision.
Measure: behaviours pinned, tests that moved after the change, and how many of those moves were intended.
Find a real intermittent defect — in your own code, or one open in a project's issue tracker.
Reproduce it reliably first. Everything after this is easy and nothing before it is possible.
Shrink the failing input until removing one more thing makes it pass.
Find the cause under a debugger with a breakpoint or watchpoint, not by scattering print statements around.
Write the test, confirm it fails on the commit before the fix, then land the fix.
Measure: reproduction rate before and after shrinking, input size before and after, and time to first reliable repro.
Pick a module with real logic — a parser, a pricing rule, a date calculation — and write unit tests for it.
Cover boundaries and error inputs, not only the happy path that you already know works.
Run a mutation testing tool over the suite and read the surviving mutants one at a time.
Coverage says a line ran. A surviving mutant says nothing checked what that line did. Read them.
Rewrite the tests that let mutants live, and re-run until the survivors are only equivalent ones.
Measure: line coverage, mutation score, and surviving mutants before and after the rewrite.
Design an FPGA module that samples an external interface and buffers it into a different clock domain.
Keep one synchronous style: one clock per domain, a documented reset strategy, and no gated clocks.
Put a two-flop synchroniser on every single-bit crossing and an asynchronous FIFO on every bus crossing.
Constrain the crossings in the timing file. An unconstrained crossing passes timing and then fails in the lab.
Close timing on the real part, then soak it on hardware at temperature for an hour looking for corruption.
Measure: worst negative slack, crossings constrained versus present, and errors seen over the soak run.
Agree a register map with whoever owns the FPGA side, include a version register, and put it in version control.
Generate the firmware's register definitions from that file rather than typing the offsets a second time.
Read the version register at boot and refuse to run when firmware and bitstream disagree.
Write the driver against the map with a timeout on every hardware wait loop. An unbounded poll hangs the device.
Load a mismatched bitstream on purpose and confirm the device stops with a reason a human can read.
Measure: boot-time checks performed, mismatches caught, and register accesses per transaction.
Write a Verilog module for something with state — a FIFO, an arbiter, or a CRC unit.
Write a reference model of the same behaviour in software, accurate at the interface every cycle.
Drive constrained-random stimulus into both and compare outputs automatically, cycle by cycle.
Add functional coverage points for full, empty, back-to-back and reset-mid-transaction cases.
Random stimulus without coverage tells you nothing about what was never tried. Read the coverage report and fill the holes.
Measure: coverage points hit and missed, cycles simulated, and mismatches against the reference model.
Build a five-stage RISC-V core in Verilog running the RV32I integer subset.
Get the single-cycle version running real programs first, verified against a reference simulator.
Pipeline it, then add forwarding for data hazards and stalls for the cases forwarding cannot cover.
Handle the load-use hazard and the taken branch. That pair is where nearly every pipeline bug lives.
Run the compliance tests and compare architectural state instruction by instruction against Spike.
Measure: compliance tests passing, cycles per instruction against the single-cycle version, and stall cycles per benchmark.
Automate five real user journeys through an application with login, forms and a checkout or payment step.
Put interactions behind page objects and setup behind fixtures, so a test reads as the journey it covers.
Keep traces, screenshots and video on failure only. A failure you cannot diagnose is not a test result.
Hand it to two people who did not build it and let them add tests without asking you how it works.
Fix whatever they got wrong in the framework itself, not in a document telling the next person not to.
Measure: journeys covered, time for a new person to add their first passing test, and total suite runtime.
Take a suite that depends on a shared seeded database and count the tests that quietly assume an order.
Make every test create its own data through the API and remove it afterwards.
Namespace what cannot be deleted — emails, accounts, tenant ids — so parallel runs never collide.
Shuffle the suite order and run it. Order dependence is the failure everybody discovers in CI instead.
Run it in parallel against one shared environment and fix every collision at source, not with a mutex.
Measure: suite runtime serial versus parallel, failures under shuffle, and rows left behind after a run.
Split the existing tests into unit, contract and end-to-end, and time each layer honestly.
Run unit and contract on every push; keep the slow end-to-end suite for the release gate.
Shard the slow suite across parallel runners, balanced by measured runtime rather than by file count.
Block the merge on red. A pipeline that anyone can override is a report, not a gate.
Push a change that breaks only an end-to-end case and confirm it reaches the release gate and stops there.
Measure: runtime per layer, feedback time on push, and defects caught per layer.
Run the whole suite twenty times against one unchanged commit and record every test that ever failed.
Open a register: test name, failure rate, and cause — timing, shared state, or a real race in the product.
Fix each at source. A retry hides the flake and keeps the bug underneath it.
Ban sleeps entirely: wait on the condition, never on a duration.
Re-run the same twenty times and confirm the register shrank rather than the retry count growing.
Measure: failure rate per test before and after, rerun rate, and flakes that turned out to be product bugs.
Implement Raft leader election and log replication across five nodes with a simple key-value state machine.
Persist term, vote and log to disk before replying to anything. This is the rule people break for speed.
Write a client that records every operation with its invocation and completion times.
Kill and restart nodes at random mid-write, the leader included, over a long run.
Feed the recorded history to a linearizability checker such as Porcupine or Knossos and read what it rejects.
Measure: histories checked, violations found, election time after a leader kill, and commit latency.
Build a replicated key-value store over five nodes with configurable read and write quorums.
Version every value with a vector clock or a timestamp you can defend, and reconcile on read.
Add read repair, so a stale replica is corrected by the read that noticed it.
Set R plus W below N deliberately and go and find the stale read instead of assuming it is rare.
Sweep the quorum settings and record how often a stale read actually appears at each combination.
Measure: stale reads per thousand at each R and W setting, read and write latency, and repairs triggered.
Take a running cluster of at least three nodes serving reads and writes under steady load.
Write down what you expect it to give up under partition — availability or consistency — before cutting anything.
Cut the network with traffic-control rules or a proxy. A stopped process is a crash, not a partition.
Record from each side what still served, what was refused, and what came back stale.
Heal the partition and check whether the sides converged, and what became of the conflicting writes.
Measure: writes accepted per side during partition, stale reads observed, and time to converge after healing.
Build lease-based leader election over a handful of workers writing to one shared store.
Issue a monotonically increasing fencing token with every lease granted.
Make the storage layer reject any write carrying a token lower than the highest it has already seen.
Pause a leader past its lease expiry with SIGSTOP and let a new leader take over while it sleeps.
Resume the old leader and confirm its write is refused. A lease alone would have let that write through.
Measure: election time after lease expiry, late writes rejected, and split-brain windows observed.
Take a public corpus of at least 500,000 documents and build an inverted index from scratch.
Write compressed postings lists with document frequency, and skip pointers for fast intersection.
Write segments and merge them in the background, so indexing never stops the world.
Index the same corpus into Lucene and run the same 200 queries against both systems.
Compare result sets, not only latency. A fast index that returns the wrong documents is not faster at anything.
Measure: index build time and size, query p95, and result-set overlap with Lucene per query.
Get a real query log — yours or a public one — of at least 50,000 queries.
Build the stages separately: intent classification, spelling correction against corpus vocabulary, and entity recognition.
Route recognised entities to structured filters rather than leaving them in the free-text query.
Measure each stage on a held-out slice on its own, or you will never learn which one is doing the damage.
Find the queries the corrector rewrote that were already correct, and add the guard that stops it.
Measure: precision and recall per stage, corrections applied to already-correct queries, and added latency per stage.
Get BM25 working as a first pass and freeze it as the baseline you have to beat.
Collect graded judgements for at least 200 queries by hand — three grades, several documents each.
Train a learning-to-rank model using only features you can compute at serving time, not offline-only ones.
Report NDCG on a held-out query set, keeping the training and held-out queries genuinely separate.
Run an interleaving test on live clicks and see whether it agrees with your offline number.
Measure: NDCG@10 baseline versus re-ranked, interleaving win rate, and re-ranking latency per query.
Take a corpus with awkward text — product codes, mixed languages, punctuation — and index it with the default analyser.
Collect the queries returning nothing and the ones returning rubbish. That list is the whole project.
Choose tokenisation, stemming, stop-word and synonym rules per field rather than one chain for everything.
Pin those queries as a regression set that runs on every change to the analysis chain.
Add a synonym that helps one query, then check the regression set for the query it just broke.
Measure: zero-result rate before and after, regression queries passing, and index size per analyser choice.
Take an interaction dataset with at least a million events — MovieLens, a retail log, or your own.
Build three candidate sources: co-visitation, recency and popularity, each returning a few hundred items.
Set the latency budget for the whole stage first, and hold every source inside it.
Measure recall per source in isolation before blending. Blended recall hides a source contributing nothing at all.
Drop each source in turn and re-measure, so you know what each one is actually paying for.
Measure: recall@500 per source and blended, latency per source, and overlap between sources.
Take implicit interactions with timestamps — views, plays, purchases — at least a million rows.
Split by time, never at random. A random split leaks the future and flatters every model you try.
Build the most-popular baseline first and score it. A great many models never beat it.
Train matrix factorisation or ALS on implicit feedback with a negative sampling scheme you can defend.
Score cold and sparse users separately. The average hides that they are the users you serve worst.
Measure: recall@20 and NDCG@20 against most-popular, overall and for users with fewer than five interactions.
Take the candidates from your generation stage and build the second-stage click model over them.
Compute every feature point-in-time, so nothing that happened after the impression leaks into training.
Train a gradient-boosted model and hold scoring inside the serving latency budget you set.
Plot a reliability curve: predicted probability against observed click rate, bucketed. Ranking work skips this and stays uncalibrated.
Calibrate with Platt scaling or isotonic regression and re-plot to show the curve straightened out.
Measure: AUC, log loss, expected calibration error before and after, and scoring latency per request.
Embed at least a million items and store the vectors somewhere you can rebuild the index from.
Compute exact nearest neighbours for a sample of a thousand queries. That is your ground truth.
Build an HNSW index and sweep its parameters, plotting recall against latency at every setting.
Pick a point on that curve deliberately and write down the recall you have chosen to run at.
Add new items, refresh the index, and re-measure recall. Freshness almost always costs some of it.
Measure: recall@10 against exact search, query p95 per parameter setting, index build time and memory.
Model accounts and entries so every movement writes two entries summing to zero, and nothing is ever updated.
Enforce the balance in the database with a constraint, not in a service where it can be bypassed.
Derive balances from entries, then add a snapshot table for speed. Never edit a balance in place.
Write the replayer: rebuild every balance from entry one into an empty database.
Replay after a run of real traffic and compare account by account with the snapshot. Any drift is a bug now.
Measure: entries replayed, replay time, and accounts disagreeing between replay and snapshot.
Draw the state machine first: authorised, partially captured, captured, expired, voided, refunded.
Store the state in a column with a check constraint and enforce the legal transitions in the database.
Drive every path through a sandbox gateway, partial capture included, rather than only the happy one.
Handle authorisation expiry. Nobody builds that path until the day it happens in production.
Fire an illegal transition straight at the database and confirm it is refused, not merely logged.
Measure: transitions defined versus exercised, illegal transitions rejected, and payments stuck in a non-terminal state.
Get three sources for the same day: a gateway settlement report, your ledger, and a bank statement.
Match three ways on amount, date and reference, and treat anything unmatched as an exception.
Give every exception a reason code and a date, and put it in a queue somebody has to clear.
A reconciliation that passes with a warning is a reconciliation that passes with a hole in it. Fail it.
Plant a discrepancy — a missing refund, a duplicated payout, an unbooked fee — and confirm it lands in the queue.
Measure: lines matched three ways, exceptions by reason code, run time, and planted discrepancies caught.
Require an idempotency key on every write that moves money, and store the response against that key.
Write the key and the effect in the same transaction. Two separate transactions is the bug.
Handle the in-flight case: a retry arriving before the first request commits must wait or be refused.
Apply the same guarantee to gateway webhooks, keyed on the event id, so a redelivery is a no-op.
Fire fifty concurrent duplicates and re-deliver yesterday's webhooks, then reconcile the ledger against expectation.
Measure: duplicate effects under concurrent retries (must be zero), key conflicts with a different body, and storage overhead.
Take a service you already run and pull a week of access logs — at least a million lines, or generate a week that looks like one.
Build the traffic profile from those logs: endpoint mix, payload sizes, think time and the daily peak, not a flat request rate.
Hold every run long enough for connection pools, JIT and caches to reach steady state. Short runs measure warm-up, and everybody reports them anyway.
Ramp until the error rate leaves its floor, and record the load where it first moved rather than where it collapsed.
Replay a uniform load at the same requests per second and show the two answers disagree.
Measure: requests per second at the first error, p50/p95/p99 at that point, and the same numbers under uniform load.
Put the service under a steady load heavy enough to be CPU-bound — a load rig or a replayed hour of real requests, not one curl.
Attach a sampling profiler to the running process and collect a flame graph over several minutes, not one burst.
Read down to the frame that actually owns the CPU time, not the widest parent. Everybody stops at the parent and fixes the wrong thing.
Fix that one frame, and change nothing else in the same commit.
Re-profile under the identical load and show the peak has moved elsewhere. If it has not, you fixed nothing.
Measure: CPU share of the top frame before and after, throughput at fixed concurrency, and where the new peak sits.
Instrument one request path with latency histograms — HDR or native buckets — over at least a million real or replayed requests.
Plot the full distribution, put the mean on the same chart, and show what the mean hides.
Split the histogram by route and by cache hit or miss until the slow mode belongs to one identifiable path.
Merge histograms across instances properly. Averaging per-instance percentiles is the mistake nearly everybody ships, and it hides the worst box.
Inject latency into the slow mode only, and confirm that mode's buckets move while the fast mode does not.
Measure: p50, p95, p99 and p99.9 per split, the mean beside them, and the request count in each mode.
