Pick one operation worth benchmarking and pin its dataset — a fixed seeded corpus of at least a hundred thousand records, checked in or content-addressed.
Write the harness with an explicit warm-up phase and a fixed measurement window, on hardware you can get back to.
Run it twenty times unchanged and record the spread. That noise band is the whole benchmark; without it every result is a coin toss.
Wire it into the merge gate so it fails only when throughput falls outside that band, never on one slow run.
Commit a deliberate regression and confirm the gate catches it, then commit a no-op and confirm it stays quiet.
Measure: mean throughput, run-to-run spread, and the smallest regression the gate detects reliably.
Take two systems holding overlapping records of the same thing — a CRM export and a billing table will do, ten thousand records each side.
Write the field-level mapping first: every field, its type, its units, and where it comes from on each side.
Write the tie-break rule for every field that can disagree, and name which system wins. This is the part left to whichever job ran last.
Run the sync, then reconcile both sides afterwards, raising a ticket per mismatch instead of overwriting it.
Change the same field on both sides between runs and show your rule applied and the loser recorded, not lost.
Measure: records compared, mismatches raised, mismatches resolved by rule, and reconciliation run time.
Stand up a real broker — Kafka, RabbitMQ or SQS — and a consumer that writes each message into a database.
Acknowledge only after the write commits, never on receipt. Acking on receipt is the default in most examples and it loses messages.
Route poison messages to a dead-letter queue carrying the failure reason and attempt count, not just the payload.
Build the replay path so a dead-lettered message can be put back through without duplicating its effect.
Kill the consumer mid-batch, restart it, and prove nothing was lost and nothing applied twice.
Measure: messages published against messages committed, duplicates after the kill (it must be zero), and dead-letter depth.
Take two real representations of the same records — a partner CSV and your own schema — a few hundred rows with the awkward ones included.
Put every field rule, unit conversion and date format in one versioned mapping file, not scattered through transform code.
Write a golden input-and-expected-output file per rule covering null, empty string and absent field. Those three differ, and mappings usually pretend they do not.
Run the suite on every change so an edited rule fails locally, long before it reaches the partner.
Change one rule deliberately and confirm the golden file fails in CI, then revert it.
Measure: rules covered, fields with a golden case for null, empty and absent, and rows failing conversion.
Sign up for a real partner sandbox — Stripe, Twilio or a public government API — and read every documented error code before writing a client.
Build the client with bounded retries and backoff that honours the partner's rate-limit headers rather than a fixed sleep.
Record a fixture for every documented error code so the certification suite runs in CI without touching the partner.
Handle the 200 carrying an error inside the body. Partners do this constantly and clients that only read status codes swallow it.
Replay the rate-limit and timeout fixtures and confirm the client backs off and gives up rather than hammering.
Measure: documented error codes with a fixture, retries per failed call, and suite run time with no network access.
Find the sequence your team copies out of the wiki — at least five steps somebody runs weekly — and wrap it in one command-line tool.
Ship shell completion and a dry-run flag that prints what would happen without doing it.
Add per-subcommand usage telemetry, local and opt-in, so you learn which commands are actually run.
Watch three people who did not write it use it unaided. Watching, not asking — what people say they need is not what they type.
Break its assumptions on purpose — wrong directory, missing credentials, stale config — and confirm it fails with an instruction, not a stack trace.
Measure: runs per subcommand over two weeks, subcommands with zero runs, and time from first invocation to a correct result.
Take a repository whose clean build exceeds five minutes and write down its current clean and incremental times on one machine.
Make every task declare its inputs and outputs explicitly, so only changed targets rebuild.
Find the targets lying about their inputs: build twice with no change and see what rebuilt anyway. That is where the cache leaks.
Turn on a shared cache and surface the hit rate in CI, where people will actually see it.
Touch one leaf file and prove exactly one target rebuilds, then touch a shared header and prove the right set does.
Measure: clean and incremental build time before and after, cache-hit rate, and targets still non-cacheable.
Take a project with at least three services and a database, and time clone-to-first-passing-test on a machine that has never run it.
Package it in dev containers with seeded data and stubbed third parties, so nobody needs a partner credential to start.
End setup in a smoke test that fails loudly when the environment is wrong, rather than leaving a half-working stack.
Tie the seed data to migrations so a schema change updates the seed. Seeds drifting from the schema is what kills these after a month.
Wipe the machine, clone from scratch, and run it yourself with a stopwatch. Then have somebody else do it.
Measure: clone-to-first-passing-test on a clean machine, steps still needing a human, and what the smoke test says when it fails.
Take a pipeline running over ten minutes and record per-job duration and queue time across its last hundred runs.
Find the critical path. Everything off it is not worth optimising, however slow it looks.
Split the test suite by measured timing rather than by directory, cache dependencies, and run independent jobs in parallel.
Keep one stage serial on purpose — the one where parallel runs would fight over shared state — and write down why.
Run the new pipeline twenty times and count the flakes parallelism introduced; a fast pipeline that fails randomly is slower.
Measure: pipeline time and queue time before and after, per-job durations, and flake rate over twenty runs.
Take a public dataset with at least a million rows across three joined tables, and a reporting question somebody would genuinely ask.
Write the queries in version control, one file each, with the filters and joins explained in a comment.
Check row counts against a known total before quoting any number. An inner join silently dropping rows is the commonest wrong answer in reporting.
Have somebody review the definitions, not just the SQL — what a filter excludes matters more than how it is written.
Change one join to a left join and show the number move. That difference is what you were nearly wrong by.
Measure: rows in against rows out per query, the reconciliation total, and query run time.
Find a real owner — a club treasurer, a team lead, anyone — and get the three questions the dashboard must answer in writing.
Agree those questions before designing anything. A dashboard designed first and justified after is a wall of tiles nobody reads.
Build one tile per question, each linked to the written definition of its metric.
Put a freshness stamp on the page showing when the underlying load last ran, and make staleness obvious.
Sit with the owner while they use it, and delete every tile they did not look at.
Measure: tiles in the first draft against tiles kept, questions answered without a follow-up, and load-to-display lag.
Find two reports of the same metric that disagree — two teams, two tools, or one number quoted twice with different totals.
Write each definition out fully: numerator, denominator, time grain, and every exclusion.
Reconcile the difference back to the definitions rather than to the SQL. The gap is nearly always an exclusion nobody wrote down.
Agree one version with both owners and put it under version control with the date it was agreed.
Recompute both historical reports under the agreed definition and show which published figures change.
Measure: the gap between the two figures, how much each exclusion accounted for, and periods restated.
Take a dataset with per-user events across at least twelve months — a public retention or transaction set works.
Group users by joining month, not calendar month, and plot retention by months since joining.
Say at which period the curve flattens rather than quoting one retention number for everybody.
Test the confounder: check whether an improving cohort is the team's change or a shift in who joined that month.
Recut the identical data by calendar month and show the two charts telling different stories.
Measure: cohort sizes, retention at 1, 3 and 6 months per cohort, and the joining-mix shift between cohorts.
Take a public dataset of at least fifty thousand rows with a continuous outcome somebody would want explained, not merely predicted.
Fit an interpretable regression and write down what each coefficient claims, in plain words.
Check the assumptions rather than assuming them: residual structure, influential points, correlated predictors. Skipping this decides whether the coefficients mean anything.
Report an interval beside every estimate, never a bare point figure.
Refit with the most influential rows removed and show how far the coefficients move.
Measure: coefficients with intervals, variance inflation per predictor, and the coefficient shift after dropping influential points.
State one hypothesis about a dataset you have not yet pulled — public data is fine, provided you have not looked.
Write down the effect size worth detecting, the required sample size and the whole analysis plan before touching the data.
Pull the data once and run the analysis you wrote. Choosing the test after seeing numbers is how a null result becomes a finding.
Report the confidence interval, not only the p-value.
Write the conclusion you would have drawn had it gone the other way, and at a p-value just past your threshold.
Measure: sample size needed, sample obtained, the effect estimate with its interval, and the test's power.
Take a dataset with timestamps and a labelled outcome — at least a hundred thousand rows — so the moment of knowledge is recoverable.
For every feature, write down when its value would have been known, and drop anything computed after the label.
Plant a leak on purpose: add a feature derived from the outcome and watch the score jump. That jump is what leakage looks like from inside.
Remove it and record how far the honest score falls.
Keep the leakage check in the test suite so a future feature computed from the future fails the build.
Measure: score with the leaking feature and without, features rejected on timing, and the check's run time.
Take an imbalanced classification dataset with a time column — fraud, churn or default — of at least a hundred thousand rows.
Split by time, never at random, and record the majority-class baseline before training anything.
Calibrate the probabilities and plot the calibration curve. An uncalibrated score cannot become a decision, and most people ship one anyway.
Choose the operating threshold from the cost of a false positive against a false negative, and write both costs down.
Re-run with a random split and show how much better the model looks than it is.
Measure: precision and recall at your threshold, the baseline, calibration error, and the gap between random and time-based splits.
Take a source that can be both replayed and streamed — a public event dataset of at least ten million records — and define the transformations once.
Build the batch path over the whole history and the streaming path over those same transformations.
Commit offsets only after the output write commits, so a restart resumes rather than repeats.
Kill a worker mid-run, restart it, then compare streaming output to the batch result row for row. That comparison is the project.
Find where the two disagree — late data, windowing, ordering — and decide in writing which one you trust.
Measure: rows in each path, rows differing after the kill, offset lag at restart, and time to catch up.
Ingest a real external source on a schedule — a public API or partner file drop with at least a hundred thousand records a run.
Write the data contract at the boundary: required fields, types, ranges, and what a valid record looks like.
Quarantine every reject with its reason and raw payload rather than dropping it or failing the load. Silent drops are the bug found six months later.
Give the quarantine table an owner and an alert when it grows faster than usual.
Feed in a malformed batch on purpose and confirm the good records still land and the bad ones stay recoverable.
Measure: records ingested, records quarantined by reason, load run time, and time to reprocess a quarantined record.
Model a daily load with at least six tasks and real dependencies in Airflow, Dagster or Prefect, over a month of data.
Put sensors on upstream freshness so a task waits for its input instead of reprocessing yesterday's file.
Make every task idempotent — delete-then-insert by partition, or merge by key — so a re-run changes nothing.
Backfill the whole month by re-running the same tasks, then compare totals to a single clean run. A difference means one task is not idempotent.
Kill the DAG halfway through the backfill, resume it, and check the totals again.
Measure: task durations, retries fired, backfill totals against a clean run, and the difference between them.
Take a pipeline you already run and a source table with at least ten columns something downstream depends on.
Version the data contract and classify every possible change as compatible or breaking, in writing.
Read the old and new shapes side by side through an overlap window rather than cutting over in one release.
Fail the load only on a genuinely incompatible change. A pipeline halting on every added column gets its checks switched off within a month.
Rename a column upstream for real and show the pipeline landing on time through the overlap.
Measure: contract versions live at once, loads through the overlap, rows failed, and landing time against the usual.
Take a transactional source of at least a million rows and two existing reports that disagree about the same number.
State the grain of the fact table in one sentence and write it into the model's documentation before building anything.
Build conformed dimensions shared across both marts rather than a dimension per report. Duplicated dimensions are exactly why the reports disagreed.
Rebuild both reports on the shared model and show them resolving to the same figure.
Insert a row below the declared grain and show the fact table's tests rejecting it.
Measure: the stated grain, fact row count against source, and the difference between the two reports before and after.
Take a warehouse with at least five raw sources and build a layered project over them in dbt or SQLMesh.
Give each layer one job: staging renames and casts, intermediate joins, marts answer a question.
Read every raw source in exactly one staging model. Two models reading the same raw table is how definitions quietly fork.
Render the dependency graph from the code, never draw it by hand.
Point a mart model straight at a raw source and confirm a lint rule or test fails the build, then revert.
Measure: models per layer, sources read more than once, graph depth, and full-run time.
Find at least ten metrics currently defined inside dashboards, and collect every existing version of each one.
Move each into one versioned metric layer that the BI tool reads instead of redefining.
Change one definition and show every report move together. That single edit is the entire point of the layer.
Add a test that fails when a dashboard reintroduces its own copy of a governed metric.
Rebuild a governed metric inside a dashboard on purpose and confirm the test catches it.
Measure: metrics governed, duplicate definitions removed, reports moved by one definition change, and test run time.
Take models fed by at least three sources and list what must be true of each: keys, ranges, allowed values, row-count bounds.
Write assertions for uniqueness, referential integrity, accepted values and row-count bounds — not just not-null on every column.
Halt the load on failure and leave the previous good tables in place. Tests that only warn are ignored within a fortnight.
Set row-count bounds from the historical range rather than a guess, so a real seasonal dip does not fail the load.
Feed in a load with duplicated keys and confirm the run halts while yesterday's tables still serve.
Measure: assertions per model, failures by type over a month, false failures, and time from failure to alert.
Take a training job you can run end to end in under an hour, on a dataset of at least a hundred thousand examples.
Pin the data snapshot by content hash, seed every source of randomness, and log config, code commit and artefacts per run.
Reproduce a run from three weeks earlier on a clean machine and compare scores. Nobody checks this until the day they need it.
Find the non-determinism you cannot remove — GPU kernels, thread scheduling — and bound it by running one config five times.
Change a line of preprocessing without touching the config and confirm the pipeline notices the code commit moved.
Measure: score spread across repeated runs of one config, the reproduction gap against the original, and full pipeline run time.
Serve a trained model behind an HTTP API taking real request shapes, not a notebook cell.
Validate input schema and ranges before inference, and return the model version with every response.
Decide what happens when a feature arrives outside the training range — reject, clamp or flag — and write down why.
Health-check a new version at start-up and fall back to the previous one when it fails, rather than serving a broken model.
Deploy a deliberately broken version and watch the fallback hold traffic on the old one.
Measure: p50 and p99 latency, requests rejected by validation, fallback events, and time to serve the previous version.
Take a served model with a measured p99 and a written latency budget somebody would sign up to.
Profile first and find where the time actually goes — preprocessing, forward pass, or serialisation. It is usually not the forward pass.
Batch concurrent requests, export the graph to a compiled runtime, and move preprocessing off the request path.
Re-score on the same evaluation set after every change, so a speed-up that quietly cost accuracy is caught.
Push concurrency past the batch window and show where latency stops improving and starts queueing.
Measure: p50 and p99 before and after per change, throughput, and the evaluation score at each step.
Take a dataset with labels stamped in time and features that change — at least a hundred thousand labelled events.
Join each feature as it stood at the moment of its label, not as it stands today.
Replay a past day through the serving path and compare served features to trained ones, field by field. Skew hides from anyone who skips this.
Fix every field that disagrees, and record which ones did.
Break one feature's point-in-time join deliberately and show the replay catching the mismatch.
Measure: features compared, fields disagreeing on replay, rows affected, and the score gap between point-in-time and naive joins.
Stand up a registry — MLflow or equivalent — in front of at least five model versions you actually trained.
Make every version carry its data snapshot hash, code commit and evaluation report; a version missing them cannot be registered.
Make promotion a recorded decision with an author and a timestamp, not a file copy.
Gate promotion on the evaluation report existing and passing. Without that gate a registry is a folder with extra steps.
Try to promote an unevaluated version and confirm it is refused, then roll a promotion back by moving the serving tag.
Measure: versions registered, promotions and rollbacks, time to roll back, and versions rejected by the gate.
Schedule retraining over a dataset that genuinely grows each week — a public feed, or your own logged events.
Have each run pull fresh data, train, and evaluate against the incumbent on a fixed holdout that never changes.
Register a candidate only when it wins. A pipeline that ships whatever it trained is a pipeline that ships a bad week.
Add data checks before training — volume, null rates, label balance — and stop and page rather than train on rubbish.
Feed in a deliberately broken week and confirm the run halts before training and alerts a human.
Measure: runs, candidates registered against runs, runs halted by data checks, and holdout score per run over time.
Take a model in service and log its input features and predictions against the training reference distribution.
Compute a population-stability or distance measure per feature, per day, rather than one score for the whole input.
Tune thresholds by replaying a period with a known distribution change, so the alarm level comes from data rather than a default.
Separate real drift from a broken upstream: a feature suddenly all-null is a bug, not a shift, and both trip the same alarm.
Corrupt one feature upstream on purpose and confirm the alarm fires and names that feature.
Measure: per-feature drift scores over time, alarms fired, false alarms per week, and lead time before accuracy moved.
Serve two model versions side by side and route a fixed small fraction of live traffic to the new one.
Compare error rate, latency and prediction distribution on the same requests, not on different traffic.
Work out from your traffic rate how long the canary must run before the comparison means anything, and write that number down first.
Wire automatic rollback when any of the three crosses its threshold, with no human in the loop.
Ship a deliberately worse model and watch it come back out on its own.
Measure: canary traffic share, time to detect, time to roll back, and the three comparison metrics per arm.
Pick a question narrow enough to answer, and write the search strings for at least two databases before reading anything.
Fix the inclusion and exclusion criteria in advance, and record a screening decision and reason per paper.
Screen on title and abstract first, then full text, keeping counts at each stage. Reading closely before screening turns a review into a reading list.
Extract the same fields from every included paper — data, method, metric, sample size — into one table.
Find the comparisons that are not like for like and say so, instead of averaging incompatible numbers.
Measure: papers screened, included and excluded by criterion, and the spread of the headline metric across included studies.
Start from a concrete case where the existing approach fails — one you can construct and show, not one you read about.
State the assumption your method needs and the regime where it should not work, before running anything.
Build the method and test it first on constructed data where you already know the answer.
Go looking for the result that would tell you the method is wrong, and run it. Skipping this is what makes a method unfalsifiable.
Run the predicted failure case and show the method failing there, as stated.
Measure: the metric on the constructed gain case and the constructed failure case, and where the crossover sits.
Pick three published approaches to one task with released code, and a benchmark with fixed public splits.
Run every method on the same splits, the same hardware and the same environment.
Give each baseline the tuning budget the proposed method got, counted in trials. Under-tuned baselines are how most reported improvements are manufactured.
Run every configuration over at least five seeds and report the spread, not the best run.
Compare your tuned baselines against the figures printed in the papers and report the gap.
Measure: score mean and spread per method, tuning trials per method, and the difference from published figures.
Pick one published result with released code and a stated number you can aim at.
Run it from the paper first, and log every gap you fill by guesswork — a hyperparameter, a preprocessing step, a split.
Record each guess as you make it. Reconstructing them afterwards is impossible, and they are the whole value of the exercise.
Pin the environment — image, versions, seeds — so the run is repeatable by someone who was not there.
Hand it to a stranger, or a clean machine, and have them reach the same numbers with one command.
Measure: the reported number against yours, gaps filled by guesswork, and the run's variance over seeds.
Pick a task small enough to train repeatedly — a character language model or a small image classifier — and get the standard block working first.
Design one variant and match it to the baseline on parameter count.
Match training compute too, plus data order, optimiser and schedule. Parameter count alone does not isolate the design, and most comparisons stop there.
Train both across at least three seeds each.
Give the baseline the variant's tuned learning rate and see whether the gap survives.
Measure: parameters, training FLOPs, wall-clock time, and the evaluation metric per seed for both.
Take a model with at least four separable components and one fixed evaluation set.
Work out your seed budget first, and how many runs each cell of the table will cost.
Remove one component at a time and report the spread across seeds beside every mean. A single-seed ablation table is noise with the error bars removed.
Test pairs as well as singles, so you catch a component contributing nothing once another is present.
Run the full model twice under different seeds and see how much of your smallest ablation effect that gap covers.
Measure: metric mean and per-seed spread per ablation, seeds per cell, and the smallest effect distinguishable at that budget.
Train the same architecture under two objectives from one initialisation, on the same data in the same order.
Pick a downstream task neither loss directly optimises, and freeze its evaluation set before training starts.
Report the downstream score, not the training loss. The lower loss is the thing being measured, which settles nothing.
Repeat over at least three seeds each and report the spread beside every mean.
Check whether the winning objective still wins at half the training budget.
Measure: final training loss per objective, downstream score per seed, and the gap at half compute.
Train at least five model sizes across a compute range you can actually afford, on one fixed dataset.
Record compute, parameters, tokens and loss for every run, including the ones that failed.
Fit the curve on the smaller points and hold the largest run out entirely.
Predict the held-out point before you look at it, and write the prediction down. Fitting on all points and calling it a law proves nothing.
Run the largest configuration and compare the result against your written prediction.
Measure: fitted exponents, predicted against actual loss at the held-out size, and the residual across fitted points.
Find a domain expert and get twenty competency questions in writing before a single class exists.
Model only the classes and relations needed to answer those questions, and nothing else.
Write a stored query per competency question that fails when a later modelling change breaks it. Ontologies without these drift until nothing answers.
Take the questions back to the expert and let their answers force changes to the hierarchy.
Move a class up or down a level on purpose and show which competency queries stop returning.
Measure: competency questions answered by a passing query, classes and relations modelled, and queries broken per modelling change.
Build a graph from at least two sources that overlap — public datasets describing the same entities work well.
Attach the source and the assertion date to every statement, not to the node.
Load a contested fact from both sources and decide what the graph stores and what the query returns. Storing only the winner is how provenance is lost.
Build retraction: remove one source's statements without rebuilding the graph.
Retract a source and confirm the contested query's answer changes while the other source's statements survive.
Measure: statements held, statements per source, contested entities, and retraction time.
Take a real collection of at least five hundred items needing classification — support tickets, product listings or documents.
Write a definition and a scope note for every term, separating it from its siblings.
Have two people classify the same hundred items independently, without discussing it. Skipping this leaves terms only their author can apply.
Rework every term where they disagreed, then re-run the exercise on a fresh sample.
Merge two terms and deprecate one, then show what happens to the records already classified under them.
Measure: inter-annotator agreement before and after rework, terms revised, and records remapped by the merge.
Take two record sets with overlapping entities — at least fifty thousand rows carrying real name and address noise.
Block on something cheap so you are not comparing every pair, and record what blocking makes unreachable.
Hand-label a set of matching and non-matching pairs, including the hard near-misses. Everything downstream is guesswork without it.
Score the match rule against that set and tune the threshold to the precision the downstream merge can tolerate.
Force a wrong merge, follow what it costs downstream, and set the threshold from that cost.
Measure: pairs surviving blocking, precision and recall against the labelled set, and true matches lost to blocking.
Collect or take a dataset with several distinct capture sessions — different days, lighting or devices — of at least five thousand images.
Hold out a whole session rather than a random split, so the test set is genuinely unseen.
Report mean average precision broken down by object size, not one headline figure. Small objects carry the failure and the average buries them.
Fix the IoU threshold you report at, then report the same number at a stricter one.
Run on the held-out session and list the conditions it fails in — glare, occlusion, distance — with example frames.
Measure: mAP by object size and by IoU threshold, per-session scores, and failure counts by condition.
Take a segmentation dataset with per-pixel masks and recorded capture conditions — at least a thousand annotated images.
Split the held-out set by capture condition rather than at random.
Report intersection-over-union per class, never averaged. One unusable class disappears completely into a healthy mean.
Overlay predictions on the worst frames and look at the boundaries, which is where the aggregate score lies most.
Halve the worst class's training data and show its per-class IoU move while the mean barely does.
Measure: IoU per class and per condition, the mean beside them, and boundary error on the worst frames.
Print a calibration target on rigid board and capture at least thirty images at several distances and angles.
Run the calibration and report reprojection error per image, not just the overall figure.
Discard the captures inflating the error — blurred, too oblique, target not flat — and recalibrate. Keeping every image because you took it is the usual mistake.
Undistort, then measure a known object at a known distance to check the calibration against reality.
Move that object to the edge of the frame, where distortion is worst, and measure again.
Measure: reprojection error per image and overall, images discarded, and measured against true length at centre and edge.
Write the labelling guide first, with an example and a counter-example per class, for a set of at least two thousand images.
Build a gold set every annotator must pass before their work counts towards the dataset.
Double-label a sample and measure inter-annotator agreement. Low agreement caps model accuracy and no amount of training fixes it.
Send every disagreement back to sharpen the guide rather than adjudicating it quietly.
Slip known-bad labels into the stream and check the gold-set process catches the annotators who accept them.
Measure: inter-annotator agreement per class, images per annotator-hour, gold-set pass rate, and labels revised after guide changes.
Take a labelled text dataset with at least twenty thousand documents and more than two classes.
Build both baselines first — majority class and a keyword rule — and record what each scores.
Train the model and report per-class precision and recall on a held-out set, never one accuracy figure.
Read at least a hundred errors by hand and sort them into a written taxonomy. That is what tells you whether it is a data or a label problem.
Relabel the class your taxonomy says is defined badly, retrain, and see whether the confusion moves.
Measure: per-class precision and recall against both baselines, errors by taxonomy category, and the change after relabelling.
Take an annotated NER corpus with character offsets — at least five thousand sentences across several entity types.
Score on exact span match, not token overlap. Overlap scoring flatters every model and hides the boundary errors.
Build a second held-out set from a source the training data never included — a different domain or a different period.
Report per-type precision and recall on both sets, not one combined number.
Score the same predictions under token overlap too, and show how far the number drops when you tighten it.
Measure: exact-span F1 per entity type on both held-out sets, and the gap between overlap and exact scoring.
Take a multilingual corpus including a morphologically rich language — Finnish, Turkish or Tamil — of at least a hundred thousand sentences.
Train at least three schemes: word-level, BPE and a unigram model, at two vocabulary sizes each.
Measure out-of-vocabulary rate and resulting sequence length per language, never averaged across the corpus.
Run the same downstream task under each scheme, because sequence length costs compute and context that OOV rate alone never shows.
Set the vocabulary deliberately too small and show what it does to the richest language's sequence length.
Measure: OOV rate and median sequence length per language and scheme, plus downstream score for each.
Take a task dataset of at least five thousand examples and freeze an evaluation set before touching a single hyperparameter.
Score the same model merely prompted, with a few examples, and write the number down. Fine-tuning cannot be justified without that baseline.
Fine-tune, tuning only against a validation split that is not the frozen set.
Evaluate the prompted baseline and the fine-tuned model on the frozen set, under identical scoring.
Build a small set of examples written after the base model's training data ends, and score both there too.
Measure: prompted and fine-tuned scores on the frozen set and the post-cutoff set, plus training cost.
Take a real surface with traffic — a site, an app, a mailing list of a few thousand people — and one change worth testing.
Write the primary metric, the guardrail metrics, the minimum detectable effect and the stopping rule before launch.
Run an A/A test first: both arms identical, which should find nothing. Skipping it ships an assignment bug as a result.
Check balance across the arms on the variables you did not randomise on.
If the A/A comes back significant, stop and find the bug rather than explaining it away.
Measure: assignment counts per arm, the A/A result with its interval, the minimum detectable effect, and the sample required.
Run a live test on the surface you built, with at least a few thousand units per arm.
Randomise at the unit that stops treatment leaking between arms — user or session, not request.
Analyse once, at the pre-declared sample size. Peeking daily until it turns significant is the commonest way these get called wrong.
Report the confidence interval and the guardrail movements beside the headline result.
Re-analyse the same data as though you had peeked daily, and count how often you would have stopped early.
Measure: units per arm, effect estimate with interval, guardrail deltas, and the peeking simulation's false-stop rate.
Take an offline model with a measured score and put it behind a live decision — a ranking, a routing choice or a threshold.
Share one piece of feature code between training and serving. Two implementations always diverge and nobody notices for months.
Log every prediction with its inputs and its decision, so an offline replay can be run afterwards.
Compare the offline replay against the live outcome and account for the gap part by part, not as one number.
Point serving at a copied version of the feature code and show where its outputs start to differ.
Measure: offline score, live outcome, the gap between them, and rows where training and serving features disagree.
Take logged decisions from a policy that recorded its action probabilities — at least a hundred thousand rows.
Build the naive replay first, and note what it assumes about actions the logging policy rarely took.
Estimate with inverse propensity weighting instead, clipping the weights and saying where you clipped and why.
Check the effective sample size after weighting. A handful of huge weights carrying the estimate is the failure people report as a number anyway.
Compare your offline estimate to the online result of an experiment already run, and report where they disagree.
Measure: effective sample size, the estimate with its interval under two clipping levels, and the gap to the online result.
Find three people who make a recurring decision from data — a weekly stock call, a spend review — and write down the decision, not the data.
Write the question each panel answers as one sentence, then drop every column that does not change one of those three decisions.
Build it over the real warehouse table, at least 100,000 rows, with a comparison period on every figure so a number means something.
Sit five people who have never seen it in front of it and say nothing. This is the part everybody skips and it is the whole project.
Record every hesitation and every question they asked out loud, cut or relabel what caused it, then test again with new people.
Measure: time to the right answer per participant, how many reached a wrong answer, and panels cut after testing.
Collect the same metric as five different teams report it — pull their actual spreadsheets and queries, not their descriptions of them.
Write one specification per metric giving the exact filter, grain, time zone, owner, and the SQL that produces it.
Run every version side by side over the same period and diff the numbers figure by figure.
Chase each difference to its cause — a filter, a late join, a different day boundary — instead of picking the number you prefer.
Take the disagreements to the owners and get one definition signed off in writing, including the cases where you were wrong.
Measure: metrics defined, the widest gap between versions, and how many definitions an owner rejected or changed.
Take a warehouse with at least ten reports written straight against raw tables, and read every one of their queries first.
Define the shared dimensions, joins and metrics once in a semantic layer — dbt metrics, LookML, Cube, whatever the warehouse takes.
Rebuild each report against the layer and diff every figure against what the old query produced, row by row.
Do not round a mismatch away. Each one is either a bug in your layer or a bug the old report already had. Say which.
Add a test on every certified metric, then break a join on purpose and confirm the build fails before a wrong figure reaches anyone.
Measure: reports rebuilt, figures that disagreed and why, and query time against the layer versus the raw tables.
Take a report somebody builds by hand every week and time how long it takes them and what they check.
Script the whole build — extract, transform, render, publish — so it runs on a schedule with no keyboard involved.
Add the checks that run before the send: source freshness, row count inside an expected band, no nulls in a key column.
Make a failed check hold the send and tell the owner. Most automated reports publish stale numbers silently, which is worse than not sending.
Withhold one source on purpose and confirm nothing was published and the owner was told exactly what was missing.
Measure: manual minutes replaced, checks that fired over a month, and how many sends were held back.
Implement Black–Scholes for European calls and puts with the analytic Greeks first, and keep it as the reference implementation.
Build a binomial tree that prices the same instruments, with the step count as a parameter you can sweep.
Price a grid of at least 500 cases — spot, strike, volatility, maturity — through both and record the difference on each.
State a tolerance and hold to it. A tree that agrees at the money and drifts deep in the money has a bug, not rounding.
Take the Greeks off the tree by finite difference and compare with the analytic ones; the bump size is where this usually breaks.
Measure: maximum and mean pricing error against closed form, steps needed to hit tolerance, and Greek error by bump size.
Take at least five years of daily returns for a portfolio you can define — a handful of liquid tickers is enough.
Produce a one-day loss estimate at 99% confidence for every day from a rolling window, using historical simulation first.
Add a second method — parametric or filtered historical — over the identical window so you have something to compare against.
Count the days the realised loss exceeded the estimate. Everybody builds the model; almost nobody counts the breaches afterwards.
Run Kupiec and Christoffersen tests on the exception count and its clustering, and say plainly which method failed.
Measure: exceptions expected versus observed per method, the test statistics, and whether the breaches arrived in clusters.
Get price data that includes delisted names. A survivorship-biased set flatters anything you build and is not worth testing on.
Split the history into walk-forward folds: fit on one window, trade the next, roll forward, never look ahead.
Write the execution model — spread, slippage, commission, financing on shorts — before you have seen a single return.
Charge those costs on every fill. A signal that survives frictionless testing and dies under real spread is the usual outcome.
Run the identical pipeline over a shuffled or random signal and confirm it earns nothing. If it earns something, your harness leaks.
Measure: return, drawdown and turnover per fold against buy-and-hold, and the cost per trade you assumed.
Price a European option by simulation where the closed-form answer is already known, so convergence has something to converge to.
Report the standard error beside every estimate and plot it against path count on a log scale.
Add antithetic variates, then a control variate, and re-run on the same seeds so the comparison is fair.
Fix and record the seed. An unseeded run cannot be reproduced, and a result nobody can reproduce is not a result.
Push it to a path-dependent payoff with no closed form and show the estimate sits inside the error bars of a much longer run.
Measure: standard error at each path count per variance-reduction method, paths needed for a stated error, and run time for each.
Pick a corpus you know well — a documentation set, a codebase — of at least 5,000 documents, so you can spot a plausible wrong answer.
Write 100 questions with their expected answers and the source document for each, by hand, before building anything. This is the part everybody skips and it is the whole project.
Build chunking and retrieval, score hit rate, then add a re-ranking pass and re-score. One change at a time.
Set a retrieval-score threshold below which the service refuses to answer, tuned on questions the corpus genuinely cannot answer.
Ask it twenty unanswerable questions and confirm it refuses rather than inventing, then wire the whole set as a build gate.
Measure: retrieval hit rate, grounded-answer rate, refusal rate on unanswerable questions, and p95 latency.
Pick a task that genuinely needs several steps — reconciling two systems, triaging a queue — not one call dressed up as an agent.
Give the loop a hard step budget, a per-step timeout and a total wall-clock cap, and decide what the user sees at each limit.
Write every step to durable state before executing it: input, tool, arguments, result. State recorded afterwards cannot be resumed.
Trace the whole run so a wrong final answer can be walked back to the step that caused it, not guessed at from logs.
Kill the process mid-run at three different steps and restart it. It must resume from where it stopped, not begin again.
Measure: steps per task, resumed runs whose output matched an uninterrupted run, and how often the budget was hit.
Embed a corpus of at least 500,000 chunks, so the index is large enough that the approximate structure actually matters.
Hash the source of every record and re-embed only what changed, so a daily run costs minutes rather than the whole corpus.
Build the index behind an alias so a rebuild can be swapped in and the old one dropped afterwards.
Run exact nearest-neighbour search over the same set on a sample of queries. Without it you have no idea what your recall is.
Rebuild and swap while a load generator queries the alias, and confirm no request failed or came back empty.
Measure: recall@10 against exact search, query p95, index build time, and records re-embedded per run.
Expose four tools over something with real consequences — a database, a ticket system — so validating arguments actually matters.
Declare a typed schema per tool and validate the model's arguments against it before anything is allowed to execute.
On a malformed call, return the validation error to the model and re-prompt, within a bounded number of attempts.
Validate the values, not only the types. A well-formed call carrying an out-of-range id is the one that does the damage.
Inject timeouts and errors into every tool in turn and confirm the loop degrades and reports rather than hanging.
Measure: malformed-call rate per model, calls repaired inside the retry budget, and behaviour at each injected failure.
Pick a task with a checkable right answer — extraction, classification, structured rewriting — over at least 200 real inputs.
Split the inputs into a tuning set and a held-out set, and do not look at the held-out set while writing the prompt.
Write the prompt as numbered, separable instructions, so a line can be removed without breaking the sentence around it.
Remove one instruction at a time and re-score. Most prompts are half superstition, and nobody checks which half.
Keep only the lines whose removal actually cost accuracy, then score the stripped prompt once on the held-out set.
Measure: accuracy per ablation, instructions kept versus written, and token count before and after.
Freeze a set of at least 150 inputs with expected answers and version it, so scores stay comparable across changes.
Write the grading rubric down before grading anything, with the borderline cases decided in advance rather than case by case.
Grade the whole set with the rubric — exact matching where the answer is exact, a model grader where it is not.
Have a second grader, a person or a different model, grade a sample and compute agreement. An ungraded grader is not evidence.
Feed the harness a deliberately worse prompt and confirm the score drops. A harness that never fails anything is measuring nothing.
Measure: score per prompt version, grader agreement rate, and cost and latency of one full run.
Take a step whose output feeds real code — a row written to a database — and collect at least 500 real inputs for it.
Declare the JSON schema, validate every response against it, and pass nothing downstream that fails validation.
Add a bounded repair loop: return the validation error to the model, retry a fixed number of times, then give up loudly.
Log every rejection with the raw output. The failure shapes are what tell you which part of your schema is unreasonable.
Add semantic checks the schema cannot express, then run the same inputs through two models and compare parse-failure rates.
Measure: parse-failure rate per model, repairs that succeeded inside the retry budget, and rejections that were valid JSON but wrong.
Take an assistant with at least three rules worth breaking — a refusal, a data boundary, a tool it must not call unattended.
Build a catalogue of at least 60 attacks from published techniques: direct injection, role play, encoding, and content hidden in retrieved documents.
Write a pass or fail check per attack that looks at the behaviour, so a polite compliance still counts as a failure.
Include indirect injection through the corpus. Everybody tests the chat box and forgets that retrieved text is also input.
Run the suite on every prompt change and record which attacks still get through, rather than reporting a clean pass.
Measure: attacks in the catalogue, the number still succeeding, and the false-refusal rate on benign inputs.
Get the business questions the model must answer, agreed and written down before you draw anything. Twenty of them is enough.
Draw the conceptual model — entities and relationships only — and walk it past the people who asked those questions.
Write the grain of every table as a sentence: one row is one what. A table with no stated grain ends up with two.
Take it down to physical tables with keys, cardinality and types, and load it at realistic volume rather than ten rows.
Answer all twenty questions in SQL against the loaded model, and record every one that needed a schema change to answer.
Measure: questions answerable without changing the model, tables and grains defined, and rows loaded per table.
Inventory every table in one real schema — at least fifty — and record who currently reads and writes each of them.
Assign an owner, a classification and a retention rule to every table, and have the owner confirm theirs in writing.
Wire the classification into access grants, so a restricted table is unreadable by default rather than by convention.
Write the job that flags any new table arriving without an owner or a classification. Governance nobody enforces is a document.
Create an unclassified table and a retention-breaching row on purpose, and confirm both are flagged before you tell anyone.
Measure: tables classified, grants changed, unowned tables caught per week, and rows the retention job removes.
Take one real domain with named sources, volumes and consumers, and write down what it must do before drawing anything.
Draw ingestion, storage, serving and access as they would actually be built, with technologies named rather than a box labelled ETL.
Write one decision record per choice: the alternative it beat, why it beat it, and what it costs.
Name the condition that would reverse each decision. An architecture with no stated way to be wrong is a preference with diagrams.
Review it with the engineers who would have to build it and record every objection, including the ones you did not accept.
Measure: decisions recorded against a named alternative, objections raised in review, and how many changed the design.
Take two systems holding the same entities — customers, suppliers — with at least 100,000 records between them and no shared key.
Match deterministically first on the identifiers that do exist, and record the proportion that matches with no fuzzy logic at all.
Apply fuzzy matching only to the remainder, with a threshold you can defend and the method recorded on every match.
Hand-label a sample of 300 pairs as match or not, and score your matcher against it. Without labels you are guessing.
Write the survivorship rule per field, then route everything between the auto-accept and auto-reject thresholds to a stewardship queue.
Measure: precision and recall against the labelled sample, records merged, and the size of the review queue per run.
Take a nightly load that moves at least a million rows from a source system into a warehouse table.
Break it into discrete steps — extract, land, transform, validate, commit — each writing to staging and recording its own completion.
Make the commit atomic: a swap or a transaction, never a truncate-then-insert that leaves an empty table if it dies.
Make each step idempotent, so re-running a completed step changes nothing. That property is what makes a restart safe.
Kill the job at every stage in turn and re-run it. It must restart from the failed step and land identical rows.
Measure: rows loaded, run time per step, and the row count after each kill-and-restart against a clean run.
Take a load with at least sixty columns across its tables and write the transformation, type and null rule for every one.
Keep the mapping in the repository beside the code, not in a spreadsheet somebody emails when asked.
Generate a test from each row of the mapping — type, nullability, range, allowed values — that runs against the loaded data.
Test for source columns the mapping does not mention. A new column that silently goes nowhere is the usual failure.
Add an unmapped column to the source and change one column's type, and confirm the build fails on both.
Measure: columns mapped and tested, tests failing on a deliberate schema change, and mapping run time in CI.
Take at least eight jobs feeding one report and draw what actually depends on what, rather than what time each runs.
Express it as a dependency graph in a scheduler, so a job starts when its inputs land, not at half past two.
Give every job a timeout and a retry policy, and decide job by job whether a retry is safe.
Set the alarm on the report's delivery deadline, not on each job finishing. Nobody is paged by a job that never started.
Hold an upstream job back by two hours and confirm the deadline alarm fires and the catch-up run fills the missed window.
Measure: critical-path length, slack before the deadline, and detection time when an upstream job runs late.
Take a full reload of a table with at least ten million rows and time what that reload currently costs.
Pick the watermark column and prove it is monotonic and always populated. A nullable updated_at loses you rows quietly.
Load incrementally on the watermark, matching updates to existing rows by key rather than appending a second copy.
Overlap the watermark window deliberately and deduplicate, because a record written during your last run is otherwise missed forever.
Run the full reload alongside the incremental for a week, comparing row counts and column sums until they agree.
Measure: run time and rows read, full versus incremental, and any rows the reconciliation found missing.
Model a domain where order matters — a per-account ledger — and produce at least 50,000 events a minute into it.
Choose the partition key for the ordering you need, and write down what ordering you bought and what you gave up.
Set replication factor, minimum in-sync replicas and producer acknowledgements deliberately, and state what each setting costs you.
Check the key distribution against real data. A key that gives you ordering usually gives you a hot partition too.
Kill a broker under load and confirm producers kept writing, no partition lost its order, and nothing acknowledged was lost.
Measure: throughput, per-partition skew, producer latency during the broker kill, and ordering violations found.
Take a stream of at least ten million events and a reference table that changes while the stream is running.
Hold the reference data in local state and join each event against the version current when that event happened.
Checkpoint state to durable storage on an interval you have chosen and can justify against the cost of a replay.
Bound the state. A job that keeps every key forever runs fine for a week and then dies at three in the morning.
Kill the job mid-stream and restart it, then diff the output against an uninterrupted run over the same input.
Measure: state size over time, checkpoint duration, recovery time, and rows differing after the restart.
Build a path ending in a sink you can count — a ledger table — over at least a million events, so the claim is checkable.
Use a transactional producer, and commit consumer offsets inside the same transaction as the writes to that sink.
Give every event an id the sink is unique on, so a replay collides rather than inserting a second row.
Name where the guarantee stops. Every path has a segment that is really at-least-once, and pretending otherwise is the error.
Inject duplicates and restart consumers mid-run, then reconcile input event ids against sink rows and account for every one.
Measure: events in and rows out, duplicates in the sink (it must be zero), and the throughput cost of the transactional path.
Take a stream with real timestamp skew — events from clients, not from one server — and at least a day of history.
Aggregate on event time with watermarks, and write down the allowed lateness and why you chose that number.
Route events arriving beyond the allowance to a side output. Never drop a late event silently.
Compute the same aggregates in batch over the same input, so the streaming totals have something to be wrong against.
Replay the stream deliberately out of order and an hour late, then diff every window against the batch result.
Measure: windows differing from batch, events sent to the side output, and watermark lag under the replay.
Take a repository with a real service and at least two environments it deploys to today.
Build one immutable artefact on merge, tagged with the commit, and promote that same artefact everywhere. Never rebuild per environment.
Put tests, a dependency scan and an image scan in the path, with a manual gate only where a human decision is genuinely required.
Keep configuration out of the artefact and inject it per environment, or you have rebuilt per environment with extra steps.
Break a test and a scan on purpose, confirm neither artefact reached an environment, then trace a running container back to its commit.
Measure: merge-to-production time, duration per stage, pipeline failure rate, and merges that reached production untouched.
Define one whole environment in Terraform — network, compute, database, DNS — rather than a single bucket.
Put state in a remote backend with locking, and make the plan output part of the pull request review.
Split it into modules with variables per environment, so staging and production differ by values rather than by copies.
Run a scheduled plan that fails when the live estate has drifted. Without it the code is a description, not a definition.
Change something in the console by hand, watch the drift job catch it, then destroy the environment and rebuild from code alone.
Measure: resources managed, full rebuild time from an empty account, and drift events found per week.
Take a service released by hand today and write down every step somebody performs, including the ones they do from memory.
Derive the version and the release notes from the commit history, so the changelog cannot drift from what actually shipped.
Sign the tag and record the artefact digest against it, so a release names exactly one binary.
Make rollback a first-class command that redeploys a version, not a scramble to revert commits and rebuild under pressure.
Roll a real release back on purpose and confirm the old code came back, then repeat it with a migration in the release.
Measure: release time end to end, rollback time, and manual steps removed.
Take three hosts doing different jobs and write the configuration for all of them as Ansible roles.
Write each role to be idempotent: a second run must report no changes at all, and that is the test.
Schedule a check-mode run that reports drift instead of silently correcting it, so somebody actually sees what changed.
Cover the things people leave out of roles — users, sudoers, cron, log rotation — because those are what drift first.
Hand-edit a managed file and stop a managed service, and confirm the drift report names both before the next apply.
Measure: changes reported on the second run (it must be zero), drift found per week, and time to configure a fresh host.
Take a service with at least a month of real request logs and list what a user actually notices when it is unwell.
Pick two or three indicators from that list — success rate, latency at a percentile — and define good and bad precisely.
Compute each indicator over the past month before naming a target. A number chosen first is a wish, not an objective.
Choose the measurement window and whether it rolls, and agree both with the people who will be paged on them.
Replay a past bad day through the definition and confirm it registers as bad, then replay a good day and confirm it does not.
Measure: each indicator's historical value, the target chosen, and how much budget the past month would have spent.
Start from objectives that already exist and compute the budget they imply over a 28-day window in absolute terms — failed requests, not percentages.
Build fast and slow burn-rate alerts, each with its own window and threshold, pointed at a real paging policy.
Put budget remaining on the dashboard instead of uptime, because uptime never tells anybody to stop shipping.
Write down what stops when the budget runs out, and get the person who would have to stop to agree beforehand.
Replay a past bad day through the alerting and check the fast alert fired within minutes and the slow one did not flap.
Measure: budget spent per week, alert lead time on the replay, and false pages over a month.
Take a staging environment close enough to production to teach you something, and three people willing to respond to a drill.
Write the severity levels, the incident lead's job and the communications channel before anything is broken.
Break something real without telling the responders what it was, and start the clock the moment you break it.
Time detection, diagnosis and mitigation as three separate numbers. One end-to-end figure hides which part is actually slow.
Fix the slowest of the three, run a second drill, and confirm that number moved rather than the total moving by luck.
Measure: detection, diagnosis and mitigation times per drill, and action items closed between the two runs.
Pick a service with at least two dependencies and one metric that tells you whether users are being served.
Write the hypothesis for each experiment before running it: what should happen, and how you will know it did.
Agree the blast radius and write an abort condition the harness enforces automatically, not one you sit and watch for.
Run the experiments during real traffic. A failure injected into an idle system is a rehearsal, not an experiment.
Kill an instance, fill a disk and add latency to a dependency in turn, and record where the hypothesis was wrong.
Measure: error rate and recovery time per experiment, hypotheses falsified, and the abort condition firing when it should.
Pick one workload with a database and real users, and write the rollback plan before you write the migration plan.
Copy the data, then verify it: row counts, a checksum per table, and a sample compared field by field.
Run both sides in parallel against the same inputs and diff the outputs until they stop disagreeing.
Keep DNS TTLs low and the old environment warm. A cutover you cannot reverse in minutes is a launch, not a migration.
Cut over a slice of traffic, break the new side on purpose, and reverse it by DNS while timing how long users saw errors.
Measure: divergences found in the parallel run, cutover and rollback times, and cost per month on each side.
Build an organisation with a separate account per environment plus a shared network account and a shared logging account.
Apply guardrails at the organisation root: required encryption, centralised logging, allowed regions, no root access keys.
Centralise the network and the log destination so a workload account cannot switch either of them off.
Vend accounts from code rather than the console, so the guardrails are already on before anybody can log in.
Create a fresh account and try to break each guardrail — unencrypted storage, a forbidden region, deleting a trail — and confirm each is refused.
Measure: guardrails enforced, time to vend a compliant account, and violations caught in the first week.
Take a workload with wildcards in its policies and pull ninety days of access logs for every principal it uses.
Build the candidate role from the actions actually called, grouped by principal rather than by service.
Ask why an unused permission is unused before deleting it. Quarterly and yearly jobs do not appear in ninety days of logs.
Replace static keys with short-lived credentials from a role, and delete the keys rather than leaving them inactive.
Write assertions that the removed actions are denied, run them in CI, and confirm the workload still works under the new role.
Measure: permissions before and after, static keys removed, denied-action assertions passing, and access-denied errors after the switch.
Pull a month of billing data at resource granularity and find how much of it you cannot attribute to any workload.
Enforce tagging so new untagged resources are rejected, then backfill the existing ones with their owners.
Define cost per unit of work — per order, per thousand requests — because total spend falls when usage falls, which proves nothing.
Right-size from observed utilisation, add storage lifecycle rules, and shut idle non-production down on a schedule.
Turn the schedule on and see what breaks. The nightly job somebody runs in staging is how you find the real dependencies.
Measure: unattributed spend before and after, saving per change, and cost per unit of work either side.
Take an estate with at least fifteen running services and list what nobody can answer today: who owns this, what does it call.
Generate the catalogue from the running infrastructure — cluster, registry, deployment metadata — rather than from a form somebody fills in.
Require ownership at deploy time, so a service without an owner cannot ship rather than appearing unowned in a list.
Derive dependencies from real traffic or traces. A hand-drawn dependency list is wrong again within a fortnight.
Delete a service and deploy a new one, and confirm the catalogue reflects both within one run with nobody editing anything.
Measure: services registered automatically, unowned services found, and catalogue staleness after a change.
Time somebody standing up a new service the current way, and write down every step and every person they had to ask.
Build a template that goes from an empty repository to a deployed URL with CI, logging, metrics and an on-call route already wired.
Make the generated service boring and current — the same libraries and base image, updatable centrally afterwards.
Write down what the path deliberately does not cover and how somebody leaves it. The unhandled exception is what kills adoption.
Sit a developer who has never seen it in front of it, say nothing, and time them to a deployed URL.
Measure: time to first deploy before and after, steps still needing a human, and services created on the path versus off it.
Find the three things teams raise the most tickets for — a database, a queue, an environment — and count the tickets and the waiting.
Define each as a declarative request in a repository, so asking for one is a pull request rather than a form.
Validate the request against limits — size, region, cost band — and apply it automatically once it passes.
Put a cost and blast-radius check in the path with a human gate above a threshold, since below it nobody is looking.
Submit a request that is too large, one that is malformed and one that clashes with an existing name, and confirm all three are refused cleanly.
Measure: tickets replaced, time from request to working resource, requests rejected by validation, and cost of what was provisioned.
Pick six rules that matter — resource limits, no floating image tags, non-root, required labels — and write them as executable policy.
Run them against everything already deployed, so you know what would break before anything is blocked.
Ship in warn mode and leave it there until violations are near zero. Enforcing on day one just gets the policy switched off.
Build the exemption path: recorded, owned and expiring, so a bypass stays visible instead of becoming a permanent hole.
Turn enforcement on, deploy a violating manifest, and confirm it is rejected with a message that says how to fix it.
Measure: violations at warn time and at enforcement, exemptions open and expired, and admission latency added.
Take two machines, virtual is fine, and get network boot working so an install starts with no keyboard attached.
Write the unattended install answer file, then hand off to configuration management for packages, users, monitoring and logging.
Keep every step in the repository, including partitioning and network configuration, so nothing lives only in somebody's memory.
Handle the secrets properly. A host key or a join token baked into the image is how an unattended build leaks.
Wipe one host and rebuild it, then diff the two machines on package lists, running services and configuration file hashes.
Measure: build time from power-on to monitored, manual steps remaining, and differences found in the diff.
Build a redundant pool over at least four disks, real or virtual, and fill it to a realistic level with real data.
Schedule snapshots with a retention policy, and scrubbing often enough to find rot before a rebuild needs that data.
Monitor capacity growth and alert on the trend, not on a fixed threshold you will cross at the weekend.
Restore from a snapshot onto somewhere else. A snapshot nobody has restored is a belief about your storage, not a backup.
Pull a disk from the running array, time the rebuild, and confirm reads stayed correct throughout it.
Measure: rebuild time, throughput during rebuild, scrub errors found, and days of headroom at the current growth rate.
Stand up two hypervisor hosts with shared storage and run at least six guests doing real work across them.
Set CPU and memory limits per guest, and write down the overcommit ratio you have chosen and why.
Add affinity and anti-affinity rules so the two halves of a redundant pair cannot land on the same host.
Test what happens when the guests actually claim their memory. Overcommit works right up until everyone wants what they were promised.
Live-migrate a running guest under load, then drain a whole host for patching and confirm nothing on it stopped.
Measure: migration time and connections dropped, overcommit ratio, and host utilisation during the drain.
Take a stock host running a real service and scan it against a published benchmark before changing anything. That scan is your baseline.
Cut packages and services down to what the application needs, confirming it still works after each cut.
Enforce access control properly — no shared accounts, keys not passwords, sudo rules recorded — and ship logs off the box.
Write the justification for every control you deliberately skip. An unexplained exception is indistinguishable from an oversight.
Re-scan, then break one control on purpose and confirm both the scan and the central log notice it.
Measure: benchmark score before and after, controls waived with a reason, packages removed, and the application's tests still passing.
Build a lab with at least six routers in containerlab or GNS3, with two paths between every pair that matters.
Run OSPF inside with deliberate areas and summarisation, and BGP at the edge to two upstream providers.
Write the filters that stop you advertising one upstream to the other. Becoming a transit by accident is the classic mistake.
Push traffic across the network continuously, so an outage is something you can see rather than something you infer afterwards.
Cut the primary link and measure how long traffic actually stopped, then tune the timers and cut it again.
Measure: convergence time per failure, packets lost during it, and routes in the table before and after summarisation.
Take at least four switches, lab or virtual, and pull every running configuration into a repository as the starting point.
Template the parts that differ per device, so a change is a variable edit reviewed as a pull request.
Push by script, with a pre-change and post-change reachability check wrapped around every apply.
Add commit-confirm or a scheduled rollback so a device that goes unreachable reverts itself. That is what saves the site visit.
Push a change that deliberately locks you out, and confirm the device rolled back on its own without help.
Measure: devices under version control, push and rollback times, and configuration drift found against the repository.
Take a flat network with at least five kinds of device on it — servers, workstations, printers, cameras, management.
Split it into VLANs by function and force all inter-VLAN traffic through one filtering hop.
Write the reachability matrix first: every pair, must reach or must not reach, with the reason recorded.
Test the must-not cells as well as the must cells. Everybody proves the allowed paths work and assumes the rest are blocked.
Put a host on the wrong VLAN, try to reach management from it, and confirm the filter refuses.
Measure: cells in the matrix, cells tested, failures found on the must-not side, and throughput cost of the filtering hop.
Find or create a real loss — a slow transfer over a link you can degrade — and capture at both ends and the hop between.
Filter to one conversation and read it end to end: handshake, window sizes, retransmissions, duplicate acknowledgements, timings.
Compare the same packets at each capture point. One capture tells you there is loss; three tell you where it is.
Write the diagnosis as a claim: this interface dropped these packets at this time, and here is the evidence for it.
Fix that interface, capture again under the identical load, and confirm the retransmissions are gone.
Measure: retransmission rate before and after, round-trip time and window size, and throughput on the same transfer.
Take one real site with a known device count and traffic profile, and write the requirements down before drawing anything.
Draw every layer with addressing, redundancy and oversubscription stated as numbers, not as the word redundant on a label.
List every single point of failure. A pair drawn twice but cabled into one chassis is still one box.
Write the failure behaviour per case: what stays up, what degrades, what stops, and for how long.
Review it with the engineers who would have to run it, and record every failure case they say you got wrong.
Measure: oversubscription per layer, single points of failure listed and removed, and objections raised in review.
Collect at least three months of per-link utilisation at five-minute granularity, so busy hour is a measurement rather than a guess.
Model on busy-hour peaks, not daily averages. An average hides the twenty minutes a day that actually hurt.
State the growth assumptions explicitly — users, traffic per user, new services — with a source behind each one.
Project each link forward and name the one that runs out first, and the date it does.
Re-run the model with the growth assumption halved and doubled, and record how far the answer moves.
Measure: busy-hour utilisation per link, months of headroom, and the sensitivity of that date to each assumption.
Take at least four sites, measure what each actually sends and receives, and compare it with what each site asked for.
Design dual-provider connectivity per site with path selection by application class, and write the failover behaviour for each.
Ask both providers for the physical path, not the logical one. Two contracts down one duct is one link with two invoices.
Cost each site against measured bandwidth with stated headroom, and record what you would drop under a failure.
Take one provider out at a low-traffic site during the day, and record what failed over, how long it took and what degraded.
Measure: measured versus contracted bandwidth per site, failover time, and cost per site before and after.
Write at least ten requirements and their weightings before contacting any vendor, and get them signed off.
Shortlist to two on paper, then pick the two claims that would actually decide it — the ones a datasheet cannot settle.
Test those two claims in a lab on your own traffic. A datasheet number was measured on the vendor's bench, not yours.
Score against the written weightings rather than against the demo, and include operational cost and support in the score.
Record what the losing option was better at, and the condition under which you would have chosen it instead.
Measure: lab results against the claimed figures, scores per requirement, and total cost over the expected life.
Take a database of at least 100GB under real write traffic, and write down the recovery time and recovery point objectives first.
Set up full backups, incrementals and continuous archiving of the write-ahead log, all shipped off the machine.
Restore to a fresh host, never to the original. A restore that reuses anything already on the server proves nothing.
Restore to a chosen point in time and check the restored data against the source rather than checking the exit code.
Drop a table on purpose, recover to the second before it, and time each phase of the restore separately.
Measure: restore time against the objective, data lost at the recovery point, and backup size and duration per type.
Turn on statement logging on a database at realistic volume and collect the ten slowest queries by total time, not by single run.
Read the execution plan for each and find where the estimated row count and the actual row count disagree.
Fix the cause — a stale statistic, a non-sargable predicate, a bad estimate — rather than pinning the plan with a hint.
Change one thing at a time, and keep the plan and the timing from before and after every change.
Re-run at production volume with a cold cache, because a query that is fast on a warm buffer pool is not fixed.
Measure: time and rows read per query before and after, and the share of total database time the top ten accounted for.
Pull index usage statistics from a database that has been serving real traffic for at least a month.
List the indexes nothing has read, plus the duplicates and prefixes another index already covers.
Measure the write cost before adding a covering index: time an insert and update batch with it and without it.
Drop the unused ones one at a time, and watch for the query that only runs at month end.
Re-run the read workload after each drop to confirm nothing regressed, then restore a dropped index to prove you can.
Measure: indexes dropped and their size on disk, read time on the target queries, and insert and update throughput per index added.
Replicate a database under continuous write traffic to a standby on another host. The traffic is what makes the lag real.
Monitor lag in both bytes and seconds and alert on it, because a standby nobody watches is not a standby.
Choose synchronous or asynchronous deliberately, and write down the data loss each choice permits.
Confirm the standby actually serves reads, rather than being silently broken behind a healthy-looking replication status.
Promote the standby under load in a rehearsal, time the failover, and count exactly which acknowledged writes were lost.
