Measure: replication lag under load, failover time, writes lost at promotion, and time to rebuild the old primary as a standby.
Take one real system you built with at least three trust boundaries — a browser, your API, a database, a third-party call — and draw the data-flow diagram.
Apply STRIDE at each boundary in turn, writing every abuse case as a sentence an attacker would say, not a category name.
Rank the abuse cases by what they would actually let someone do, not by how many you found. This ranking is the part everybody skips.
Turn each ranked abuse case into a failing test before you touch the code, so the fix has something to turn green.
Fix the top findings, watch the tests pass, then try one you chose not to fix and confirm it still fails on purpose.
Measure: findings per trust boundary, how many became tests, and how many are still open at the end.
Take a repository with real git history and pull its past security fixes — the commits that patched a vulnerability are your training set.
Write custom static-analysis rules that would have caught those bugs before they merged, not generic lint the scanner already ships.
Run each rule over the whole history and measure how often it fires wrongly. Tuning the false-positive rate is the part everybody skips.
Wire the rules into CI so a match blocks the merge instead of leaving a comment nobody reads.
Reintroduce one of the old vulnerable diffs on a branch and confirm the gate refuses it.
Measure: true and false positives per rule over the history, and merges blocked versus merges only commented.
Take one host or container image you run and score it against the matching CIS benchmark before changing anything.
Apply the controls as code — a script or Ansible run — and write down each exception with the reason it cannot be met.
Rebuild the host from that baseline on a clean machine to prove nothing was quietly fixed by hand. This rebuild is the part everybody skips.
Set up drift detection that re-scans on a schedule and alerts when a setting moves off the baseline.
Change one hardened setting by hand and confirm the drift alert fires.
Measure: benchmark score before and after, exceptions carried, and time from drift to alert.
Run three different scanners — code, dependencies and container image — over one real service and export everything they report.
Deduplicate the output into one record per real finding, because the same bug shows up three times with three names. This merge is the part everybody skips.
Give every record a named owner and a due date driven by severity, not by when the next scan runs.
Track time to fix against the policy clock and build the view that shows what is overdue.
Feed the scanners a knowingly vulnerable dependency and confirm it lands as one record, not three.
Measure: raw findings versus deduplicated findings, findings with an owner, and time to fix per severity band.
Pull a labelled set of at least 200 past alerts that a human already closed as true or false positive.
Write the triage decision tree as explicit steps, not instinct — what you check, in what order, and what each answer means.
Replay the labelled alerts through the tree and score each verdict against the analyst who originally closed it.
Read the disagreements one by one and rewrite the steps they exposed. Working the disagreements is the whole project, and the part everybody skips.
Add one alert the tree has never seen and confirm it reaches a verdict rather than falling through.
Measure: agreement with the human before and after the rewrite, and alerts the tree could not decide.
Take the noisiest handful of detections in a SIEM and count how many alerts each raised over a real week.
Rewrite them as version-controlled Sigma rules with every exclusion justified in a comment inside the rule itself.
For each exclusion, replay the technique it silences and confirm the real attack still fires. Proving it cut noise not coverage is the part everybody skips.
Run a simulated attack, such as Atomic Red Team, through the tuned rules end to end.
Add an exclusion that is deliberately too broad and confirm the replayed attack now slips past, so you see the failure mode.
Measure: alerts per rule per week before and after, and true positives that still fire after tuning.
Take one real service and write its escalation path — who is paged at each severity, and the criteria for each, agreed before any incident.
Run a simulated out-of-hours incident against the path with the people who would really be on call.
Time every handoff and note each point where the page reached somebody who could not act. Timing the handoffs is the part everybody skips.
Fix the steps the drill exposed and write down who is allowed to raise severity mid-incident.
Re-run the drill with the on-call person unreachable to prove the fallback actually leads somewhere.
Measure: time to reach someone who could act, handoffs per incident, and steps that dead-ended.
Collect authentication, endpoint and network logs from a set of hosts, real or from a public breach dataset with a known intrusion in it.
Normalise every clock to one time source first, because a wrong offset silently reorders the story. Fixing the clocks is the part everybody skips.
Correlate the three sources into a single per-host timeline keyed on host and account.
Replay the recorded intrusion through it and check the timeline shows the entry point without being told where to look.
Skew one host's clock by ten minutes and watch the timeline put events in the wrong order, so you see how much it matters.
Measure: hosts with disagreeing clocks, events correlated per host, and whether the entry point was found unaided.
Take a real telemetry source — endpoint or network logs over a meaningful window — and pick a technique you think might be present.
Write the hypothesis and the exact data it needs before you run a single query. Writing it first is the part everybody skips.
Run the hunt and record the outcome in a log, including the hunts that found nothing, because those are most of them.
Promote any hunt that found something into a scheduled detection so it runs without you.
Run one hunt you expect to fail and log it honestly rather than quietly dropping it.
Measure: hunts run, hunts that found something, and hunts promoted to detections.
Pull two or three real threat feeds into one store with a common schema for indicators.
Score each indicator by source reliability and age rather than treating every feed as equal.
Expire indicators automatically on a clock so the store does not fill with stale ones. The expiry is the part everybody skips, and it is why the pipeline stays useful.
Match the live indicators against your own telemetry and report how many would actually have fired.
Let a batch of indicators pass their expiry and confirm the detections relying on them go quiet rather than erroring.
Measure: indicators ingested, indicators matching own telemetry, and store size before and after expiry runs.
Build an isolated analysis lab — no route to your network or the internet — and load one real malware sample from a research corpus.
Recover its persistence and command-and-control configuration both statically and by detonating it in the lab.
Write a YARA rule from what you found.
Run the rule over a large corpus of clean files to see what it wrongly matches. Testing against clean files is the part everybody skips.
Give the sample a sandbox check to evade and confirm whether your lab is convincing enough that it still runs.
Measure: config recovered, false matches per thousand clean files, and whether the sample detected the lab.
List the detections protecting one real environment and map each to the ATT&CK technique its name claims to cover.
For every technique you claim, execute an atomic test that actually performs it.
Mark the map from what fired, not from what the rule was named. Testing the claim rather than trusting the name is the whole project.
Note every technique you believed was covered that produced no alert.
Run one technique you have no detection for to confirm the map shows a real gap and not a false green.
Measure: techniques claimed, techniques that fired under test, and the gap between the two.
Take one real system and a named control framework, and list the controls in scope.
For each control, collect the evidence an auditor could open unaided — a config, a log, an export — not the owner's word for it.
Mark each control from that evidence alone. Refusing to score from description is the part everybody skips.
Rank the gaps by what each would actually let happen, not by how many there are.
Take one control the owner swears is in place and check the evidence really shows it, expecting at least one to fail.
Measure: controls assessed, controls passing on evidence, and gaps ranked by impact.
Build a risk register for one real system with a defined scoring scale, a named owner and a review date on every entry.
Write down what each band of the likelihood and impact scale actually means, so two people score the same risk the same way.
Take a past incident and walk it backwards through the register to see whether the risk that caused it was ever listed.
If it was listed, find out why it was never treated. That backwards walk is the part everybody skips.
Add a risk whose owner has left and confirm the register flags it as unowned rather than hiding it.
Measure: entries with an owner and a review date, entries past their review date, and whether the incident's risk was present.
Pick a handful of controls over one real system whose evidence today is gathered by hand.
Write a job that pulls each artefact from its source system on a schedule.
Record the query, the timestamp and the operator beside every artefact, because evidence with no provenance is worthless to an auditor. Recording provenance is the part everybody skips.
Prove it by re-evidencing a sampled control from scratch without asking anybody.
Backdate a screenshot by hand and show why your scheduled evidence is trustworthy where the screenshot is not.
Measure: controls with automated evidence, collection runs completed, and time to re-evidence a sampled control.
Pull live entitlements from one real system, not last quarter's export, for every account it holds.
Route each entitlement to the manager who owns the person, not to a shared inbox.
Revoke anything not confirmed by the deadline rather than leaving it because nobody objected.
Re-read the entitlements afterwards to prove the revocation landed in the system, not only in the spreadsheet. Checking that it actually happened is the part everybody skips.
Plant an account nobody will claim and confirm the campaign forces a decision on it instead of skipping it.
Measure: entitlements reviewed, entitlements revoked, and revocations confirmed present on re-read.
Take one real organisation or unit and write its security governance model — who owns what, who decides what.
Assign every control to a named person rather than a team, because a team owns nothing.
Stand up a steering forum with a decision log and a monthly metric set.
Trace one real decision from the day it was raised to the day it closed to show the model carried it. Following a real decision end to end is the part everybody skips.
Run a case where the control owner disagrees with the security team and confirm the model says who wins.
Measure: controls with a named owner, decisions logged and closed, and the age of the oldest open decision.
Gather the risks currently accepted across one real system and put them in one register.
For each, name the person who accepted it in writing, state the compensating control, and set an expiry date.
Reopen every acceptance that has quietly passed its date and put it back in front of its owner. Reopening the expired ones is the part everybody skips.
Write the rule for who is senior enough to accept which level of risk.
Take an acceptance whose accepter has left and confirm the register forces it to be re-decided rather than inherited silently.
Measure: acceptances with a named owner and expiry, acceptances found past their date, and acceptances re-decided.
Take one real organisation's security needs and list the controls you would propose over a year.
Price each control against the risk it reduces, and price the do-nothing option beside it. Costing the do-nothing option is the part everybody skips.
Separate licence, headcount and run costs so the second year of the plan is visible before the first is signed off.
Rank the controls and decide which one to drop when the budget will not stretch.
Write the argument to the sponsor for the control you dropped, so the decision survives being questioned later.
Measure: controls priced, first-year versus second-year cost, and the risk reduction per pound of the marginal control.
Take the controls over one real system and the framework the external auditor will use.
Run a dry-run audit using the same sampling method the real auditor would, not a hand-picked easy set.
Record each finding with an owner and a due date in a log.
Re-test the closed findings rather than accepting a claim that they were fixed. Re-testing instead of trusting the tick is the part everybody skips.
Expect at least one finding to fail on re-test, and work out what that says about how it was closed.
Measure: findings raised, findings closed, and findings that failed re-test.
Stand up a lab replica of a real web application — a deliberately vulnerable app like Juice Shop is fine — and write the scope before you start.
Test methodically, and for every finding record the exact request that reproduces it, not a screenshot.
Score each finding with a full CVSS vector rather than a bare severity word, so the rating can be argued. Justifying the vector is the part everybody skips.
Have the fix applied, then retest to either close the finding or say why it is still open.
Rate one finding lower than a developer would expect and be ready to defend it from the vector.
Measure: findings with a reproducing request, findings by CVSS score, and findings that closed on retest.
Take a lab build of software with a known memory bug — an old CTF binary or a deliberately vulnerable target — and get a reproducible crash.
Work the crash into controlled execution, one primitive at a time.
Re-run the exploit with platform mitigations — ASLR, DEP, stack canaries — switched back on to see which breaks it. Turning them back on is the part everybody skips.
Run it against the patched build to confirm the fix actually stops it.
Note what an attacker would need to defeat the mitigation that broke your exploit.
Measure: steps from crash to execution, mitigations that stopped it, and whether the patch closed it.
Stand up a lab host running a realistic stack and start from a low-privileged foothold on it.
Escalate to administrator, documenting every step of the chain as you go.
Collect the logs each step produced, so the defenders can see the attack from their side. Gathering the defender's-eye logs is the part everybody skips.
Mark which steps left no log at all.
For one silent step, work out what would have to be deployed to make it visible.
Measure: steps in the chain, steps that left a log, and steps that left nothing.
Write the rules of engagement for a test against one real system — scope, exclusions, testing windows, evidence handling and the number to call when something breaks.
Define the boundary precisely enough that a host is unambiguously in scope or out.
Run discovery and deliberately let an out-of-scope host appear in the results.
Prove the process catches it and stops before touching it. Rehearsing the stop rather than assuming it is the part everybody skips.
Write what you would do if you found evidence of a live intruder halfway through the test.
Measure: hosts in scope versus discovered, out-of-scope hosts touched (must be zero), and time to halt on the drill.
Take a real cloud account with resources defined in Terraform and turn on continuous posture monitoring over it.
Deduplicate the findings into one record per resource, with the owning account named, instead of a flat scanner dump.
Compare the live configuration against the Terraform that was meant to produce it, so drift shows up against the code. Diffing against the source is the part everybody skips.
Handle the findings that are real but deliberate so they do not reappear every day.
Misconfigure a bucket on purpose and time how long it takes to surface.
Measure: findings per account, time from misconfiguration to alert, and drift items against the Terraform.
Take a real service's container images and pin every base image by digest, not by a floating tag.
Add a scan to CI that fails the build for a fixable critical rather than printing a warning.
Schedule a rebuild so an upstream fix reaches production unattended, because a scan that never rebuilds is a snapshot. The rebuild schedule is the part everybody skips.
Push a knowingly vulnerable image and watch the pipeline refuse it.
Introduce a critical with no fix available yet and decide, in writing, who lets the image ship anyway.
Measure: builds blocked by the gate, mean age of base images, and vulnerabilities cleared by scheduled rebuilds.
Take a real Terraform codebase and write policy-as-code guardrails, such as OPA, over it.
Evaluate them against the plan in CI so a violation fails before anything is applied.
Write unit tests for the policies themselves, because a policy that silently stopped matching passes everything. Testing the policies is the part everybody skips.
Give every exception an expiry date instead of letting it live forever.
Break a policy on purpose so it matches nothing and confirm its unit test catches the change.
Measure: plans blocked before apply, policies with unit tests, and exceptions past their expiry.
Find the long-lived cloud keys a set of real services use and list what each one is for.
Replace them with federated workload identity issuing short-lived credentials scoped to one role per workload.
Delete the static keys outright, because keys that still exist are still a risk. Deleting rather than rotating is the part everybody skips.
Let the pipeline run to prove nothing was quietly depending on the deleted keys.
Force a token to expire mid-request and watch what breaks first.
Measure: static keys removed, credential lifetime before and after, and failures caused by expiry under load.
Take one real host and capture its build as a versioned image plus an Ansible run, nothing done by hand.
Rebuild the host from that build on a clean machine.
Diff the rebuilt host against a live fleet member to find every setting somebody once applied by hand. The diff is the part everybody skips, and where the drift hides.
Fold each found setting back into the build or delete it deliberately.
Rebuild once more and confirm the diff comes back clean.
Measure: settings the diff found outside the build, time to rebuild a host, and diff size before and after.
Take a fleet of real servers, even a small one, and define a canary ring that patches ahead of the rest.
Agree a maintenance window and run the monthly patch through the canary first.
Rehearse the rollback rather than assuming it works, because the first real use of an untested rollback is during an outage. Rehearsing it is the part everybody skips.
Report patch state per host from the machines themselves, not from the ticket that said it was done.
Ship a patch that breaks the canary and confirm the fleet behind it stays unpatched until you roll back.
Measure: patch lag per host, canary breakages caught, and time the fleet sat unpatched.
Take a real system with backups and stand up an isolated network to restore into.
Restore from the backup media alone, with no access to the live system.
Time the whole restore and check the restored data is actually usable, not merely present. Checking usability rather than presence is the part everybody skips.
Compare the time against the recovery time the business actually asked for.
Change the retention policy and repeat the rehearsal to confirm the older restore point still works.
Measure: restore time, data usable versus present, and the gap against the required recovery time.
Take a directory, a lab Active Directory is fine, and give it an organisational-unit structure that matches how the org is actually run.
Replace shared domain-admin accounts with rights delegated per organisational unit.
Pilot every group policy change in one unit before it reaches anybody else.
Add a scheduled job that disables accounts not authenticated inside the agreed window. Handling the accounts it should not disable is the part everybody skips.
Point the job at a service account that logs in rarely and confirm your exclusion keeps it alive.
Measure: accounts disabled by the job, service accounts wrongly caught, and admins with delegated versus shared rights.
Take a real problem and design the solution in C4 layers — context, container, component.
Behind each significant choice write an architecture decision record naming the option you rejected and why.
Walk the design through two real scenarios and one failure mode with the engineers who would build it. Walking it with the builders is the part everybody skips.
Fix the parts the walkthrough exposed and update the affected ADRs.
Take one failure mode and trace what the design actually does when it happens, rather than assuming it copes.
Measure: decisions with an ADR, scenarios walked, and design changes the walkthrough caused.
Take one real integration and build it twice as spikes against the same interface — once synchronous, once event-driven.
Put both under the same load.
Kill the downstream dependency mid-load and watch which spike loses data and which only slows. Killing it under load is the part everybody skips.
Write the choice up with the conditions that would reverse it.
Push the load until the surviving pattern also fails, so you know both boundaries.
Measure: data lost per pattern under failure, latency under load, and the load at which each breaks.
Take a real system and collect its non-functional requirements as the business states them — usually adjectives like fast and reliable.
Turn each into a stated target: latency, availability, recovery time, data retention, as numbers.
Write the test that fails when each target is missed, so a requirement cannot quietly stop being true. Writing the test per target is the part everybody skips.
Run the tests against the built system.
Find the target the design cannot meet and write down what you would trade to get close.
Measure: requirements turned into targets, targets with a test, and targets currently met versus missed.
Take a real project and run structured interviews with at least three stakeholder groups — operations, finance and engineering.
Write each requirement down against the person who asked for it.
Trace each requirement forward to the design element that satisfies it and back to its owner. Keeping the two-way trace is the part everybody skips.
Find the requirements that contradict each other.
Take one contradiction back to the two people and resolve it on the record instead of quietly picking a side.
Measure: requirements captured, requirements traced both ways, and contradictions resolved on the record.
Design a landing zone for a real or sandbox cloud estate so a new account arrives with its networking, logging, identity and guardrails already applied.
Build the vending as a pipeline, not a runbook someone follows by hand.
Vend one account and check every baseline control from the API, not from a console. Checking from the API rather than eyeballing the console is the part everybody skips.
Work out what happens to accounts that existed before the landing zone.
Vend an account and try an action a guardrail should block to prove the baseline is really applied.
Measure: baseline controls verified per vended account, time to vend, and pre-existing accounts brought into line.
Take a real estate of workloads and assign each rehost, replatform or rebuild against a stated reason, not a default.
Pick one workload and move it end to end.
Rehearse the cutover and test the rollback before the window, because an untested rollback is not a rollback. Testing it beforehand is the part everybody skips.
Leave the old system running until the data reconciles between old and new.
Trigger the rollback on purpose during the rehearsal to confirm it lands you back safely.
Measure: workloads dispositioned with a reason, cutover time, and rows reconciled between old and new before decommission.
Take a multi-account cloud org and set service control policies that draw the hard boundary of what any account may do.
Replace standing admin with permission sets granted per role.
Write an exception path that expires rather than granting a permanent hole. The expiring exception is the part everybody skips.
Attempt a forbidden action from inside a member account to prove the boundary holds, rather than trusting the policy document.
Grant one real exception, let it expire, and confirm the access is gone afterwards.
Measure: forbidden actions blocked under test, standing admin accounts removed, and exceptions granted versus expired.
Design the network for a real multi-account estate as hub-and-spoke with centralised egress, private endpoints and cross-account name resolution.
Build it in a sandbox with traffic flowing across the spokes.
Fail an availability zone and trace which flows kept working and which quietly depended on a single subnet. Tracing the dependency rather than assuming redundancy is the part everybody skips.
Fix the flows that broke and re-run the zone failure.
Take the hub itself down and work out the blast radius.
Measure: flows surviving a zone failure, single-subnet dependencies found, and the blast radius of a hub outage.
Take a real service and define its SLOs from event-level good-against-valid counts, not host averages.
Agree the error budget policy before the first breach, so the argument happens when nobody is angry. Agreeing it in the calm is the part everybody skips.
Set burn-rate alerts at two windows so a slow burn and a sudden one page differently.
Watch the SLI over real traffic to see whether the objective matches what users notice.
Burn the budget on purpose by injecting errors and confirm both alert windows behave as designed.
Measure: budget consumed per window, alerts fired by burn rate, and the gap between the SLO and observed user pain.
Take three real services where one talks to the next through a queue and instrument them with OpenTelemetry.
Carry the trace context through the queue hop, which is where it is normally lost. Threading context across the queue is the part everybody skips.
Use tail-based sampling that keeps the errors and the slow traces rather than a flat percentage.
Add latency in one service and locate it from the trace alone, not from the code.
Leave a message in the queue for an hour and check what that does to the trace's duration.
Measure: hops with unbroken context, traces kept by tail sampling, and the span that held the regression before and after.
Stand up a metrics pipeline over a real service with a collector layer in front of storage.
Add recording rules for the expensive queries so dashboards do not recompute them on every load.
Set a cardinality budget and enforce it by dropping offending labels at ingest, because unbounded labels are what actually kill a metrics store. The budget is the part everybody skips.
Measure storage and query cost per series before and after dropping a label.
Add a high-cardinality label on purpose and watch the budget catch it at ingest.
Measure: active series, storage and query cost per series, and cardinality rejected at ingest.
Take a real service and instrument its code paths with OpenTelemetry spans, metrics and structured logs.
Make all three share one set of attribute names, so a trace, a metric and a log line about the same request agree.
Write a test that fails the build when a new handler ships without its span or with an attribute the convention does not know. The convention test is the part everybody skips.
Add a handler with no span and confirm the build goes red.
Decide what you deliberately will not instrument and note how you would notice if it turned out to be the slow part.
Measure: handlers covered by the convention, builds failed by the test, and attribute names outside the convention.
Take a real cloud bill, or the public billing export format, and build a cost allocation model over it.
Push shared and untaggable spend out to teams on a stated key instead of leaving it in an unowned bucket. Allocating the shared spend is the part everybody skips.
Reconcile the model to the invoice to the cent, because a model that does not tie out will not be believed.
Walk the teams being charged through the model before using it for anything.
Change the split key and show which team is worst off under each, so the choice is deliberate.
Measure: spend allocated versus unowned, reconciliation gap against the invoice, and each team's share under the chosen key.
Take the billing export for a real workload and find its steady-state usage, not the console's recommendation.
Model commitment coverage against that steady state.
Hold back the portion of usage that is genuinely variable, because committing to spikes is how commitments go to waste. Separating steady from variable is the part everybody skips.
Track coverage and utilisation every cycle so an under-used commitment surfaces before it expires.
Retire the workload the commitment was bought for and work out what the commitment now costs you.
Measure: coverage and utilisation per cycle, steady versus variable usage, and stranded commitment if the workload goes.
Take a real cloud bill and build showback so each team sees its own spend in units it recognises, not raw resource lines.
Write a dispute process so a team can challenge its bill.
Reconcile the figures against the invoice every month so an argument is about the driver, not about whether the number is right. Reconciling monthly is the part everybody skips.
Put the bills in front of the teams.
Run a real dispute through the process and change something as a result.
Measure: teams with a recognisable bill, reconciliation gap per month, and disputes raised and resolved.
Take a real estate and define the tags every resource must carry.
Enforce them by failing the deployment when a required tag is missing, not by reporting on it a month later. Enforcing at deploy is the part everybody skips.
Backfill the existing estate from ownership records.
Report untagged spend as a figure with a named owner rather than an unattributed remainder.
Deploy a resource with a tag missing and confirm the pipeline refuses it.
Measure: deployments blocked for missing tags, estate tagged versus untagged, and untagged spend remaining.
Take a directory and the authoritative people record, an HR export, for the same organisation.
Model each identity as an explicit state rather than an active flag.
Reconcile the two and report every account with no matching person and every person with no account. Reconciling both directions is the part everybody skips.
Close the orphaned accounts and fix the process that had been creating them.
Create an account with no matching person on purpose and confirm the next reconciliation flags it.
Measure: orphaned accounts found, people with no account, and orphans closed versus reclaimed as service accounts.
Take a real application and integrate single sign-on over OIDC or SAML.
Map the group claims to application roles rather than granting everyone the same access.
Set session and token lifetimes deliberately instead of leaving the defaults.
Disable the local password login so the identity provider is the only door. Closing the fallback login is the part everybody skips, and the whole point.
Disable a user in the provider mid-session and time how long their active session survives.
Measure: login paths remaining after SSO, token and session lifetimes, and the gap between disabling an account and its session ending.
Take a real system and pull the entitlements people actually exercise, not the ones they were granted.
Collapse them into roles the owners could name.
Test each role against real jobs to see what it grants that nobody in that job has ever touched. Checking for unused grants is the part everybody skips.
Trim the roles down to what the job uses.
Find the role that ended up too broad and work out how to split it without making one role per person.
Measure: entitlements granted versus exercised, roles built, and unused grants per role.
Take a real HR event feed and wire joiner, mover and leaver provisioning off the event rather than a ticket.
Make the mover case remove the old access, not only add the new — this is the case everybody gets wrong.
Drive a test identity through all three transitions.
After the move, check each downstream system directly to see what old access survived. Checking the mover for leftover access is the part everybody skips.
Run the leaver step and time how long the account's access actually survives.
Measure: transitions automated, old access left attached after a move, and survival time of a leaver's access.
Take a real set of systems — databases, object stores and logs — and scan them for personal data instead of sending a questionnaire.
Record the purpose and lawful basis beside each field the scan finds.
Trust the scan over the survey, because the questionnaire always misses a field somebody forgot about. Believing the scan is the part everybody skips.
Schedule the scan to re-run so a new column of personal data is found by the map, not by an incident.
Add a column of personal data to a log field and confirm the next scan catches it.
Measure: personal-data fields found, fields the team swore were not there, and new fields caught on re-scan.
Take a real dataset with a processing job over it and build consent capture that stores the purpose, the wording shown and the version consented to, with a timestamp.
Enforce consent where the data is read, so a withdrawal actually stops the processing rather than being noted for later. Enforcing at read time is the part everybody skips.
Withdraw consent for a test subject and watch the downstream job skip that record.
Work out what happens to data already processed under a consent that was just withdrawn.
Re-run the job to confirm the withdrawn subject stays out.
Measure: records processed versus consented, time from withdrawal to enforcement, and records still in flight at withdrawal.
Take a real schema and list every field it collects.
Tie each field to a stated purpose, and stop collecting the ones that cannot be tied to one. Actually cutting the untied fields is the part everybody skips.
Shorten what the logs keep to match.
Re-run the test suite and the reporting to show which questions the estate can no longer answer.
Find the field somebody fights to keep and make them state its purpose.
Measure: fields collected before and after, log retention before and after, and reports broken by the cut.
Take a real set of stores that all hold data about the same people.
Build a run that assembles one subject's records from every store once the requester is verified.
Redact the third parties who appear in the same rows, because a raw dump leaks other people. The redaction is the part everybody skips.
Time the whole run against the statutory deadline instead of assuming it fits.
Verify the requester is the data subject without collecting more personal data to do it, and write down how.
Measure: stores covered per request, third-party fields redacted, and run time against the deadline.
Take a real product idea and recruit at least five people from its actual audience to interview.
Fix the interview guide before you recruit, so every conversation asks the same things.
Build an opportunity tree from what people described, not from what they asked for.
Name the riskiest assumption and test it with a prototype before any engineer is asked for an estimate. Testing the assumption before building is the part everybody skips.
Let the assumption fail and stop building whatever depended on it.
Measure: interviews run, opportunities found, and assumptions tested versus assumptions that failed.
Take a real backlog and write the criteria you will score items against.
Have more than one person score independently, so the ranking is not one person's opinion.
Keep a visible record of what was dropped and why, because the rejected items are where the argument goes later. Keeping the rejects is the part everybody skips.
Re-run the ranking under a changed constraint to see which items are genuinely at the top and which were only there by ordering.
Rank the loudest stakeholder's item below something else and prepare the case for it.
Measure: items scored, agreement between scorers, and rank changes when the constraint changed.
Take a real product and build a metric tree from the north star down to the inputs a single team can actually move.
Give each number one written definition and a tracked event behind it.
Have two people pull the same figure on the same day and confirm they get the same answer. Nailing the definition so it does not drift is the part everybody skips.
Find a metric a team could improve while making the product worse, and add the guard against it.
Change the event definition on purpose and watch the two pulls disagree, so you see why the definition matters.
Measure: metrics with one written definition, figures that reconcile between two people, and metrics with a guardrail.
Take a real opportunity and size it bottom-up from counts somebody can go and check, not from an analyst's market figure.
Put every assumption on its own line, so each one can be argued separately. Listing the assumptions openly is the part everybody skips.
Build the estimate from those counts.
Vary the least certain assumptions and show how far the answer moves.
Find the assumption the answer is most sensitive to and say what you would do to reduce its uncertainty.
Measure: the estimate, the range across the sensitivity runs, and which assumption moved it most.
Take one real epic from a product you use and write out the work behind it — at least 20 stories' worth.
Slice it so each story ships on its own and a user can see the difference. A layer is not a slice.
Write acceptance criteria into each story, because a story with none is where the two estimates diverge.
Hand the set to two engineers who estimate cold, separately, with no walkthrough from you.
Compare the two estimates story by story and rewrite every one they read differently, then re-estimate with a third person.
Measure: stories written, how many the two estimates disagreed on by more than a factor of two, and rewrites forced.
Pick one feature with at least six user-visible behaviours — a checkout, an invite flow, a permissions screen.
Write each behaviour in Given/When/Then form, one criterion per behaviour, with no compound conditions.
Enumerate the edge and failure cases: empty, offline, permission denied, duplicate submit, expired session. Everybody skips these and they are where the defects live.
Walk QA and engineering through the set before build starts, and log every question they had to ask.
Have QA try to write a test that passes while the feature is broken. Rewrite every criterion that allows it.
Measure: criteria written, questions raised at review, criteria QA rejected, and defects later traced to a missing one.
Collect a month of real feedback — 200 items or more from app store reviews, support tickets or a public forum.
Write the rubric before reading anything: severity levels, frequency bands, and a definition for each theme.
Code every item against the rubric, adding a theme only by amending the written codebook first.
Have a second person code a 30-item sample blind. This is the part everybody skips and it is the only thing that makes the ranking reproducible.
Compare, report where you disagreed, resolve each one, and rewrite the definitions that caused the disagreement.
Measure: items coded, agreement rate between the two coders, and the top five themes by severity times frequency.
Take a product with event data you can query — your own instrumented app, or a public clickstream dataset of 100,000 events or more.
Pull each feature's original spec and write down the case that was made for it, before you look at a number.
Query usage per feature: unique users, repeat use, and what people do instead. Keep the query next to the result.
List the caveats — tracking gaps, cohort skew, seasonality. A number without its caveats is not evidence for a removal.
Recommend one removal in writing, then hand the same data to someone else and let them try to break the recommendation.
Measure: users touching each feature, repeat rate per feature, and the size of the tracking gap you could not close.
Take one real delivery with at least two stakeholders who want different things — a club project, a freelance job, a team deliverable.
Interview both separately and write what is in scope as deliverables, not as intentions.
Write the out-of-scope list next to it. This is the half everybody skips and the only half anybody ever argues about.
Take it back to both and get it signed, including the sentence each of them wanted removed.
Run it for a few weeks, hold every new request against the document, and record the refusal and what the requester did next.
Measure: requests received, how many the baseline refused, and how many forced a change to the baseline itself.
Start a RAID log for a live delivery running six weeks or more, with four or more people involved.
Seed it with every risk, assumption, issue and dependency you can name, each with a named owner and a review date.
Assumptions are the ones everybody omits. Write each as a statement that could be false, and name who can confirm it.
Walk the whole log at a fixed weekly slot with the owners in the room, not by email.
When a risk becomes an issue, go back to what the log said the week before and record the gap between the two.
Measure: entries opened and closed, average age of an open entry, and issues that arrived with no risk predicting them.
Take a delivery with a baselined scope and six weeks left to run, and put one intake route in front of it — one form, one log, no corridor requests.
Define the assessment before the first request arrives: effort, schedule impact, what it displaces, and who approves at what size.
Assess every request, including the small ones. The small ones are what actually move the date, and they are what gets waved through.
Record the decision and the reason in one log, with the refusals sitting next to the approvals.
Push a change in at the last minute on purpose and see whether the assessment happened or was skipped under pressure.
Measure: requests logged, approved and refused, total assessed schedule impact, and the slip actually observed.
Take a delivery with at least 30 tasks and real dependencies between them, not a flat to-do list.
Build the network: duration, predecessors and dependency type on every link.
Derive the critical path by hand once before letting any tool do it, so you can tell when the tool is wrong.
Compute the float on every non-critical task. Float is what everybody skips and it is the thing that tells you which slip matters.
Re-run the network after each real slip and publish which milestone moved, the same week it happened.
Measure: path length, float per task, and how many tasks moved onto the critical path over the delivery.
Take a programme with three or more teams that must ship in some order — yours, or a documented open-source roadmap.
List every technical constraint between them: what must exist before what, and why. Ask the engineers, not the managers.
Sequence from the constraints first and fit dates afterwards. Doing it the other way round is how roadmaps become fiction.
Publish the dependent milestones under each item, so a slip is visibly attached to everything it moves.
Replan monthly against what actually shipped, and let one milestone slip in public rather than quietly re-baselining it.
Measure: milestones planned versus delivered per month, and days of slip propagated into dependent milestones.
Pick a service genuinely about to go live — real users, a fixed date, and somebody who will be on call afterwards.
Write the bar before the review: rollback rehearsed, alerts firing, on-call named, load test run, runbook written.
Make every gate a yes or no with named evidence. A gate that reads "mostly ready" has never stopped a launch.
Run the review with the owners present and record who said yes to what, by name.
Fail a gate on purpose — unrehearse the rollback — and see whether the process actually holds the date.
Measure: gates passed and failed at first pass, evidence missing per gate, and days between the review and the launch.
Find two teams building either side of one interface, with nothing written down between them yet.
Write the contract: fields, types, error cases, and the date each side commits to. Send it to both.
Error cases are what everybody leaves out and what every integration then fails on. Name each one and what the caller does about it.
Get the disagreement onto the page rather than into a meeting, and record who gave way on what.
Back it with a contract test running in both builds, then push a breaking change and confirm the other side's build fails.
Measure: fields and error cases agreed, breaking changes the test caught, and days from first draft to both signatures.
Take a change going to real users and define three stages: internal, a cohort of about one percent, then everyone.
Write entry and exit criteria per stage — the metric, the threshold and the soak time — before the first stage ships.
Rehearse the rollback before stage one, not after. A rollback first attempted during an incident is not a rollback.
Ship stage one, hold for the full soak, and promote only on the written exit criteria, not on how it feels.
Roll one stage back deliberately, time it, and record the residue — half-migrated rows, stale caches, emails already sent.
Measure: time to roll back, users affected per stage, and the state the rollback did not undo.
Take a real queue with at least 100 tickets over a month — a lab, a society, a small team's IT requests.
Define the categories first and force one onto every ticket at intake, not at close where the answer is already known.
Measure first-contact resolution and reopen rate per category. Reopens are what everybody leaves out of the headline number.
Take the largest recurring category and write the self-serve fix: a page, a script, or a permission change.
Publish it, wait a full month before claiming anything, and check the category shrank rather than moved into another one.
Measure: tickets per category before and after, first-contact resolution, reopen rate, and time to close.
Take a real estate of spend with at least 20 line items across a year — a cloud account, a department's tool list.
Split every line into licence, infrastructure and support, and attach it to the service it exists for.
Forecast three months forward from usage drivers — headcount, storage, request volume — not from last month plus a percentage.
Reconcile against actuals every month and name the cause of each variance. "Rounding" is not a cause and hides the real one.
Change one driver on purpose and check the forecast moves the way the model says it should.
Measure: spend per service, forecast versus actual per month, and the largest variance with its named cause.
Build a register of at least ten real contracts — the tools a team actually pays for, with the paperwork in hand.
Record renewal date, notice period and exit clause for each. The notice period is the one that quietly costs a year's fee.
Pull actual use per seat or unit from the vendor's own admin console and set it against what is licensed.
Diff entitlement against use and rank the gaps by annual value, not by seat count.
Take one renewal back to the vendor with the under-use evidence rather than the sales figure, and record what they offered.
Measure: seats licensed versus active per contract, annual value of the gap, and days of notice remaining on each.
Pick two or three services with real users and write down what a user can actually see going wrong.
Turn each into a level with a threshold and a window, phrased from the user's side, never from what a server reports.
Wire the measurement to ticket and monitoring data, so the number is computed rather than reported by the team it judges.
Write down what the level deliberately does not cover, and why the line sits there. An uncovered case discovered later is a broken promise.
Simulate a breach out of hours and time whether escalation reached a named person inside the stated window.
Measure: attainment per service per month, time to escalate in the drill, and the share of incidents outside the definition.
Take one real task in a product you can study and map every screen it touches, trigger to done — usually eight to fifteen.
Add the branches most flows omit: empty state, error, permission denied, expired session, partial success.
Build it clickable at grey-box fidelity. No colour, no type choices — the flow has to survive being judged on its own.
Walk five people through it cold and note where they hesitate, which matters more than where they fail.
Change the flow rather than the visuals wherever they hesitated, then rerun the same tasks with different people.
Measure: branches mapped, hesitation points per participant, and steps in the task before and after.
Take a screen with at least six actions on it, one of which destroys something the user cares about.
Specify every action in four states: loading, optimistic, failed and undone. Most specs stop at the first.
The failed state is what everybody skips. Say exactly what the user sees, what they keep, and what they must retype.
Prototype the destructive action twice — once behind a confirmation dialogue, once with a real undo.
Put both in front of the same people and watch which one they use and which one they misfire on.
Measure: states specified per action, misfires per prototype, and undo use rate versus confirmation dismissal rate.
Build a clickable prototype of one flow, six to ten screens, then throw out every placeholder before anyone sees it.
Load real data: the longest names, the empty list, the 47-item list, the currency with no symbol.
Add the real latency. Instant transitions hide every loading state and every decision about what to show while waiting.
Find the screens that only worked because the data was polite, and rewrite them rather than trimming the data.
Test cold with people who have not seen it, and record what realistic data broke that placeholder data was hiding.
Measure: screens broken by real data, longest content the layout survives, and task completion with latency switched on.
Find a pattern rebuilt three or more times in one product and propose it as a single component.
Specify variants, every interactive state, and content guidance including what happens when the label runs long.
Write the rule for when not to use it. Without that rule a component gets used for everything and then quietly rewritten.
Take it to the teams who would have to adopt it, before it is built, and record every objection they raise.
Rebuild one existing screen on the component and find out what the component could not do.
Measure: existing uses it would replace, objections raised at review, and how many were fixed in the component versus the guidance.
Pick one core task in a real product and wireframe three genuinely different versions of it at low fidelity.
Count for each version the steps, the decisions demanded of the user, and the fields they have to type.
Check what each version hides. Moving four steps behind a menu is not removing them, and the count must say so.
Put all three in front of people on paper and have them complete the same task on each.
Keep the shortest version people actually finished, and write down what the user lost when the step went.
Measure: steps and decisions per version, completion rate per version, and time to finish the task.
Take a product with at least 40 pages or features and put every one on its own card.
Write the tree-test tasks now, before the sort. Writing them afterwards lets you test the structure you already like.
Run an open card sort with 15 or more real users and record the labels they wrote, not the ones you expected.
Build the structure from the clusters, keeping the users' words over the internal names.
Tree-test the new structure on the pre-written tasks, and test the old structure on the same tasks as a baseline.
Measure: success rate and directness per task, old structure versus new, and the labels the sort changed.
Pick one customer journey and interview at least eight people who have actually been through it.
Map from the trigger before the product to the moment after it, including the phone call, the email and the paperwork.
The off-product steps are what everybody leaves off and usually where the pain sits. Ask what they did before opening the app.
Trace every pain point to a quoted interview or a support ticket. Anything traced to a workshop opinion comes off the map.
Walk the finished map back to two people who lived it and correct everything they say is wrong.
Measure: steps on and off the product, pain points with evidence versus without, and the stage carrying the most.
Watch at least six people perform the core task on the current build, helping and explaining nothing.
Break it into real sub-steps from what they did, including the workarounds and the second window they opened.
Time every sub-step on the current build. This baseline is the part everybody skips, and without it the redesign proves nothing.
Build the redesign, then time the same participants on the same tasks, counterbalancing the order.
Report every sub-step the redesign made slower next to the ones it made faster, before deciding whether to ship.
Measure: time and error count per sub-step, before and after, and which sub-steps got worse.
Take the densest screen in a real product — a dashboard, a settings page, a checkout with 20 or more elements.
Rank what the screen is for: one primary action, a few supporting, the rest reference. Write the ranking down first.
Build the hierarchy from weight, size and space. Colour alone fails for a tenth of your users and washes out in sunlight.
Run five-second tests with at least ten people: what is this screen for, and what would you do next?
Record what they read first. Where it is not what you ranked first, change the design rather than the ranking.
Measure: correct answers to both questions, and the element read first per participant, before and after.
Take a real interface of 30 screens or more and list every colour, space and type decision it contains.
Name every token by the role it plays — surface, border, text-muted, danger — never by the value it currently holds.
Apply them everywhere and delete the hard-coded values. A half-applied token set is worse than none, because it looks done.
Swap the whole interface to a dark theme by changing values only, touching no component.
Anywhere that needs a new token or a one-off override is a naming failure. Rename it and run the swap again.
Measure: tokens defined, hard-coded values remaining, and new tokens or overrides the dark swap forced.
Choose a ratio, generate the scale, then pull the longest and densest real content the product has — never sample copy.
Set line length and line height at every level, and write down why each level exists at all.
Set the real content in it, including the 90-character heading and the eight-word button label everybody designs around.
Take it to a 320-pixel viewport and find the levels that collapse, wrap to three lines, or stop being distinguishable.
Add manual exceptions only where the ratio genuinely fails, and write the reason next to each one.
Measure: levels in the scale, line length per level at each breakpoint, and the exceptions the real content forced.
List every foreground and background pairing a real interface of 20 screens or more actually produces.
Measure each with a contrast tool against WCAG 2.2. Judging by eye is what put the failures there in the first place.
Include disabled, focus, error, placeholder and text over images. These are the pairings an audit always misses.
Fix each failure by changing the colour or by changing how it is used, and record which you chose and why.
Simulate the three common colour-blindness types and find everything that only worked because of hue.
Measure: pairings tested, pairings failing before and after, and how many relied on hue alone.
Take one feature with a real engineer building it, and write the problem statement before drawing anything.
Go sketch, wireframe, high fidelity, keeping each stage so the decisions stay separable afterwards.
Sit with the engineer during the build rather than handing it over. The questions they do not ask are the ones that get guessed.
Log every difference between spec and built screen, and decide each one explicitly: accept, or send it back.
Compare the shipped screen against the spec at two breakpoints after it is live, not from memory.
Measure: differences logged, accepted versus sent back, and the questions engineering had to come and ask.
Take one flow of six to ten screens and commit to three stages: grey box, wireframe, high fidelity.
Test the grey-box structure with people before any visual weight exists on the page.
Solving a layout problem with colour is the trap. If a screen only works once it is coloured, the structure is still wrong.
Move to wireframe, fix what the structure test found, and test again on the same tasks.
Only then add type, colour and imagery, and record in the version history which decision happened at which stage.
Measure: structural problems found at each fidelity, and how many surfaced only after visual work had begun.
Take a set of screens engineering is about to build — eight or more — and write the handoff spec before the kickoff.
Specify tokens, spacing, breakpoints, and every interactive state: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error.
Specify what happens when content runs longer than the design assumed. This is the question engineering always has to come back and ask.
Hand it over with no walkthrough and take every question in writing rather than in conversation.
Treat each question as a hole in the spec: fix it, count it, and do not defend it.
Measure: questions asked per screen, states specified, and build differences traced to a missing line in the spec.
Design the flow at 320 pixels wide first, with the real content, before any larger viewport exists.
Add at each breakpoint rather than removing. Designing wide and cutting is how mobile ends up with the leftovers.
Build it and open it on a real low-end handset. A browser preview has no thumb, no keyboard overlay and no slow network.
Watch five people use it one-handed and note every action they stretch for or miss.
Move the primary action into thumb reach, retest, and check nothing important now sits under the keyboard.
Measure: mis-taps per participant, one-handed completion rate, and the reach zone of each primary action.
Pick one product and one question it can answer. Write the tasks, the success criteria and the sample size — six to eight participants — before recruiting anyone.
Pilot with one person to find the tasks that are impossible or that give the answer away, then lock the script.
Moderate without helping. The urge to rescue a stuck participant destroys the data and it is the hardest part of the job.
Score every task against the criteria written in advance, not against how the session felt afterwards.
Trace each finding through to the change it caused, then retest the changed flow with fresh participants.
Measure: task success and time per participant, findings raised versus acted on, and how many were retested.
Write the screener before recruiting: quotas, disqualifying answers, and a target of 8 to 12 qualified participants.
Hide what a right answer looks like. A question that signals the answer recruits people who want the incentive.
Pilot the screener on ten people and cut every question they could guess their way through.
Screen a real pool and log every rejection with its reason, not only the people who got in.
Describe the sample you actually achieved, including who you failed to reach, and state which claims that rules out.
Measure: screened, qualified and rejected counts, quota fill per cell, and the groups missing from the achieved sample.
Take transcripts or session notes from at least eight sessions of real research, not from memory or sticky notes.
Write the codebook first, with a definition and an example for each code, and version it as codes are added.
Code everything, linking each quote to its timestamp so any claim can be walked back to raw evidence.
Have a second person code a 20 percent sample blind. Skipping this is what makes synthesis a matter of opinion.
Report where the two of you disagreed and what happened to those themes, including the one that did not survive.
Measure: sessions coded, codes in the book, agreement rate on the double-coded sample, and themes dropped after review.
Recruit 12 to 15 participants for a two-week study, expecting to lose some, and fix the research question before day one.
Design the capture so an entry takes under two minutes. A photo and one line beats a form nobody fills in.
Set the timed prompts, and write the drop-off plan before it happens: when you nudge, how often, and when you stop.
Check completion daily and act on that plan rather than hoping people return in week two.
Analyse for behaviour that only appears over time — the abandoned attempt, the workaround, the weekly rhythm a single session cannot show.
Measure: entries per participant per day, drop-off by day, and the findings visible only after week one.
Pick a short explainer sequence, 20 to 30 seconds, with a real script and a real point to make.
Block it in keys only — the extreme poses that carry the action, nothing between them.
Review the blocking with someone else before drawing a single inbetween. Polishing a pass that does not read is the expensive mistake.
Add breakdowns to define the arcs, and only then the inbetweens.
Export the blocking pass and the finished pass side by side and check the action still reads in the blocking alone.
Measure: keys, breakdowns and inbetweens per shot, and whether the action reads without the inbetweens.
Take one motion sequence of about ten seconds and chart it frame by frame before any drawing is cleaned up.
Write the timing chart per action: how many frames it takes, and where the spacing bunches at each end.
Play it back at the delivery frame rate. Scrubbing the timeline flatters everything and hides every timing problem you have.
Mark the actions that float — even spacing, no ease, no sense of weight.
Fix each by deciding whether the fault is timing or spacing, and change only that one thing so you can see the effect.
Measure: frames per action, the spacing chart before and after, and the actions still floating at full speed.
Rig one character with a full body and a face — enough that naming and hierarchy actually matter.
Build named controls, joint limits and IK/FK switching, setting the limits from the poses the sequence really needs.
Hand it to another animator with no walkthrough and no documentation. Anything they cannot find is a rig fault, not theirs.
Watch them pose it and write down every control they broke, could not find, or used in a way you had not planned.
Fix each one, then hand it to a third person and see whether the fixes held.
Measure: controls exposed, breaks per handover, and how many fixes landed in the rig versus in the naming.
Board a full sequence of 60 to 90 seconds, deciding staging, camera and every cut on the board.
Record or obtain the final audio first. Boarding to a temp track and retiming later is where sequences die.
Cut the boards into a timed animatic against that audio, holding every panel for its real duration.
Show it to people who do not know the story and ask them what happened. The shots they cannot describe do not read.
Rewrite or cut those shots and re-cut the animatic before a single frame is animated.
Measure: shots boarded, shots cut or rewritten at animatic stage, and the animation days that would have cost.
Pick a component that already exists somewhere with more than ten props, and take its job as the brief.
Write the five hardest real use cases as code against an API that does not exist yet.
Design for composition — slots and children — rather than a prop per variation. Every prop you add is one you cannot remove.
Implement it, and where a use case wants a prop you did not anticipate, change the API rather than adding the prop.
Give it to a second consumer and let them try to break it with a case you never wrote down.
Measure: props exposed versus the original, use cases satisfied without new props, and API changes forced by real use.
Take a real interface and put every colour, space and type value — at least a hundred of them — into one source file.
Generate the CSS custom properties and the typed constants from that source in a build step, never by hand.
Wire the generation into CI so a token change lands as a reviewable diff rather than a mystery visual change.
Add a lint rule that fails the build on a hard-coded colour. Without the gate the pipeline decays within a fortnight.
Delete a token on purpose and confirm the build breaks at the components using it, not at runtime in front of a user.
Measure: tokens generated, hard-coded values remaining, and build failures the lint gate produced over a week.
Build four interactive components against the WAI-ARIA authoring practices: menu, dialogue, tabs and combobox.
Implement roving focus, focus trapping and escape handling, returning focus to where it came from on close.
Run an automated scan and note the pass, then set it aside: a scan passes components a screen reader cannot operate.
Drive the whole flow with the keyboard alone, then with a screen reader, writing down what it announces at every stop.
Fix everything unreachable or unnamed, then retest with a second screen reader on a different platform.
Measure: components passing the scan, failures the screen reader found anyway, and keyboard-only completion of the flow.
Take a component library of at least 20 components and enumerate every state each one has.
Render each state in both themes and at every breakpoint, and snapshot them in CI on a fixed image.
Kill the flake first — fonts, animation, dates, random data. A noisy gate gets approved blindly and stops being a gate.
Push a one-pixel spacing change and confirm the build stops it and names the components affected.
Write the review rule: who approves a diff and what an approval must say, then run it for a fortnight.
Measure: states snapshotted, diffs raised, false positives per week, and real regressions caught before merge.
Take a product with instrumented events — your own, or a public clickstream dataset with at least 100,000 sessions.
Define the steps from events the user causes, not from page views, and fix the attribution window before querying.
Compute the drop between each step and name the worst one.
Segment it by platform, cohort and traffic source. A drop that is one browser or one release is a bug, not a behaviour.
Hunt the tracking gap: a step whose event fires late, twice, or not on mobile fakes a cliff. Check this before concluding anything.
Measure: conversion between each step, drop-off by segment, and the size of the events you know are missing.
Take one flow with at least 15 events in it and write the tracking plan first: every event, its properties, its types, its exact firing condition.
Review the plan with the engineer who will implement it, before implementation, and settle every ambiguous condition in writing.
After it ships, validate the live stream against the plan event by event. This is the step everybody skips, and it is why dashboards lie.
Hunt the three classic faults: fires twice, fires on the wrong action, never fires on one platform.
Add an automated conformance check so an event missing a required property is flagged the day it appears.
Measure: events specified versus arriving, faults found per event type, and days between a fault appearing and being caught.
Get event data with signup dates covering at least six months and 10,000 users.
Write the definition of a retained user, and the reason for it, before plotting anything.
Build the curves by signup cohort, never blended. A blended number moves when acquisition moves and says nothing about the product.
Recompute under a stricter definition and a looser one, and put all three side by side.
Say which cohorts flatten and which keep falling, and check that a flattening cohort is not simply a much smaller one.
Measure: retention at day 1, 7, 30 and 90 per cohort, cohort sizes, and how the curves move under each definition.
Inventory every event a real product already sends — usually a few hundred, many of them duplicates of each other.
Write the convention: the naming pattern, the required properties every event carries, and a named owner per event.
Map the legacy events onto it and decide each one, remap or retire, writing down the decision and who it costs.
Migrate, keeping both streams running long enough to reconcile counts between old and new event by event.
Add a CI check that rejects a non-conforming event, then submit a bad one on purpose and watch the build fail.
Measure: events inventoried, remapped and retired, count reconciliation between the two streams, and non-conforming events blocked.
Take a programme with three or more teams and list every dependency between them, including the ones only ever agreed verbally.
Write each as a named person, a dated commitment, and the thing that breaks if it slips. Any two of the three is not a dependency.
Review weekly with both sides in the room. A dependency confirmed only by the receiving team is not confirmed at all.
Escalate anything with no owner immediately, rather than leaving it to be discovered at launch.
When one slips, record how many days before the milestone you knew, and whether the register told you or a person did.
Measure: dependencies tracked, how many were unowned at first pass, days of warning per slip, and slips found only at the milestone.
Open a register for a real programme running two months or more, with a delivery date somebody cares about.
Give every entry a probability, an impact, a named owner and a trigger condition — the observable thing that says it is happening now.
The trigger is what everybody leaves out. Without it a register is a list of worries that nobody ever acts on.
Review at a fixed cadence and close each entry with what actually happened, rather than letting it age quietly.
When a risk materialises, write it up against what the register predicted, and separately list the ones it missed entirely.
Measure: risks opened and closed, triggers that fired, and issues that arrived with no matching risk.
Take a delivery with four or more milestones and write the exit criteria for each before agreeing any date.
Make every criterion checkable by someone outside the team, with named evidence attached.
Agree the dates only after the criteria exist. The other order is what produces green statuses over unmet criteria.
Assess each milestone against its criteria on the day, and refuse to mark it green on partial evidence.
Move a date in public when the criteria are not met, and record what people did next.
Measure: milestones met on criteria versus on date, days moved, and how many were declared green then reopened.
Take a real programme running six weeks or more and write the report as a decision request, not a summary of activity.
State what is at risk, what changed since the last report, and what must be decided this week.
Name the decision maker for each ask. A decision addressed to everybody is a decision addressed to nobody.
Send it at a fixed time for at least six weeks and track whether each report actually produced a decision.
Rewrite the format after the reports that were ignored, and record what you changed and whether it worked.
Measure: decisions requested versus made per report, days to decision, and how many reports produced none.
Facilitate planning for one real team over at least five sprints — one board, one sprint goal per sprint.
Build the capacity forecast by subtracting leave, support duty and known interruption before anything is pulled in.
Interruption is the subtraction everybody omits and usually the largest. Measure it for two sprints before you dare estimate it.
At each sprint end, compare the forecast against what actually finished, per person and in total.
Correct the model, not the team. A forecast 20 percent high three sprints running is a model that is 20 percent high.
Measure: forecast versus completed capacity per sprint, sprint goal met or missed, and the drift in the model over time.
Start an impediment log for a real team and record every blocker for at least six sprints.
Capture who raised it, when, what it blocked, and the date and cause of it clearing.
Age is the number that matters. A log without open-duration lets a three-week blocker look like a one-line note.
Sort by recurrence and take the top one to its source outside the team, instead of working around it again.
Record what that cost politically, and whether the blocker actually stopped coming back in the sprints afterwards.
Measure: impediments raised and cleared, age of each at close, and recurrence rate before and after the source fix.
Facilitate six consecutive retrospectives for one real team, rotating the format each time.
Bring the sprint data into the room — cycle time, carry-over, incidents — so the discussion argues with evidence rather than memory.
Cap the output at two or three actions, each with an owner and a date. Ten actions is the same as none.
Open every retro by checking whether the previous actions closed. Skipping this is why retros stop being taken seriously.
When an action fails to close twice, take it out of the retro and escalate it rather than re-agreeing it.
Measure: actions raised per retro, share closed by the following one, and how many had to be escalated out.
Take a team's board with at least 60 completed items of history and pull every column-change timestamp.
Compute cycle time per item and plot the distribution. Report the 50th and 85th percentiles, never the average.
Split each item's time into working and waiting per stage. The waiting is usually most of it, and it is what nobody measures.
Find the stage with the longest queue and trial a work-in-progress limit there, changing nothing else at the same time.
Re-measure the same way after at least three weeks, and look for what else moved — team size, work type, holidays.
Measure: cycle time percentiles before and after, waiting time per stage, and queue length at the limited stage.
Find a real change wanted by two groups who want different things — a process, a tool, a system somebody actually uses.
Interview each group separately first, with a written question set, and record who said what.
Write each requirement with its rationale and the named person it came from. A requirement with no source cannot be defended later.
Run the workshop only after the interviews, and put the contradictions on the wall instead of smoothing them over.
Resolve each conflict in writing with a named decider. Averaging two requirements produces something neither group asked for.
Measure: requirements captured, contradictions found, and how many were resolved in writing before sign-off.
Pick a real process with at least three people and two hand-offs, and watch it run end to end twice.
Draw it in BPMN from what you saw, not from the procedure document. The document describes the process somebody intended.
Mark every hand-off and every point where work sits waiting, with how long it waited.
Walk the map back to the people who do the job and let them cross out the steps nobody actually follows.
Record the exceptions they handle by hand and never mention, and put every one of them on the map.
Measure: steps, hand-offs and exceptions mapped, waiting time per hand-off, and the steps the document had wrong.
Pick one real capability at least three people depend on and write its current and target state before listing a single gap.
List every gap between them, each with the capability it needs and a named owner.
Split them: what a process change can close, and what genuinely needs a build. Calling everything a build turns this into a wish list.
Put an order-of-magnitude cost on each — days, weeks or months — and write down what that estimate assumes.
Recommend two gaps stay open, with the reason and what would change your mind, then take the list to the owner to be argued with.
Measure: gaps found, the split between process and build, estimated cost per gap, and how many were left open deliberately.
Take a change with at least 30 requirements and pull the requests, the build tickets and the test cases into one sheet.
Link each stakeholder request forward: to its requirement, to the build ticket, to the UAT case that accepts it.
Find the requirements with no test. These ship untested, and nobody notices until UAT has already been signed off.
Find the build items with nothing behind them, and go and ask who asked for each one.
Take both lists to the delivery meeting and record what happened to every orphan on them.
Measure: requirements traced end to end, requirements with no test case, and build items with no requesting stakeholder.
Take one real system somebody depends on — a club's booking process, a lab's stock sheet — and sit with at least three of its actual users.
Number every requirement you hear. One line, one behaviour. A line holding two behaviours becomes two lines.
Write an acceptance test beside each line, precise enough that two people running it reach the same verdict. This is the part everybody skips.
Put a named owner on every line, and send the ambiguous ones back in writing rather than guessing at what was meant.
Read the catalogue back line by line until each is signed off, and record every line that changed under challenge.
Measure: requirements captured, lines changed at review, lines still without an owner, and elapsed time to sign-off.
Pick an old system with an awkward data shape — a legacy CSV export, a SOAP service, a spreadsheet somebody still maintains by hand.
Write the field-level contract first: every field, its type, its units, and what a missing value means on each side.
Build the anti-corruption layer so nothing downstream ever sees the legacy shape, its names or its codes.
Replay a full day of real records through both the old path and the new one, and diff every field rather than sampling.
Reconcile every difference before switching anything, and record which side turned out to be wrong each time.
Measure: records replayed, fields that disagreed, differences explained, and unexplained differences remaining (target zero).
Take one real decision with three plausible answers — a queue, a database, a hosting model — for a system you are actually building.
Agree the criteria and their weights with whoever pays for it, in writing, before you read a single vendor page.
Score all three on paper from documentation, and mark honestly which of those scores are guesses.
