Build a throwaway spike of the two shortlisted options against your own workload. The spike is what turns a guess into a measurement.
Re-score from the spike and show at least one score that moved, or say plainly why none did.
Measure: weighted score per option before and after the spike, and the spike's own numbers — throughput, latency, setup time.
Take two services that already talk to each other — yours and a friend's, or two of your own — and write down exactly what crosses.
Specify every field with a type and a range, every error code, the retry rule, and who owns each failure case.
Write down what happens when the downstream side is gone for a day. Most specifications stop before this, and that is the gap.
Turn the specification into contract tests and put them in both pipelines, so either side breaking it fails its own build.
Break it on purpose: rename a field on the producer and confirm the consumer's pipeline goes red before anything deploys.
Measure: fields under contract, error cases specified, failure cases with a named owner, and the build result on the deliberate break.
Take a real application heading for a release — your own project, or an open-source one with a dated milestone.
Write what is covered at unit, integration and system level, and name what is deliberately not covered at all.
Write the entry and exit criteria as numbers a release can be checked against, not as adjectives.
State the cost of each uncovered area if it bit. The gaps you name in advance are the strategy; the ones you do not are excuses.
Hold an actual release against the exit criteria, and record whether you shipped, blocked or waived, and who agreed.
Measure: criteria met and missed at the gate, defects found per level, and defects that escaped past all of them.
Take a bug tracker with real traffic — an open-source repository where you can triage the incoming queue will do.
Write the severity and priority scale down before triaging anything, with an example defect sitting at each level.
Triage every incoming defect against the scale, and record a two-line reason whenever you argue a severity down.
Set severity from customer impact, never from the tone of the report. Loud tickets outranking quiet ones is the failure everybody falls into.
Track each defect from report through to a fix you verified yourself, not to a developer saying it was fixed.
Measure: defects triaged, severity changes on appeal, open counts by severity per release, and the trend across releases.
Take a system with real users and list every way it can fail that would actually cost somebody something.
Score each by likelihood and by cost of failure, with the cost agreed by whoever carries it rather than guessed by you.
Aim the regression effort at the top of the map, and write the low-risk areas down as deliberately uncovered.
Wait for an escaped defect, then find where it sat on the map. If it sat low, the map was wrong, not unlucky.
Re-rank after each escape and keep the earlier version, so the map's own history stays visible.
Measure: risks ranked per band, share of regression effort on the top band, escapes per band, and re-rankings forced by escapes.
Take a regression suite with at least a hundred cases and a run history you can actually read.
Record every case's outcome across many runs and find the ones that have never failed, ever.
Before deleting one, replay it against the commits that introduced past defects. A case that catches nothing on replay has earned deletion.
Add a case for every defect that reached production, written from the reproduction rather than from the fix.
Cut the suite until it fits inside the release window, then replay every previously escaped defect and confirm each is still caught.
Measure: suite run time before and after, cases retired and added, and escaped defects still caught on replay.
Take an application with a real interface and at least twenty journeys worth automating.
Build the fixture layers — session, per-suite, per-test — and create and destroy test data inside the run, never leaving rows behind.
Make the report readable by somebody who does not test: what failed, on what data, with the evidence attached.
Hand it to another developer with no explanation and watch them add a suite. Every question they ask is a defect in your framework.
Fix what they had to ask about, then repeat with a second person and see whether the questions changed.
Measure: suites added by other people, questions asked per newcomer, and time from clone to first passing test.
Take a web application with at least eight screens and write end-to-end tests for its main journeys.
Move every locator and every wait into page objects, so a test body contains user steps and nothing else.
Ban the brittle locators — positional XPath, generated class names — and the fixed sleeps, and write down what you banned and why.
Rewrite the front end's markup: rename classes, reorder the DOM, replace a component. Do not touch the tests.
Repair the whole suite inside the object layer alone. If you had to open a test file, the layer leaked.
Measure: files changed to repair the suite, test files touched (target zero), and suite pass rate after the rewrite.
Take an automated suite that already takes too long — twenty minutes or more on a single runner.
Wire it into CI as a required check on pull requests, so a red run blocks a merge rather than being ignored.
Shard it across parallel runners, splitting by measured duration rather than by file count.
Attach logs, a screenshot and a video to every failure. A red build nobody can diagnose without a rerun is worse than no build.
Break a test on purpose and diagnose it from the attached artefacts alone, without running anything locally.
Measure: wall-clock time on one runner and sharded, runner count, reruns needed per failure, and merges blocked by real failures.
Take a suite that runs often enough to have history — several hundred runs across a month at least.
Record every result per test, not just the run outcome, and compute a pass rate for each individual test.
Rerun each failure once automatically, and treat a pass on rerun as noise recorded, not as a green build to move past.
Quarantine the unstable ones out of the merge gate behind a written bar: a run of consecutive passes readmits, nothing else does.
Take the worst offender and find the real cause — a shared fixture, a clock, a race — rather than adding a wait and moving on.
Measure: flake rate per test, merge-gate red builds before and after quarantine, tests quarantined, and tests readmitted.
Take a feature with a written requirement list of at least twenty lines, and write one case per line.
Give every case preconditions, the exact data, the steps, and one expected result you could argue in front of a developer.
Write the data down as values, not descriptions. "A valid user" is where two testers stop agreeing.
Hand the pack to somebody who has never seen the feature and let them run it with no help from you at all.
Record every place they hesitated, guessed or asked, and rewrite those steps. Their questions are the defects.
Measure: cases written, questions asked per run-through, and verdicts that differed between the two testers.
Take a release with a numbered requirement list and a test pack somebody else already wrote.
Build the matrix: every requirement against the cases that exercise it, and against the run that passed or failed them.
Find the requirements with no case at all. Every project has some, and finding them before sign-off is the whole point.
Find the cases mapped to no requirement, and decide honestly whether they are extra coverage or dead weight.
Run the pack, fill in the results, and take the matrix to sign-off with the gaps shown rather than smoothed over.
Measure: requirements with no coverage, cases with no requirement, cases per requirement, and gaps still open at sign-off.
Take an assembled build with every component wired together and nothing stubbed, and load it with production-shaped data rather than ten tidy rows.
Write the end-to-end scenarios as the business would describe them, and fix their order before you start.
Execute in that order and attach evidence to each: screenshots, logs, and the database state afterwards.
Test the joins between components, not the components. A defect a unit test could have caught means you are testing at the wrong level.
Hold the build against the exit criteria when the date arrives, and record what you blocked or waived and who agreed.
Measure: scenarios executed and passed, defects found only at system level, and exit criteria met at the gate.
Take a feature ready for release and recruit at least five people who will actually use it, not colleagues who built it.
Write the scripts in the business's own vocabulary, with no product jargon and no field names lifted from the database.
Sit with each user while they run the script, and say nothing. The temptation to help is what destroys a UAT round.
Sort everything raised into defects, misunderstandings and change requests, and take the misunderstandings back to the documentation.
Close with a written sign-off listing the known open items by name, so nobody can claim later that they were hidden.
Measure: users run, items raised per user, the split between defect and misunderstanding, and open items at sign-off.
Take an application you did not build and write six charters, one area each, before you touch it.
Time-box each session to ninety minutes and keep notes as you go: what you tried, what you noticed, what you did not reach.
Do not investigate during a session. Note it and carry on — investigating mid-charter is how a session becomes an afternoon.
Debrief each session: what was covered, what was found, and what the charter should have said instead.
Turn every finding into a scripted case, so the same ground can be covered by anyone next cycle without you.
Measure: charters run, session time, findings per charter, and scripted cases produced from them.
Take ten real bug reports with vague steps — an open-source tracker has plenty — and work them one at a time.
Reproduce each on a clean build, with the version, configuration, data and settings written down as values.
Cut steps until it stops reproducing, then put the last one back. The shortest sequence is what a developer will actually run.
Hand each write-up to somebody else and have them reproduce it from the words alone. If they cannot, the write-up is not finished.
Keep the ones that never reproduced in a separate list with everything you tried, rather than closing them as invalid.
Measure: steps before and after reduction, write-ups reproduced by a second person first time, and reports left unreproducible.
Pin one build by its exact commit or artefact digest and one data set, and let neither move mid-cycle.
Order the cases so the highest-risk journeys run first, because the cycle will run out of time and something will be left.
Record pass, fail or blocked per case with evidence attached, treating blocked as its own outcome rather than folding it into fail.
When a defect is found, do not fix and re-run against a fresh build. Finish the cycle on the pinned one or the results mean nothing.
Report what was untested when time ran out, named case by case, and say how you chose what to drop.
Measure: cases executed, passed, failed and blocked, cases left unrun, and cycle wall-clock time.
Pull the real analytics for a site with traffic and rank browsers, versions, screen sizes and operating systems by actual usage.
Cut the matrix at a stated share of users — ninety-five per cent, say — and write down who you are choosing not to support.
Build from what people use, not from what hardware is on your desk. The desk matrix always over-tests the newest phone.
Run the core journeys across every cell, including at least one real low-end handset rather than only an emulator.
Capture each layout or behaviour difference with a screenshot and the console log, and separate cosmetic from blocking.
Measure: cells tested, share of users covered, differences found per cell, and how many of those were blocking.
Take a system with real interfaces — an API, a CLI, a message consumer — and drive it from outside through those, not from inside.
Record every input sequence the harness sends, with its data and its version, so any run can be replayed exactly.
Make a recorded failure re-runnable by one command. A repro you have to reconstruct by hand is not a repro.
Take a real reported bug and turn it into a failing harness run before anybody writes a line of the fix.
Fix it, watch that run go green, keep it in the suite, then revert the fix and confirm the run fails again.
Measure: recorded failures replayable, time from bug report to failing run, and regressions the harness caught coming back.
Take a system with at least a database and one external dependency, and write its whole environment down as a definition file.
Pin every version by digest — images, packages, the language runtime. "Latest" is how a suite starts failing on a Tuesday.
Seed the data from a script that runs on every start, so every run begins from identical state.
Destroy the environment while a suite is running, then rebuild it from the definition alone with no manual step.
Bring it up on a machine that has never seen the project and confirm the suite passes without anyone touching a console.
Measure: cold provision time, versions pinned, and suite results on the rebuilt environment against the original.
Take a running service and build a traffic profile from its real access logs — mixed endpoints, realistic think time, not a flat line.
Ramp until latency stops being linear, and record the concurrency where that happens.
Hold it there for several hours. The soak is what finds the leaks, the pool exhaustion and the full log disk, and everybody skips it.
Take a profile under load rather than after it, and name the bottleneck from that instead of from what you suspected.
Fix one thing, re-run the identical profile, and record it honestly if your first diagnosis turned out to be wrong.
Measure: the knee concurrency, p95 and p99 there, memory and connections across the soak, and throughput before and after the fix.
Take a system of at least three services with a real database and a message broker between them.
Run the dependencies as containers per suite rather than mocking them. The mocks agree with you, which is exactly the problem.
Seed data inside each test and tear it down after, so a failure means a defect and not a row left by the previous test.
Assert on what crosses the wire: serialised payloads, headers, retries, and what the consumer actually stored.
Break the contract deliberately — change a field type on the producer — and confirm the suite catches what the unit tests passed over.
Measure: suite run time, wiring and serialisation faults found, and the unit-test result on that same deliberate break.
Take an application with at least two environments and make the pipeline build exactly one artefact per commit.
Promote that same artefact by digest through staging into production. If anything rebuilds between environments, you tested a different thing.
Put a human approval gate in front of production, showing the digest and its test results at the gate.
Make the production deployer refuse any digest the pipeline did not produce and sign, so a laptop build cannot land.
Try to deploy a locally built image on purpose, confirm it is rejected, and read the audit record of the attempt.
Measure: artefacts built per release, promotions without rebuild, out-of-band deploys rejected, and time from merge to production.
Take a project whose build works on your machine and run it in a clean container. Whatever breaks is what you are about to pin.
Pin every dependency and the toolchain itself by version or digest, and commit the lock file.
Strip the non-determinism — timestamps, file ordering, build paths, embedded hostnames. This is the part everybody skips and it is why builds drift.
Build the same commit twice on different machines and compare the artefact digests byte for byte.
Check out a commit from six months ago, rebuild it, and confirm you get back the artefact that shipped then.
Measure: digest matches across machines, sources of non-determinism removed, and build time cold and cached.
Take a repository with real history and adopt a commit convention that carries the change type in the message.
Derive the next version from the commits since the last tag, with no human choosing the number.
Generate the changelog in the same run and sign the artefact, so a tag points at exactly one build nobody can swap.
Decide what happens to a breaking change committed as a patch — who catches it, who may override — and write that rule down.
Push a breaking change labelled as a patch on purpose, and confirm the pipeline stops or corrects it rather than shipping quietly.
Measure: releases cut without manual version entry, mislabelled commits caught, and tag-to-artefact matches on verification.
Stand up an artefact repository and push every build of a real service into it, addressed by digest rather than by a moving tag.
Make the store immutable: an existing digest can never be overwritten, and prove it by trying to push over one.
Promote between environments by reference — the same digest gains a staging then a production label, never a rebuild.
Write the retention policy and enforce it as a job, keeping every promoted release and expiring the rest.
Pull a release from months ago by digest and run it unchanged. If it needs a rebuild to work, the store is not doing its job.
Measure: artefacts stored and total size, overwrite attempts rejected, retention deletions, and the old release's run result.
Take a real support queue — an open-source project's issues will do — with enough traffic to see a week's shape.
Write the severity rubric first, in terms of customer impact: what is broken, for how many, and whether a workaround exists.
Triage against it daily, and route each ticket to the team that owns the component rather than to whoever answered last.
Keep the angry tickets and the calm ones on the same scale. Severity following tone is the failure everybody falls into.
Review the mis-routed and re-severitied tickets weekly, and change the rubric rather than blaming the person who triaged.
Measure: tickets triaged, mis-routes per week, severity changes after review, and rubric revisions made.
Collect at least twenty real log bundles from failures you have already diagnosed, with the answer known for each.
Write the script that finds the failure window in a bundle: the first error, the request id, and the surrounding minutes.
Turn each diagnosed failure into a signature — the pattern, what it means, and the fix or the next question.
Run the matcher over bundles it has never seen, and record what it got right, what it got wrong, and what it silently missed.
Plant the false positive deliberately: a benign line that resembles a known signature, then tighten until it stops firing.
Measure: signatures in the library, bundles matched correctly, false positives, and time to first diagnosis with and without it.
Take ten reported faults where the reporter's environment differs from yours — versions, operating system, configuration, data volume.
Rebuild each environment to match: the same version, the same configuration file, the same shape of data at the same scale.
Ask for the configuration before guessing at it. Most "cannot reproduce" outcomes are a setting nobody wrote down.
Reduce each reproduced fault to the smallest case a developer can run in a minute, and hand it over with the environment definition.
Separate product faults from configuration faults, and close each configuration one with a written fix and a documentation change.
Measure: faults reproduced, the split between product and configuration, steps in each reduced case, and time to reproduce.
Take a queue with real timestamps and agreed targets, or set targets per severity yourself and state them before measuring anything.
Compute first response and resolution time per ticket, per severity, and plot the distribution rather than the average.
Read the tail, not the mean. An average inside target hides the ten customers who waited three days.
Group the breaches by cause and find the repeat issue sitting behind the biggest cluster.
Remove that cause — write the knowledge-base article and change the default that produced it — then measure the same window again.
Measure: response and resolution percentiles by severity, breaches and their clustering, and ticket volume for the removed cause before and after.
Write the question set before any call: data volumes and growth, authentication, network egress, data residency, compliance, and who signs off.
Run discovery with a real team — a friend's company, a society, an internal team — and ask every question even where you think you know.
Write the answers down as answers rather than impressions, and send the record back to them for correction.
Sketch the design, then check it line by line against the record. The answer that kills your favourite design is the one you needed.
Where an answer is missing, go back and get it rather than assuming, and mark which parts of the design rest on an assumption.
Measure: questions asked and answered, answers that changed the design, and assumptions still unresolved at proposal.
Get one blocking technical objection in writing — "it cannot handle our file sizes", "it will not work behind our proxy" — before building anything.
Get their own sample data, anonymised if need be, rather than the tidy sample you would have chosen yourself.
Build only what tests that objection. A proof of concept that grows into a product is a proof of nothing.
Define pass and fail as numbers before the first commit, and agree them with the person who raised the objection.
Run it and record the result honestly, including the answer you would have given had it failed.
Measure: the threshold agreed beforehand, the result measured against it, data volume used, and build time.
Take two real systems that need to exchange data, and draw what crosses, in which direction, at what volume and how often.
Name the authentication method, the retry rule, the backfill path and the owner of every failure case, in writing.
Draw what happens when their side is unavailable for a day: where data queues, how long it survives, and who is told.
Wire the thin end end to end — one record, all the way through, with real credentials — before proposing anything.
Cut their side off for an hour with data flowing, then restore it and confirm the backfill closed the gap without duplicates.
Measure: records queued during the outage, backfill catch-up time, duplicates after recovery (target zero), and failure cases with a named owner.
Take a real questionnaire — SIG Lite or CAIQ are public — and answer it for a system you actually run.
For each control, link the configuration, policy document or screenshot that proves it, not a sentence saying yes.
Mark the gaps as gaps. An unbacked yes is the answer that ends a deal at the audit, and marking it honestly is the skill.
Have somebody else try to verify ten of your answers from the evidence alone, and fix the ones they could not.
Turn the recurring questions into an answer library with an owner and a review date on every entry.
Measure: controls answered, answers with evidence attached, gaps declared, and answers a reviewer could verify unaided.
Pick a real estate you can look at — a small charity, a society, a lab — and get written permission before you scan anything.
Build the inventory from the running systems: what is actually installed, running, exposed and out of support.
Interview the people who use it, and record every place where what they describe differs from what the inventory shows.
Rank the findings by business risk and cost to fix, using the organisation's view of cost rather than your own.
Verify the top five against the live systems before writing them down. A finding taken from documentation alone is a rumour.
Measure: assets inventoried, findings per risk band, documentation-versus-reality mismatches, and findings verified against live systems.
Take a real assessment's findings — your own from the previous project — and list every change worth making.
Draw the hard dependencies: what genuinely cannot start until something else finishes, and what only feels that way.
Cost each step in money and in staff time and give it a named owner, or it is a wish rather than a step.
Sequence by dependency and budget year rather than by what is most interesting to do first.
Put a decision point on each step, then run the halved-budget exercise: which items go, and what breaks when they do.
Measure: steps per year, cost per step, dependency depth, and items surviving the halved-budget cut.
Take a real choice with at least four candidates — a ticketing system, a backup product — for an organisation that genuinely needs one.
Agree the criteria and their weights with the client in writing before booking a single demo.
Score the long list from documentation, shortlist two or three, then run each on a trial with the client's own data.
Score the demo separately from the trial. A polished demo scoring instead of the trial is how the wrong vendor wins.
Write up why the loser lost, in enough detail that the decision survives being reopened in six months.
Measure: weighted scores from documentation and from the trial, the gap between them, and criteria whose weight changed on review.
Take a real buying decision and model five years, not one, across at least two options including doing nothing.
Include the lines people leave out: migration effort, training, internal staff time, exit cost, and the year-three price rise.
Put every assumption in its own cell with a source, so a finance director can change one number and watch the total move.
Run the sensitivity: shift each assumption by a quarter in turn and see which one moves the answer most.
Show it to somebody who will argue — a finance person, a sceptical engineer — and record which assumption they attacked.
Measure: five-year total per option, cost lines included, and the assumption with the largest effect on the total.
Take a real product or your own project and script the demo environment: schema, seed data, users and state, all from one command.
Get reset under a minute, so a broken run costs you nothing and you can rehearse twenty times.
Write the story as a sequence of what the customer cares about, not as a tour of screens.
Rehearse with the network throttled to a bad conference connection, then rehearse again with it cut off entirely.
Break it mid-demo on purpose — kill the API, empty the data — and practise the sentence you say next, because that is the real skill.
Measure: reset time, rehearsals run, steps that failed under throttling, and recovery time from a broken step.
Take a real public RFP — governments publish them — with at least fifty technical requirements, and answer it for a product you know.
Answer each as compliant, partial or not supported. No fourth category, and no prose hiding the verdict.
Back every compliant answer with a document reference or a working configuration you can show, not a claim.
Write the honest "not supported" answers with the workaround beside them. Winning on an unbacked yes costs more at delivery than losing did.
Have an engineer review every claim before submission, and record how many they downgraded.
Measure: requirements answered per verdict, claims with evidence attached, and claims downgraded at engineering review.
Start a log and record at least twenty real technical objections in the words the customer used, not in your paraphrase.
Beside each, record the evidence that answered it — a benchmark, a document, a configuration — or record that there was none.
Record whether the objection actually closed, which is a different question from whether you had an answer ready.
Group the recurring ones and take them to the people who build the thing, with the frequency attached rather than as an anecdote.
Take the objection you could not answer and get it answered properly, or get it written down as a known limitation.
Measure: objections logged, share with evidence attached, share that actually closed, and recurrence rate per theme.
Take a real workload and run it at a known volume — a thousand users, a million records — on hardware you can measure.
Measure throughput, storage growth per record and per day, and resource use as volume rises. Two points make a line; take four.
Check whether it scales linearly before assuming it does. Most sizing rules of thumb are a straight line drawn through one measurement.
Build the model so every line traces to a measured number, with the customer's own volumes as the inputs.
Double the input volume, run it for real at that volume, and say plainly where the model and the run diverge.
Measure: throughput and storage per unit at each tested volume, the model's prediction against the measured run, and the volume where it stops holding.
Take a real onboarding — a product, a tool rollout, a club's member intake — and write down every step as it currently happens.
Put an owner and a completion check on each step, so "done" is something observable rather than somebody's opinion.
Time each step across at least three successive customers, including the waiting, because that is where the time actually goes.
Find the step that consistently blocks the rest. It is usually a wait on somebody else, not a task anyone is doing.
Remove or parallelise it, run the next customer through, and record what broke because that step used to catch it.
Measure: end-to-end time per customer, time per step, and the blocking step's duration before and after.
Take a real dataset of at least a hundred thousand rows with a target schema that does not match the source.
Write the extract, transform and load as a script that runs again from scratch, not as a sequence of manual steps.
Reconcile row counts and per-column checksums on both sides, and reconcile the money columns to the penny separately.
Route the rows that will not map — bad dates, missing references, duplicates — into a rejects table rather than dropping them silently.
Run it, then run it again on the same source, and confirm you get the same result rather than double the rows.
Measure: rows extracted, loaded and rejected, checksum mismatches per column, and full run time.
Take a real switch-over — a database move, a hosting change — and write the runbook as timed steps with a clock beside each.
Set the freeze window and the go and no-go criteria as things you can check, and name who makes the call.
Rehearse the whole thing end to end on a copy and time it. The rehearsal always runs longer than the plan claims.
Execute the rollback during the rehearsal, all the way back. A rollback nobody has run is a paragraph, not a plan.
Correct the runbook from what the rehearsal found, then rehearse again and see whether the timings held.
Measure: rehearsed cutover duration against planned, rollback duration, and steps corrected between the two rehearsals.
Take a multi-tenant application and write one definition covering the database, configuration, single sign-on and seed data for a tenant.
Provision three tenants from it and diff them. Anything that differs and should not is a value you left outside the definition.
Include the awkward parts — the identity provider registration, the DNS entry, the first admin — instead of leaving them as a manual note.
Destroy a tenant completely and rebuild it from the definition, with no console, no clicking and no copy-paste.
List honestly what is still manual and why, rather than pretending the process is finished.
Measure: provision time per tenant, differences between tenants, manual steps remaining, and rebuild time from destroyed to working.
Take a real support or on-call queue and write the escalation tiers with a trigger for each, in numbers rather than in feelings.
Write the handover template: what is broken, the impact, everything already tried, and what the next person should not repeat.
Put the customer update on a fixed clock — every thirty minutes at the top tier — whether or not there is news.
Send the update with no news in it. The silence during an outage is what customers remember, and filling it is the whole discipline.
Run at least three real escalations through it, and close each with an agreed written statement of what changed.
Measure: time from trigger to escalation, updates sent against the clock, handovers where work was repeated, and time to agreed closure.
Take a failure that has now happened at least three times, so you are analysing a pattern rather than an incident.
Build the timeline from evidence — logs, deploys, configuration changes — before anybody in the room offers a theory.
Keep asking why past the first plausible answer. The first answer is the symptom, and stopping there is why the ticket comes back.
Write it twice: once for the customer in their terms, once for the owning team with the change or condition named.
Track the corrective action to done, then watch the same window afterwards to see whether the failure actually stopped.
Measure: recurrence rate before and after, time to root cause, corrective actions closed, and analyses later found to be wrong.
Get real usage data for a product with a decent user base — your own project's analytics will do — covering at least a month.
List what each account pays for and what each account has actually opened, and put the two side by side.
Trust the data over the call. The feature everyone says they love is often the one nobody has opened in six weeks.
Pick the biggest paid-for and unused feature and find out why by talking to five users who have never touched it.
Run one targeted enablement session, then read the same metric a fortnight later rather than asking whether it helped.
Measure: active users per feature, paid-for features with zero use, and usage of the targeted feature before and after.
Take at least fifty accounts whose outcome you already know — renewed, churned, downgraded — and hide the outcome from yourself.
Build the score from inputs you can genuinely get: support volume, usage trend, open escalations, days since last login.
Score each account as it stood three months before its outcome. Scoring with hindsight is the mistake that makes every model look brilliant.
Compare the scores with what actually happened, and find which inputs separated the two groups and which did not.
Drop the inputs that predicted nothing, re-score, and check whether the score improved or you merely overfitted fifty accounts.
Measure: accuracy against known outcomes, precision and recall on churn, inputs dropped, and lead time before the outcome.
Take a real API with at least fifteen endpoints and get its OpenAPI description generated from the code, not written by hand.
Generate the reference from that description, so signatures, types and required fields cannot drift from the implementation.
Write the parts a generator cannot: what each endpoint is for, when to use it, and what the error cases actually mean.
Extract every example from the docs and run it in CI against a live test instance, asserting the response rather than the exit code.
Rename a field in the code and confirm the documentation build goes red instead of quietly misleading a reader.
Measure: endpoints documented, examples executed in CI, and the build result on the deliberate rename.
Move a real documentation set into the code repository and delete the copy that lived anywhere else.
Put it through the same pull-request review as code, with a reviewer required rather than merely suggested.
Add link checking, anchors and external links included, and a style linter carrying rules the team agreed to first.
Agree the style rules before switching the linter on. A linter imposed without agreement gets disabled within a fortnight.
Break a link and violate a style rule on purpose, and confirm the build fails on each independently.
Measure: broken links found on the first run, violations per style rule, build failures caught, and docs shipped in the same release as their code.
Take a documentation site of at least forty pages and pull its search queries and page analytics.
List the tasks readers arrive with, from the searches and the support tickets, not from the product's own menu structure.
Run a card sort with fifteen or more participants, fixing the card set before recruiting anybody. Changing it mid-study makes the results meaningless.
Draft the new structure and tree-test it on those tasks with a fresh set of participants, before rebuilding a single page.
Rebuild, then redirect every old path — the links in other people's posts are the traffic you are about to break.
Measure: task success rate in the tree test, first-click accuracy per task, broken inbound paths, and searches returning nothing before and after.
Take the ten how-to topics with the most traffic and rewrite each as one task, splitting the ones that hide two.
Give each prerequisites, numbered steps, and a stated way for the reader to check the result themselves.
Watch five first-time readers work through them, one at a time, and say nothing. Helping destroys the only data you came for.
Note every place they stopped, re-read, guessed or went elsewhere, and treat each as a defect in your words.
Rewrite, run five fresh readers through the same topics, and follow the support tickets for those areas for a month.
Measure: completion rate and time per task, stopping points per topic, and ticket volume for those areas before and after.
Take a real API with a sign-up flow and instrument every step from account creation to the first successful call.
Define "first successful call" precisely and log it as one event, or you will be measuring three different things.
Watch the funnel long enough to have real numbers, and find the two steps where most people stop.
Sit with five newcomers going through it live. The funnel tells you where they left; only watching tells you why.
Fix the worst step in the SDK and the documentation rather than in a support reply, then read the funnel again a fortnight later.
Measure: conversion at each funnel step, median time to first successful call, and both again after the fix.
Build a sample application that does something real with an SDK, not a hello world with a spinner on it.
Make it run from a fresh clone with one command, credentials supplied by environment variable and nothing else to configure.
Add CI that installs it from scratch in a clean container and runs the happy path end to end.
Run it against the newest SDK release on a schedule, not only on your own commits. The sample breaks when the SDK moves, not when you type.
Publish a pre-release SDK with a breaking change and confirm CI catches it in the sample before any developer meets it.
Measure: clone-to-running time, CI runs against SDK releases, and breakages caught in the sample before release.
Write a quickstart that reaches a visible working result in under fifteen minutes, and time yourself doing it on a clean machine.
Extract the commands from the page itself, so the page and the tested script cannot drift apart.
Run them verbatim in CI on a clean container with nothing pre-installed. Your machine has years of setup the reader does not have.
Watch a genuine first-timer follow it live without helping, and note every question and every pause.
Rewrite each step they stopped at, then break a command on purpose and confirm CI goes red.
Measure: time to working result for the author and for first-timers, questions asked per run-through, and the CI result on the broken command.
Read every issue, forum thread and support message about an SDK across a real period — three months at least — and record each complaint verbatim.
Add what you saw in recorded onboarding sessions, because the complaints nobody bothers to file are the important ones.
Group them by theme and count them, so the argument to engineering arrives as a number rather than an anecdote.
Turn each recurring theme into an issue with a failing snippet attached that reproduces it in about ten lines.
Take them to the owning team, accept the rejections, and record the reason for each instead of quietly re-filing it.
Measure: complaints collected and grouped per theme, issues filed with a reproduction, and how many landed in a release.
Run four validator processes on one machine, each with its own disk, socket and signing identity.
Implement the propose, vote and commit rounds with a leader that rotates on a timeout.
Persist every vote before it goes on the wire, never after. Skip this and a restarted node votes twice at the same height.
Partition the validators three against one, then two against two, and record what each group commits.
Kill a node mid-round and restart it; assert it rejoins the same chain and never contradicts its own log.
Measure: rounds to recovery after each partition, committed height per group, and any height holding two distinct blocks.
Sync a full node from genesis on a public testnet whose history takes hours rather than minutes.
Run it unattended under a process manager that restarts it, with rotated logs and a disk alarm set before it fills.
Export sync height, peer count, block lag and disk growth to a dashboard, and write down what healthy looks like.
Kill it mid-sync with kill -9 rather than a clean shutdown, restart, and confirm the database is not corrupt.
Write the restore runbook, then wipe the data directory and rebuild from snapshot using only the runbook.
Measure: time to sync from genesis, time to restore from snapshot, and disk used at each height milestone.
Build a signing service holding the key in a separate process the application host cannot read.
Allocate nonces from one ledger table, reserved inside the same transaction that records the send.
Add rebroadcast so a stuck transaction is resent at a replacement fee on the same nonce, never a fresh one.
Fire fifty concurrent sends from one account and assert every nonce is used exactly once, with no gaps.
Kill the signer mid-send and restart it; confirm no nonce is burned and nothing is signed twice.
Measure: nonce gaps and duplicates under concurrency (both must be zero), and time to clear a stuck transaction.
Index balances and transfers into Postgres over at least 100,000 blocks of a public testnet.
Write the resumable cursor in the same transaction as the rows its batch produced, not afterwards.
Store the block hash beside every row, so a rewrite can find exactly what an orphaned block wrote.
Force a reorganisation on a local chain, unwind the indexer's own writes and re-apply the new branch.
Re-query every affected balance against the node's own state and assert they agree row for row.
Measure: reorg depth handled, rows unwound, time to reconverge, and balances that disagreed after replay.
Write a Solidity system that moves real value — an escrow or auction of at least three contracts calling each other.
Apply checks-effects-interactions in every function that sends value, and make payments pull rather than push.
Cover it in Foundry including the revert cases, not only the paths where everything goes right.
Deploy to a public testnet and verify the source, so a stranger can trace the deployed bytecode to its origin.
Have somebody else call it from a wallet with no instructions from you, and fix whatever they could not work out.
Measure: deployment gas, functions covered, revert cases asserted, and the calls a stranger failed to complete.
Take a working contract of your own and commit a gas snapshot per function before changing anything.
Repack storage into fewer slots, take arrays from calldata rather than memory, and cache repeated storage reads.
Re-snapshot after every single change, not at the end. Batched changes hide the one that made things worse.
Find one optimisation that costs readability for a trivial saving, revert it, and write the reasoning into the file.
Re-run the full test suite after each change and confirm behaviour is identical, not merely cheaper.
Measure: gas per function before and after, storage slots saved, and deployment cost in both versions.
Write down four properties that must always hold — total supply equals the sum of balances, and three more.
Build a Foundry invariant handler that calls your contracts in random order with random, bounded arguments.
Bound the handler carefully. A fuzzer that can never reach a valid state proves nothing and passes every time.
Run it until an invariant breaks, then shrink the failing sequence to the shortest calls that still break it.
Keep the shrunken sequence as a named regression test and fix the contract rather than weakening the invariant.
Measure: runs and depth per campaign, invariants asserted, sequences that broke one, and shrunken length.
Write a deliberately vulnerable withdraw function and an attacker contract whose fallback calls back into it.
Run the attack and drain the contract. Do not move on until the balance is actually gone.
Keep the exploit in the suite as a case that must revert from now on, rather than deleting it once fixed.
Fix it with checks-effects-interactions first, re-run the exploit, and only then add a reentrancy guard.
Write a second attack the guard does not stop — cross-function or read-only reentrancy — and show it working.
Measure: funds drained before the fix, exploit tests retained, and the attacks the guard alone still permits.
Build one scene with a real task — sort ten objects into labelled bins — on a headset you can put on people.
Implement grab, ray and poke affordances, each with audio and haptic confirmation the moment it takes effect.
Fix the task and the success criterion before recruiting anybody, then run five people who have never worn a headset.
Watch without helping. The urge to explain destroys the study, and the failures are the entire point of it.
Change the affordances people missed, and change nothing by adding an instruction panel.
Measure: task completion per participant, time to first successful grab, and failures per affordance before and after.
Take a scene heavy enough to miss the headset's refresh rate — real geometry and real materials, not test cubes.
Capture CPU and GPU frame time on the device before touching anything; the editor's numbers are not the device's.
Batch draw calls, bake the static lighting and cut overdraw, recapturing frame time after each change on its own.
Count reprojected frames on the device. Reprojection hides dropped frames and makes a failing scene feel acceptable.
Load the scene until it drops frames again on purpose, and name whether CPU or GPU gave out first.
Measure: CPU and GPU frame time per change, draw calls, overdraw, and reprojected frames per thousand.
Build a scene where a tracked hand drives something precise — a slider the user must land on an exact value.
Predict poses forward to the display deadline rather than rendering the last sample you were handed.
Decide what happens the instant a hand leaves the tracking volume before writing the happy path. Most applications just freeze.
Measure motion-to-photon with a high-frame-rate camera filming hand and screen together, not with an in-app timer.
Walk the hand out of the tracking volume mid-gesture and confirm the fallback fires instead of a jump or a freeze.
Measure: motion-to-photon latency, prediction horizon used, and tracking losses per minute of continuous use.
Mark three fixed positions on a real floor with tape and place virtual content on each through a persistent anchor.
Save the anchors, quit the application fully, restart it and reload them into the same physical room.
Measure drift with a tape measure against the floor marks. Eyeballing it is why people claim anchors work when they do not.
Relight the room — curtains open, lamps off, a different time of day — and relocalise from the same saved anchors.
Rearrange the furniture until relocalisation fails, and confirm the application says so rather than placing content wrongly.
Measure: drift in centimetres per anchor per session, relocalisation time, and failures across ten restarts.
Build a planner for a six-joint arm in simulation, checking collisions against an occupancy map rather than a fixed obstacle list.
Build the benchmark first: twenty cluttered scenes with start and goal states, saved and version-controlled.
Fixing the scene set before tuning is the part everybody skips; without it every improvement is chosen after the fact.
Run two planners over the identical set and record success rate, planning time and path length per scene.
Tighten the clutter until success rate collapses, and name the scene geometry that breaks each planner.
Measure: success rate, median and worst planning time, path length, and the clearance at which each planner fails.
Take a real arm you can command — a hobby six-axis is enough — and measure each link's mass and length yourself.
Write the URDF from those measurements, with joint limits from the datasheet and inertias from the geometry.
Solve inverse kinematics with joint limits enforced and singularities handled explicitly, not left for the solver to trip over.
Command twenty poses and measure where the tool actually landed with a dial gauge, pose by pose.
Drive the arm through a singularity on purpose and record what the solver and the joints do.
Measure: position error per pose in millimetres, worst-case error, and how much of it geometry, mass or calibration explained.
Drive a wheeled robot over a measured twenty-metre track with marked waypoints, logging odometry, inertial and camera together.
Fuse them into one pose estimate, recording the raw error of each sensor alone before fusing anything.
Set the covariances from each sensor's measured noise rather than the defaults. Guessing them is why filters diverge.
Drop each sensor in turn mid-run — cover the camera, unplug an encoder — and record what the estimate does.
Drive the same track on a slippery surface so odometry lies, and show which sensor the filter leans on instead.
Measure: position error against ground truth per run, error with each sensor dropped, and time to reconverge.
Close a position loop on one real actuator at a fixed rate, with the loop period measured rather than assumed.
Record a step response using the gains taken straight from simulation, and keep that plot.
Add anti-windup and output bounds before tuning anything. A loop that winds up makes every tuning result meaningless.
Tune on the hardware one gain at a time, recording a step response after each change.
Load the actuator until it saturates, hold it there, then release, and show the loop recovering without a lurch.
Measure: rise time, overshoot, settling time and steady-state error before and after, plus loop period jitter.
Build circuits with known exact answers — a Bell state and a small Grover instance — on a free cloud device.
Run them on the ideal simulator first and write down the exact distribution you expect before submitting anything.
Run the same circuits on hardware with at least 8,192 shots, and again on a different day to see the drift.
Build a noise model from the device's reported gate and readout errors, simulate through it, and compare all three.
Deepen the circuit until the hardware distribution becomes indistinguishable from uniform, and record that depth.
Measure: total variation distance from ideal for hardware and for noisy simulation, shots used, and the depth signal disappears at.
Run standard randomised benchmarking on one qubit pair of a public device, with at least thirty random sequences per length.
Sweep sequence length far enough that the survival curve actually decays, rather than fitting three points.
Take confidence intervals from repeated runs on different days, not from one session's fit error. One session is a snapshot.
Run interleaved benchmarking for the two-qubit gate specifically and compare it against the reference number.
Rerun immediately after a device recalibration and record how far the same number moves.
Measure: error per Clifford single- and two-qubit, interval width, and the spread across calibration cycles.
Pick an observable whose exact value you can compute, on a circuit small enough to simulate by hand.
Measure it unmitigated on hardware and record the error against the exact value with its shot noise.
Calibrate the readout confusion matrix and apply measurement-error correction, then re-measure the same observable.
Add zero-noise extrapolation by stretching the gates, and record the extra shots each mitigation cost.
Find a circuit where mitigation moves the answer further from the exact one, and keep that case in the write-up.
Measure: absolute error mitigated and unmitigated, shots per estimate for each, and the cases mitigation made worse.
Run relaxation, Ramsey and echo experiments across at least five qubits of one public device.
Fit T1, T2 star and T2 echo per qubit, with the delay sweep long enough to see each curve flatten.
Repeat the whole set across three separate calibration cycles. One session's numbers are a snapshot, not a characterisation.
Work out the deepest circuit each qubit supports from its coherence time and the device's gate duration.
Run a circuit at that depth and one at twice it, and show where the result stops carrying information.
Measure: T1, T2 star and T2 echo per qubit per cycle, their spread, and the circuit depth each implies.
Simulate at least a million reads from a reference genome, so every read's true position is known.
Simulate with a realistic error and indel profile. Perfect reads make every aligner look equally good.
Align with two aligners under matched settings and record mapping rate, mismatch profile and mapping quality.
Score each read as correctly placed or not against its known origin, split by repeat content.
Raise the error rate and shorten the reads until both aligners fall over, and record which one goes first.
Measure: mapping rate, correctly placed fraction overall and inside repeats, and run time per million reads.
Take a public benchmark sample with a published truth set and confident-region file — GIAB provides both.
Build the workflow from alignment through duplicate marking to calling, with every tool version pinned.
Score inside the confident regions only. Scoring outside them is how people report precision they have not earned.
Report precision and recall separately for substitutions and indels, broken down by depth bin.
Downsample to a quarter of the depth and rescore, so the depth dependence is shown rather than claimed.
Measure: precision and recall per variant class per depth bin, and the filter that moved each of them most.
Write a Nextflow pipeline of at least five processes over a real dataset, each tool pinned inside its own container.
Declare every input and output explicitly, so the resume cache can tell a changed step from an unchanged one.
Kill the run mid-process by cutting the machine rather than stopping cleanly, then resume and confirm it restarts at the right step.
Run the whole pipeline on a second machine and checksum every output file against the first run.
Chase the outputs that do not match — timestamps, thread counts, unseeded randomness — and pin them out.
Measure: wall time cold and resumed, outputs matching by checksum across machines, and the ones you could not make match.
Take an assembled bacterial or small eukaryotic genome that already has a curated reference annotation.
Predict genes with a trained caller and assign function by homology search, keeping the evidence behind each call.
Compare at exact-boundary level, not only gene level. Gene-level agreement alone flatters an annotation badly.
Split the disagreements into missed genes, spurious calls and boundary shifts, and count each category.
Break the assembly into shorter contigs on purpose, re-annotate, and show which calls fragmentation destroys.
Measure: genes called, exact-boundary agreement, missed and spurious counts, and short-gene recall specifically.
Take at least thirty de-identified discharge summaries with a reference code set you keep sealed until afterwards.
Code every one for ICD-10-CM and CPT from the record and the guidelines alone, without opening the key.
Record sequencing as well as codes. Principal diagnosis order is where most of the real disagreements live.
Open the key and score per case, separating misses from extras from wrong sequencing.
For each disagreement, name the guideline or coding clinic that settles it, and mark the ones nothing settles.
Measure: exact agreement per case, agreement by code category, sequencing errors, and disagreements with no clear rule.
Define every data element in writing — source field, allowed values, what counts as missing — before opening a chart.
Build the abstraction form so each element can only be entered as defined, never as free text.
Have a second abstractor do twenty of the same charts blind to your entries. Skipping this is skipping the project.
Compute agreement element by element rather than as one overall figure, and list the ones that fell short.
Rewrite the definitions the disagreements exposed, then re-abstract a fresh sample under the new wording.
Measure: agreement per element before and after the rewrite, charts double-abstracted, and time per chart.
Write the procedure: authorisation validity checklist, minimum-necessary rule per request type, and a turnaround clock.
Build a request log recording what was asked, what was released, and the authorisation each release rests on.
Write fifteen deliberately defective requests — expired, unsigned, over-broad, wrong patient — mixed with a few valid ones.
Run the whole batch through the procedure blind and confirm every defective one is refused with a stated reason.
Include a valid request asking for more than the minimum necessary, and show what your procedure releases instead.
Measure: defective requests correctly refused, valid ones released in full, turnaround per request, and the judgement calls.
Define what makes a chart deficient — missing signature, missing report, undictated summary — with a due day for each.
Build the workflow over at least a hundred simulated charts, so the queue behaves like a backlog rather than a demo.
Route each deficiency to the responsible clinician by name, with an escalation after a stated number of days.
Track the delinquency rate week by week against the standard and chart it, rather than reporting one figure.
Change one thing in the routing, run four more weeks, and show whether the rate moved or the backlog merely shifted.
Measure: delinquency rate weekly, days to close per deficiency type, and the deficiencies no reminder ever cleared.
Capture a schematic for a real board: a microcontroller, a switching regulator and one high-speed peripheral at minimum.
Name every net, place decoupling per device pin as each datasheet asks, and draw the power and reset tree on its own sheet.
Read every datasheet's power sequencing section before routing. This is where boards that never boot come from.
Run the electrical rules check and clear every warning, including the ones you are tempted to suppress.
Get a review from somebody who has actually built a board, and close each finding in the file rather than in a reply.
Measure: ERC warnings raised and closed, review findings by type, and pins left without decoupling.
Lay out the schematic on four layers, with the stack-up and impedance targets written down before routing starts.
Keep a continuous reference plane under every fast net and check each one for a plane split it crosses.
Trace the return current of your fastest net across the whole route by eye. The gap under a split is what bites later.
Length-match the differential pairs and the parallel bus, and run design rules against the fabricator's real rule set.
Submit for manufacturability review, fix every query, then order the board and confirm it arrives without a question.
Measure: DRC and DFM violations per pass, plane splits crossed, matched-pair skew, and fabricator queries raised.
Take one high-speed interface on a board you designed and build its channel model from the real stack-up and IBIS files.
Simulate the eye at the receiver before fabrication and record the predicted opening and jitter.
Decide how you will probe before the board arrives. A long ground lead is why measurement and simulation never agree.
Probe the built board at the same point with a proper ground spring and capture the measured eye.
Degrade the channel on purpose — remove termination, extend the trace with a flying lead — and show both eyes closing.
Measure: predicted and measured eye height and width, jitter, and the difference the probe itself contributed.
Write the bring-up plan before power is applied: rails, then clocks, then reset, then each bus in order.
Bring the rails up on a current-limited supply and measure each one before enabling the next stage.
Check current draw against your own estimate at every step. A board drawing twice what you predicted is telling you something.
Scope the clocks and the reset release, then bring up each bus and confirm one known device answers on it.
Take the first fault you hit and trace it back to the schematic or the layout, writing the fix into the file.
Measure: current per rail at each stage, clock frequency and jitter, reset timing, and the stage each fault appeared at.
Pick a real load-bearing part and write down loads, constraints and material properties before opening the solver.
Model a cantilever or thick cylinder with a closed-form answer first, and match it within a stated tolerance.
Match the textbook case before trusting the real one. Everybody skips this and then defends a number nothing has checked.
Model the real geometry, stating every simplification — fillets removed, bolts as constraints — as a line in the write-up.
Change one boundary condition to something equally defensible and show how far the peak stress moves.
Measure: peak stress and deflection, error against the closed-form case, and the spread across boundary-condition choices.
Take one model and one quantity of interest — peak stress, drag, outlet temperature — chosen and written down first.
Build at least four meshes at increasing density, recording skewness and aspect ratio distributions for each.
Refine where the gradients are, not everywhere. A uniformly fine mesh burns hours and still misses the boundary layer.
Solve the identical case on every mesh and plot the quantity of interest against cell count.
Coarsen deliberately until the answer moves by more than your tolerance, and record the cell count where that happens.
Measure: cells per mesh, worst skewness and aspect ratio, the quantity of interest per mesh, and solve time.
Take a case that runs and monitor residuals, domain imbalances and one physical quantity at a point, all three together.
Write the convergence criterion down before running: residual levels, imbalance percentage and a settled monitor point.
Watch the imbalance, not only the residuals. Residuals fall on a wrong answer just as happily as on a right one.
Force divergence on purpose — bad initialisation, too large a time step, aggressive relaxation — and record how it fails.
Recover the same case by changing relaxation and time step only, and note which change actually did the work.
Measure: iterations to criterion, residual levels reached, domain imbalance percentage, and the monitor point's remaining drift.
Choose a published experiment with readable data — a backward-facing step or a pipe bend with measured profiles.
Build the same geometry and conditions, and pick the turbulence model with the reason written into the case notes.
Check resolved y-plus against what your wall treatment requires and remesh if it does not match. This is the usual silent error.
Solve and compare against the published profiles station by station, not against a single headline number.
Rerun with a second turbulence model, unchanged in every other respect, and show how far the answer moves.
Measure: y-plus range, profile error against the experiment per station, and the spread between turbulence models.
Take one small module — a limit checker or a mode selector — and write its high- and low-level requirements first.
Write the test cases from the requirements alone, without reading the implementation. Doing it the other way is the whole failure mode.
Hold a review of requirements, code and tests, recording each finding with its disposition rather than fixing it silently.
Run the tests with structural coverage to MC/DC and list every branch the requirements-based tests never reached.
For each uncovered branch decide: missing requirement, dead code or deactivated code, and write the justification.
Measure: requirements, test cases, MC/DC from requirements-based tests alone, and uncovered branches by category.
Write a control loop against a simulated plant with real dynamics — an attitude or altitude hold, not a step function.
Allocate everything at start-up, run at a fixed rate, and bound every loop and buffer at compile time.
Define the safe state before the control law. Deciding what safe means after the code exists never produces a real answer.
Inject sensor faults one at a time — stuck value, out of range, slow drift, dropout — and confirm each is detected.
Inject the plausible-but-wrong reading last, since it is the one range checks miss, and show what catches it.
Measure: loop jitter, worst-case stack use, faults injected against faults detected, and time to enter the safe state.
Give every requirement an identifier and carry it in code comments and test names, across at least fifty requirements.
Write the tool that reads all three sources and generates the matrix, rather than maintaining one by hand.
Trace in both directions. A one-way matrix hides the tests that prove nothing anybody asked for.
Wire it into CI so an untraced requirement or an orphan test fails the build.
Delete one requirement's test and rename another's identifier, and confirm the build goes red for both reasons.
Measure: requirements traced both ways, orphan tests found, derived requirements with no parent, and CI failures raised.
Build a task set of at least five periodic tasks on a real board, each with a stated period and deadline.
Assign priorities by deadline rather than importance, and write the rate-monotonic analysis down before measuring anything.
Measure response times on the target with a pin and a scope under a loaded bus, not with a printf on an idle board.
Construct a priority inversion with a shared mutex and a low-priority task, and show the high-priority task missing its deadline.
Enable priority inheritance, rerun the identical scenario, then raise the load until something misses again.
Measure: worst-case response per task, deadline misses, inversion duration before and after, and CPU utilisation.
Build one Classic AUTOSAR software component with its interfaces defined in ARXML before any C is written.
Generate the RTE and reach every port through it, keeping all hardware access inside the abstraction layer.
Do not reach past the RTE just this once. That one call is what makes the driver swap impossible later.
Run the component on a target or virtual ECU and confirm it works against a real driver.
Swap the underlying driver for a different implementation and show the application code compiling and running unchanged.
Measure: files changed by the swap (application files must be zero), RTE-mediated calls, and direct hardware calls found.
Write ECU application software on a fixed cycle schedule, with real work in the 1ms, 10ms and 100ms tasks.
Add a windowed watchdog and define the safe state the ECU enters when a cycle is missed.
Measure execution time with a pin toggle, not a timer read inside the task. The instrumentation cost is the trap here.
Load the 10ms task until it overruns, and show the safe state being entered rather than the schedule quietly sliding.
Starve the watchdog on purpose and confirm the reset happens where and when you expected it.
Measure: task jitter and worst-case execution time per cycle, CPU load, overruns, and time to safe state.
Build a CAN stack on two real nodes with a DBC file defining every message and signal on the bus.
Generate the packing and unpacking code from the DBC rather than writing bit offsets by hand.
Expose the transmit, receive and bus-off counters to diagnostics. Nobody does this until an outage forces them to.
Fault the bus — short CAN-high to ground, remove the terminator — and record the counters climbing into bus-off.
Flood the bus from a higher-priority node and record which of your messages lose arbitration and by how much.
Measure: bus load percentage, error counters through the fault, time to recover from bus-off, and messages lost under flood.
Take one vehicle function and run a hazard analysis, arguing severity, exposure and controllability for each hazard.
Derive the safety goals, pick one, and design a single safety mechanism that addresses it.
Write the fault list your mechanism claims to detect before implementing it, or the coverage figure afterwards means nothing.
Implement the mechanism and inject every fault on that list, recording detected, undetected and detected too late.
Inject three faults deliberately outside the list and record what the mechanism does with them.
Measure: hazards and ASIL per hazard, faults injected against faults detected, detection latency, and diagnostic coverage claimed.
Draw the state machine on paper first — authorised, captured, partly captured, voided, refunded, expired — with every legal edge.
Build it in Postgres with the legal transitions held by a constraint or trigger rather than by application code.
Enforce it in the database. Application-level state machines get bypassed by the first background job somebody writes.
Write a test reaching every terminal state, and one attempting every illegal transition and asserting the database refuses it.
Fire a capture after the authorisation has expired, and a refund exceeding the capture, and show both rejected.
Measure: states and legal transitions, terminal states covered by tests, and illegal transitions attempted against refused.
Generate a month of captures across several merchants, with timestamps landing either side of a stated daily cut-off.
Build the run that batches a day's captures into one payout file per merchant, with the cut-off explicit in the query.
Read by transaction time, never by now. A run that depends on when it executes can never be replayed.
Replay any past day and diff the payout file against the original, byte for byte.
Corrupt one day's first run on purpose, replay it, and show the correct file produced without paying a merchant twice.
Measure: payout totals per day, replay diffs against the original, transactions within a second of cut-off, and run time.
Stand up a simulated issuer you control that can approve, decline, partly approve, delay and silently drop a request.
Build the client with a timeout shorter than the issuer's, and treat partial approval as a first-class outcome.
Send a reversal for every request whose response never arrived. Everyone leaves this out and it holds real money.
Drop one response in ten at the simulator and run a thousand authorisations through.
Assert the simulator holds no authorisation your client does not know about, and none your client believes it reversed.
Measure: authorisations sent, responses lost, reversals fired, orphaned authorisations at the issuer (must be zero), and timeout spread.
Load a public sanctions list and build fuzzy name matching over it, handling transliteration, name order and initials.
Build the labelled set first: two hundred pairs of known matches and deliberate near-misses that must not match.
Labelling before tuning is the whole project. Tune first and you will pick the threshold that flatters the demo.
Sweep the threshold across the labelled set and record precision and recall at each point.
Write every alert to a case record an analyst can decide, reopen and audit, then reopen a decided case and check the trail.
Measure: precision and recall per threshold, alerts per thousand onboardings, and the alert rate one analyst could clear.
Put a FHIR R4 facade over a store of synthetic patients — Synthea will give you several hundred.
Validate every resource against its published profile on write, and refuse the write when validation fails.
Support the standard search parameters, not a bespoke query shape. Custom search is what makes a facade useless to a partner.
Run a public conformance suite against it and fix every failure or record it as a stated deviation with its reason.
Post a resource that satisfies the profile but is clinically nonsense, and decide and document what your facade does.
Measure: resources validating, conformance tests passing, deviations recorded, and search parameters supported against the profile's list.
Build a synthetic patient store — never real records — with identifying fields encrypted individually rather than as one blob.
Decide access per record and per role, evaluated in one place that every read must pass through.
Log the refusals as well as the grants. A log that records only successes cannot show you an insider probing.
Add break-glass: access is granted, a review case is filed automatically, and the user is told that it was.
Attempt reads that must be refused, use break-glass once, and confirm both appear in the log with actor and reason.
Measure: reads refused against reads attempted, break-glass uses, log completeness, and encryption overhead per read.
Build a SMART on FHIR application that launches in patient context from a public EHR sandbox, not as a standalone page.
Pick one decision a clinician actually makes and put only what that decision needs on the screen.
Time the task with three clinicians or stand-ins before your application exists. Without the before, the after is only an opinion.
Run the same task through your application with the same people, recording where they stopped, hesitated or clicked away.
Remove what the walkthrough showed nobody read, then rerun the timing with the reduced screen.
Measure: task time before and after, clicks per task, participants run, and elements removed after watching.
Model consent as grants carrying scope, purpose and expiry, so one patient can hold several with different limits.
Check every read against the grants at one enforcement point, refusing when no grant covers the stated purpose.
Require the purpose on every request. A read that does not say why it is reading cannot be checked against consent at all.
Withdraw a grant mid-session and confirm the very next request is refused, not the next login.
Expire a grant by clock, attempt the same read, then produce the trail showing which grant permitted an earlier release.
Measure: reads refused by reason, time from withdrawal to first refusal, expired grants honoured, and releases traceable to a grant.
Build one trigger per object across two related objects, delegating everything to handler classes.
Remove every query and DML statement from inside a loop, and add a recursion guard that survives a second update.
Test with 200-record batches from the start. Single-record tests pass on code that dies the moment a data loader runs.
Add a second automation — a flow or another trigger — updating the same records, and confirm your guard holds.
Load ten thousand records through the data loader and confirm no limit exception and no partially applied batch.
Measure: SOQL queries and DML statements per transaction against the limit, CPU time, and records loaded without failure.
Build a component backed by a wire adapter over real records, deployed from a scratch org through the CLI.
Implement loading, empty and error as real branches, each with markup you can point at.
Build the error state first. Written last, it always ends up a blank box or a silent failure nobody notices.
Walk the component by keyboard alone and then with a screen reader, fixing whatever cannot be reached or named.
Force the wire adapter to fail and then to return nothing, and confirm the right state appears each time.
Measure: Jest tests per state, states rendered under forced failure, keyboard-reachable controls, and missing screen-reader labels.
Load an org to a realistic record count — at least a million rows on the object your reports read.
Read the query plan for every reporting query before changing anything, recording cost and rows scanned.
Read the plan rather than the run time. A query that is fast on sandbox data tells you nothing about production.
Filter on indexed fields, remove leading wildcards, and split the queries whose filters can never be selective.
Push one query past the selectivity threshold on purpose and record the error the platform returns.
Measure: plan cost and rows scanned per query before and after, and the queries left non-selective.
Run a full data-loader batch through your existing automation and record queries, DML rows and CPU time per transaction.
Instrument with the Limits methods and log consumption, rather than waiting for an exception to tell you.
Find which limit you hit first. Most people assume SOQL and it is usually CPU time or DML rows.
Move the work that does not fit into Queueable or Batch Apex, writing down why each piece went where it did.
Rerun the identical batch, then double it until something fails again, and record which limit gave way.
Measure: queries, DML rows and CPU time per transaction against each limit before and after, and the batch size that still fails.
Get a sandbox S/4HANA system and configure one process end to end — order to cash or procure to pay, all the way through.
Set up the organisational structure and chart of accounts first, writing down every value you chose and why.
Write the configuration document as you go, with the transaction path per setting. Reconstructing it afterwards is where it goes wrong.
Write a test script a stranger can execute: data to use, steps to take, and the exact result expected at each one.
Hand it to somebody else and let them run it without answering questions, recording every point they got stuck.
Measure: settings documented with their paths, test script steps, steps the second person could not complete, and questions asked.
Model the as-is process from the documents alone first, with every step, decision point, exception and owner named.
Walk it through with at least four people who actually do the work, one at a time rather than in a room together.
Ask what they do when it goes wrong. The exception path is where the real process lives and no document holds it.
Redraw the as-is wherever their account differed from the written one, and mark each difference you found.
Draw the to-be at the same level of detail and take it back to the same people for a second pass.
Measure: steps and exceptions in each model, differences found per interview, and exceptions nobody had documented.
Take at least forty requirements from a real process and mark each fit, gap or partial against the standard process.
Demonstrate the standard process in the system for every requirement you call a fit, rather than trusting the documentation.
Test the fits. Half the gaps in any register are settings nobody looked for, and half the fits do not actually exist.
Give every gap three resolutions — standard configuration, process change, development — with the effort of each.
State the consequence of each option, including what the business loses by changing its process rather than the system.
Measure: requirements by category, fits confirmed in the system, gaps closed by configuration, and effort per resolution path.
Build a migration template for one master data object over at least two thousand records from a real extract.
Write the validation rules — mandatory fields, formats, check-table values, duplicates — and run them before any upload.
Dry-run first and read the rejects report line by line. A success count is not evidence that anything correct was loaded.
Correct and repeat until nothing is rejected, keeping each round's rejects report as the record of the data's condition.
Load a batch you know is bad on purpose and confirm the template refuses it rather than partly loading it.
Measure: records per round, rejects by rule, rounds to a clean load, and records checked by hand in the system afterwards.
